text: # Achilles Tendinitis ## Overview Achilles tendinitis is a common condition marked by irritation and swelling of the large tendon that runs down the back of the lower leg. The Achilles tendon is the largest tendon in the body, connecting the calf muscles to the heel bone (calcaneus). This tendon makes walking, running, climbing stairs, jumping, and standing on tiptoe possible. Despite its ability to withstand large forces during athletic activity, the Achilles tendon commonly develops tendinitis due to overuse. ## Description Tendinitis refers to acute inflammation of a tendon, a normal response of the body to injury, typically showing up as swelling, pain, or irritation. The term "tendinopathy" describes a condition where a tendon has undergone microscopic breakdown from prolonged, cumulative damage. The terms tendinitis, tendinosis, and tendinopathy essentially describe similar underlying processes.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The term "tendinopathy" describes a condition where a tendon has undergone microscopic breakdown from prolonged, cumulative damage. The terms tendinitis, tendinosis, and tendinopathy essentially describe similar underlying processes. Achilles tendinitis is different from an Achilles rupture, in which the tendon tears away from the heel bone or splits lengthwise. Ruptures typically result from a sudden injury. This article focuses on tendinitis rather than rupture. ### Two Types **Noninsertional.** This type affects the middle portion of the tendon (above where it attaches to the heel). Fibers in this area gradually break down, developing microscopic tears that lead to swelling and thickening. Younger, physically active people, especially runners, are more commonly affected. **Insertional.** This type involves the lower part of the tendon, where it attaches to the heel bone. Damaged fibers may gradually calcify (harden).

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Younger, physically active people, especially runners, are more commonly affected. **Insertional.** This type involves the lower part of the tendon, where it attaches to the heel bone. Damaged fibers may gradually calcify (harden). Bone spurs frequently form at the back of the heel with the insertional type. While it occurs across all activity levels, runners are still the most commonly affected group. Tight calf muscles frequently contribute to insertional tendinitis by creating excess stress at the attachment site. ## Cause Achilles tendinitis is usually not linked to a specific injury. Instead, repeated stress on the tendon causes the condition, often from placing too much demand on the body without enough time to adapt. Contributing factors include: - **A sudden increase in activity.** Dramatically increasing running distance without allowing the body to adjust creates irritation and inflammation. - **Changes in footwear.** Switching shoes can increase strain on the Achilles tendon.

text: Contributing factors include: - **A sudden increase in activity.** Dramatically increasing running distance without allowing the body to adjust creates irritation and inflammation. - **Changes in footwear.** Switching shoes can increase strain on the Achilles tendon. - **Tight calf muscles.** Restricted calf muscles pass on more stress, particularly at the point where the tendon attaches to the heel. - **Haglund's deformity.** An abnormal bony enlargement at the back of the heel can irritate the tendon, causing inflammation and pain. ## Symptoms Common symptoms include: - Pain and stiffness along the Achilles tendon, especially in the morning - Pain in the tendon or back of the heel that worsens with activity - Severe pain the day after exercising - Thickening of the tendon - Bone spur formation (particularly with insertional cases) - Persistent swelling that gets worse throughout the day with activity - Heel pain aggravated by contact with the shoe

Severe noninsertional cases may show calcification within the middle part of the tendon.

text: ## Nonsurgical Treatment Most cases of Achilles tendinitis respond well to conservative treatment, though symptom improvement typically takes several months. Pain may persist beyond three months even with early treatment. **Rest.** Reducing or stopping activities that worsen pain is the foundation of treatment. Replacing high-impact exercise (like running) with low-impact alternatives reduces stress on the Achilles tendon. Cross-training options such as cycling, elliptical machines, and swimming allow continued activity while reducing strain. Doctors may recommend an ankle brace or boot to support this transition. **Ice.** Applying ice to the most painful area of the tendon is helpful and can be done repeatedly throughout the day. Sessions should last about 20 minutes at most, ending earlier if the skin becomes numb. A helpful trick is freezing water in a foam cup, then peeling back the rim to create a custom-shaped ice pack, as it can conform to the shape of the tendon with repeated use.

text: A helpful trick is freezing water in a foam cup, then peeling back the rim to create a custom-shaped ice pack, as it can conform to the shape of the tendon with repeated use. Extended use beyond one month should be discussed with a primary care physician. **Physical therapy.** Therapeutic exercise is particularly beneficial. Calf stretching involves leaning against a wall with one knee straight and heel on the ground, stepping the other leg forward with the knee bent, then pushing the hips toward the wall in a controlled way. Hold the stretch for 30 seconds and repeat 10 times per foot, aiming to feel it in the calf and heel cord without causing pain in the Achilles tendon itself. Eccentric strengthening is particularly beneficial for noninsertional cases. Eccentric contraction means the muscle tightens while it lengthens. These exercises should initially be done under the supervision of a physical therapist, since performing them incorrectly risks damaging the tendon. Some discomfort may occur but should not become unbearable:

These exercises should initially be done under the supervision of a physical therapist, since performing them incorrectly risks damaging the tendon. Some discomfort may occur but should not become unbearable: - **Bilateral heel drops.** Stand at the edge of a stair with only the front of the foot on the step, allowing the heels to move up and down. Keep balance and hold a rail for safety. Raise the heels, then slowly lower them as far down as possible. Repeat 20 times slowly and deliberately; moving too quickly risks injuring the tendon. Difficulty can be increased with hand-held weights as pain improves. - **Single-leg heel drops.** Similar to the bilateral technique, but with all the weight on one leg; this should only be attempted after the bilateral version has been mastered. Research shows they significantly weaken tendon integrity. **Platelet-rich plasma (PRP).** Other injectable substances, including PRP, have been studied for tendinitis. Several studies show pain improvement with PRP, but there isn't yet enough evidence to confirm its true effectiveness. **Night splinting.** A removable brace that holds the foot with the toes pointed upward during sleep can provide substantial morning pain relief upon waking. This position keeps the calf flexible and reduces tension on the Achilles tendon. **Supportive footwear and orthotics.** Insertional tendinitis often improves with specific shoes and orthotic devices. Softer shoes or those open at the heel reduce irritation of the tendon. Heel lifts are another option that decreases strain on the tendon. Severe pain may call for temporary use of a walking boot, allowing the tendon to rest before starting therapy.

text: Softer shoes or those open at the heel reduce irritation of the tendon. Heel lifts are another option that decreases strain on the tendon. Severe pain may call for temporary use of a walking boot, allowing the tendon to rest before starting therapy. Extended use of a boot risks weakening the calf muscle. **Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT).** This treatment applies low- or high-energy shockwaves to stimulate healing of damaged tendon tissue. High-energy versions can be completed in a single session, requiring local or general anesthesia. Low-energy versions are spread across three to four sessions and don't require anesthesia. Recent studies show improvements in pain and function, particularly when combined with eccentric exercises. More research is needed before it becomes a routine recommendation. ESWT has minimal risk and negligible complications, making it worth considering before surgery. ## Surgical Treatment Surgery is only considered when pain persists beyond six months despite conservative treatment.

text: More research is needed before it becomes a routine recommendation. ESWT has minimal risk and negligible complications, making it worth considering before surgery. ## Surgical Treatment Surgery is only considered when pain persists beyond six months despite conservative treatment. The specific surgical approach depends on the location and extent of the tendinitis. **Debridement.** This procedure involves removing ("cleaning up") damaged tissue. For insertional cases, removing the bone spur at the heel along with the damaged tendon tissue commonly produces good outcomes. After the unhealthy tissue is removed, the remaining tendon is reattached to the heel bone using metal or plastic anchors and strong sutures. After debridement, most patients can walk within two weeks using a removable boot or cast, though the timeline varies with the severity of the tendon damage. When more than half of the Achilles tendon needs to be removed, the remaining segments are not strong enough on their own. A tendon transfer becomes necessary to restore the ability to push off the ground.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: When more than half of the Achilles tendon needs to be removed, the remaining segments are not strong enough on their own. A tendon transfer becomes necessary to restore the ability to push off the ground. The flexor hallucis longus tendon (which controls downward flexion of the big toe) is the most common option for a transfer. Movement of the big toe remains intact afterward. **Gastrocnemius recession.** This surgery lengthens the calf muscle. Because tightness in the calf increases stress on the Achilles tendon, this procedure benefits patients who continue to have limited ankle flexibility despite consistent stretching. The procedure lengthens one of the two muscles that make up the calf, improving the ankle's range of motion. It can be done through a traditional open incision or minimally invasive approaches using an endoscope (a camera-containing instrument). Complication rates are low but can include nerve injury.

text: It can be done through a traditional open incision or minimally invasive approaches using an endoscope (a camera-containing instrument). Complication rates are low but can include nerve injury. **Minimally invasive surgery.** Minimally invasive approaches are becoming more popular for various musculoskeletal conditions, including Achilles tendinitis. Techniques use small incisions that accommodate a camera and instruments to visualize and remove damaged, inflamed tendon tissue. Small openings also allow placement of anchors into the heel bone to secure the tendon in position. Other minimally invasive surgeries use small holes to release portions of the tendon and muscle from the bone surface. These methods may become more common, but there is currently limited data on their effectiveness. They may also be less effective in patients with substantial tendon damage. **Outcomes.** Achilles tendinitis surgery generally produces excellent results.

text: These methods may become more common, but there is currently limited data on their effectiveness. They may also be less effective in patients with substantial tendon damage. **Outcomes.** Achilles tendinitis surgery generally produces excellent results. Research on tendon debridement reports that about 75% of patients return to their pre-surgery activity level, with 90% patient satisfaction. Gastrocnemius recession similarly shows favorable outcomes, with substantial pain reduction and functional improvement after surgery. The extent of tendon damage is the main factor determining recovery. More extensive tendon involvement is associated with a longer recovery and a lower chance of returning to sports. Physical therapy is a critical part of recovery. Many patients need about 12 months of rehabilitation to reach maximum improvement. Between 20% and 30% of patients experience some lingering pain after surgery, which is the most common complication. Wound infections can also develop and can be difficult to manage given the location of the surgery.

text: # Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injuries ## Anatomy of the Knee ### Bones Three bones meet to form the knee joint: - The femur (thighbone), which sits above the knee - The tibia (shinbone), which sits below the knee - The patella (kneecap), which sits in front of the joint Bones are connected to other bones by ligaments. There are four primary ligaments in your knee. They act like strong ropes to hold the bones together and keep your knee stable. ### Ligaments **Collateral ligaments.** These are found on the sides of your knee. The medial collateral ligament (MCL) is on the inside, and the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) is on the outside. They control the side-to-side motion of your knee and brace it against unusual movement. **Cruciate ligaments.** These are found inside your knee joint.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: They control the side-to-side motion of your knee and brace it against unusual movement. **Cruciate ligaments.** These are found inside your knee joint. They cross each other to form an X, with the ACL in front and the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) in back. The cruciate ligaments control the front and back motion of your knee. - The ACL runs diagonally in the middle of the knee. It prevents the tibia from sliding out in front of the femur and provides rotational stability to the knee. - The PCL keeps the shinbone from moving backward too far. It is stronger than the ACL and is injured far less often. ### Cartilage The ends of the femur and tibia, and the back of the patella are covered with articular cartilage. This slippery substance helps your knee bones glide smoothly across each other as you bend or straighten your leg. ### Meniscus

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The ends of the femur and tibia, and the back of the patella are covered with articular cartilage. This slippery substance helps your knee bones glide smoothly across each other as you bend or straighten your leg. ### Meniscus Two wedge-shaped pieces of fibrocartilage act as shock absorbers between the femur and tibia. These are menisci. The menisci help to transmit force from one bone to another and play an important role in knee stability and smooth joint motion. Commonly, people who tear their ACL will also suffer a meniscal tear on the outside of their knee. ### Tendons Bones are connected to muscles by tendons. These are fibrous connective tissues that allow for joint movement and provide stability. The role of all the tendons is to transfer force from muscles to bones.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Tendons Bones are connected to muscles by tendons. These are fibrous connective tissues that allow for joint movement and provide stability. The role of all the tendons is to transfer force from muscles to bones. Although the quadriceps tendons are not directly affected when you tear your ACL, their stability and strength play an important role in both ACL tear recovery and future injury prevention. ## Description A "torn ACL" refers to the rupture of the ligament. This can happen within the ligament itself or at the point where the ligament connects to bone. A rupture occurs when the force applied to the ligament is too much for the ligament to bear. Injuries to the ACL often occur along with damage to other structures in the knee, such as the MCL, lateral meniscus, and medial meniscus.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Injuries to the ACL often occur along with damage to other structures in the knee, such as the MCL, lateral meniscus, and medial meniscus. It is important to identify if you have any related injuries so you and your surgeon can make informed decisions about your treatment and ensure the best possible outcome. ### Classification of ACL Tears Injured ligaments are classified on a three-grade sprain system based on the degree of injury to the ligament. Your doctor will use a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to see how much ligament damage there is. **Grade 1 Sprains.** The ligament is mildly damaged. It has been slightly stretched but is still able to help keep the knee joint stable. The ACL is intact. **Grade 2 Sprains.** A Grade 2 sprain stretches the ligament to the point where it becomes loose. This is often referred to as a partial tear of the ligament.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The ACL is intact. **Grade 2 Sprains.** A Grade 2 sprain stretches the ligament to the point where it becomes loose. This is often referred to as a partial tear of the ligament. **Grade 3 Sprains.** This type of sprain is most commonly called a complete tear of the ligament. The ligament has been torn in half or pulled directly off the bone. The knee joint is unstable. In addition, the ACL Injury Severity Scale (ACLISS) documents any damage to the meniscus, cartilage, bones, and/or other ligaments that happened at the same time as the ACL tear. ## Risk Factors for ACL Tears - Being female. Female athletes experience ACL injuries at rates 2 to 8 times higher than males. This may be due to differences in knee morphology, biomechanics, and hormonal influences. Other suggested causes include differences in pelvis and leg alignment.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Female athletes experience ACL injuries at rates 2 to 8 times higher than males. This may be due to differences in knee morphology, biomechanics, and hormonal influences. Other suggested causes include differences in pelvis and leg alignment. - Having a higher body mass index (BMI) - Having more joint laxity (looser joints) - Being younger - Decreased lower leg strength ## Cause The ACL can be injured in several ways: - Changing direction rapidly - Stopping suddenly - Slowing down while running - Landing from a jump incorrectly - Direct contact or collision, such as a football tackle ## Symptoms When you injure your anterior cruciate ligament, you might hear a popping noise, and you may feel your knee give out from under you. Other typical symptoms include: - Pain with swelling. Within 24 hours, your knee will swell. The swelling and pain may go away on their own.

text: Other typical symptoms include: - Pain with swelling. Within 24 hours, your knee will swell. The swelling and pain may go away on their own. However, returning to normal activities often worsens the feeling of instability and risks further damage to the surrounding structures in your knee. - Loss of full range of motion. - Tenderness along the joint line. - Discomfort while walking. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination and Patient History During your clinic visit, your doctor will ask about the following: - The specific movement or impact that caused the injury - Your current symptoms (swelling, bruising, etc.) - What you have tried to help manage your symptoms and what has worked During the physical examination, the physician will check all the structures of your injured knee and compare them to your non-injured knee. Often, this will be enough to diagnose your injury, but advanced imaging is usually included to remove any uncertainty and evaluate for other possible injuries. ### Imaging Tests

text: Often, this will be enough to diagnose your injury, but advanced imaging is usually included to remove any uncertainty and evaluate for other possible injuries. ### Imaging Tests **X-rays.** X-rays do not specifically show ligament injuries. However, they are a quick and useful tool for identifying any related injury to bone. When an ACL tears at the spot where it attaches to bone, it sometimes pulls away a small piece of bone. This is called an "avulsion fracture." The piece of bone can be seen on an X-ray. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan.** An MRI offers the best view of your injured ligaments or cartilage. An MRI is not required to make the diagnosis of a torn ACL, but it allows your doctor to look for injuries to other soft tissue structures in the knee (e.g., meniscus, cartilage). It also offers better insight into the severity of the ACL injury. ## Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: It also offers better insight into the severity of the ACL injury. ## Treatment Treatment for an ACL tear will depend on the patient's individual needs and desired goals for recovery. Non-operative management is always an option. The decision about whether to have surgery begins with a conversation between you and your orthopaedic surgeon to establish goals, review surgical options, and optimize post-surgery recovery plans. Broadly, surgical options include repair or reconstruction. Reconstruction remains the most common surgical treatment. Repair is typically reserved for: - Tears close to where the ligament attaches to the bone - Partial tears that are causing symptoms Your surgeon will help you determine which treatment option is best for you.

text: # Sprained Ankle ## Overview Ankle sprains are the leading cause of missed participation in sports and occur frequently across all age groups and activity levels. These injuries happen when the strong ligaments that support the ankle are stretched beyond their normal range and tear. The ligaments on the outer side of the ankle are most commonly affected. The severity of a sprain varies considerably depending on how many ligaments are involved and how much they have torn. However, medical evaluation is necessary if the ankle continues to swell or hurt for several weeks despite home care, or if putting weight on it becomes difficult. When conservative treatment fails, surgery to repair or reconstruct the damaged ligaments may be appropriate. Untreated or inadequately rehabilitated severe sprains create chronic weakness in the ankle, substantially increasing the risk of re-injury. Repeated sprains can lead to persistent pain, chronic ankle pain, arthritis, and instability. ## What Is an Ankle Sprain?

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Repeated sprains can lead to persistent pain, chronic ankle pain, arthritis, and instability. ## What Is an Ankle Sprain? Ligaments are fibrous connective tissues that link bones throughout the body. The ankle has numerous ligaments that keep the bones properly aligned and provide the joint stability needed for standing, walking, and running. A sprain occurs when one or more of the ankle-stabilizing ligaments are damaged. About 90% of ankle sprains involve an inversion injury (the foot turns inward) to the anterior talofibular (ATFL) and calcaneofibular (CFL) ligaments, located on the outer side of the ankle. Less often, medial ankle sprains result from an eversion injury (the foot turns out) to the deltoid ligament on the inner side of the ankle. Tearing severity ranges from microscopic fiber damage to a complete tear.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Less often, medial ankle sprains result from an eversion injury (the foot turns out) to the deltoid ligament on the inner side of the ankle. Tearing severity ranges from microscopic fiber damage to a complete tear. When a ligament tears completely, the ankle may become unstable once the initial swelling goes down. Progressive instability can damage the underlying bone and cartilage surfaces over time. ## Causes of Ankle Sprains A typical injury involves twisting the foot or ankle, sometimes accompanied by an audible or felt "pop" when the ligament tears severely. These injuries can happen unexpectedly during activities including: - Walking, working, or exercising on uneven ground - Falls or trips - High-demand sports involving cutting movements or jumping (trail running, basketball, tennis, football, soccer) Risk factors include: - Poor balance - Naturally loose or hypermobile ligaments - Misaligned ankle structure - Footwear that lacks adequate foot and ankle support - Shoes with insufficient traction

Swelling and inflammation often make this exam uncomfortable, and it typically involves:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Diagnosing an Ankle Sprain ### Physical Examination Doctors diagnose ankle sprains by asking about how the injury happened and performing a detailed examination of the foot and ankle. Swelling and inflammation often make this exam uncomfortable, and it typically involves: **Observation.** The doctor visually compares the injured ankle to the uninjured side. Sprains typically show swelling and bruising directly over the damaged ligaments. **Palpation.** Tenderness is localized specifically over the injured ligaments. The doctor gently presses around the ankle to identify which ligaments are damaged. **Range of motion testing.** The doctor moves the ankle in various directions, though stiffness and swelling may limit movement. **Stability testing.** The doctor applies controlled pressure and pulling motions in different directions to assess joint stability. Doctors can often estimate the severity of a sprain based on the amount of swelling, pain intensity, degree of bruising, and results of stability testing.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Doctors can often estimate the severity of a sprain based on the amount of swelling, pain intensity, degree of bruising, and results of stability testing. Difficulty bearing weight or tenderness over bone calls for additional testing to rule out a fracture. ### Imaging Tests Ankle sprains are primarily diagnosed clinically, based on how the injury happened, reported symptoms, and physical exam findings. Doctors sometimes order imaging to rule out a fracture or injury to nearby tissue. **X-rays** show dense structures like bone well. Depending on symptoms and exam findings, doctors may order X-rays of the ankle and foot bones. Severe ankle sprains can have a similar degree of pain, bruising, and swelling as a fracture, which makes it hard to tell the two injuries apart from symptoms alone. **Stress X-rays** are specialized images taken while the doctor pushes on the ankle in different directions using controlled force. They reveal whether ligament damage has compromised the ankle's stability.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Stress X-rays** are specialized images taken while the doctor pushes on the ankle in different directions using controlled force. They reveal whether ligament damage has compromised the ankle's stability. **MRI** is not required to diagnose a standard ankle sprain but may be ordered to: - Evaluate soft tissues like ligaments, cartilage, and tendons that plain X-rays cannot show - Assess for a "high ankle sprain" involving the connection between the lower leg bones - Investigate symptoms that persist beyond 6 to 8 weeks despite conservative treatment ## Classification of Ankle Sprains After the examination, doctors assign a grade to the sprain to guide treatment, based on the extent of ligament damage. **Grade 1.** Minor stretching of the fibers with microscopic tearing, mild localized pain, bruising, and swelling. Weight-bearing typically causes no pain, and stability testing shows no instability.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Grade 1.** Minor stretching of the fibers with microscopic tearing, mild localized pain, bruising, and swelling. Weight-bearing typically causes no pain, and stability testing shows no instability. **Grade 2.** Partial ligament tearing, causing moderate localized pain, bruising, and swelling. Weight-bearing causes mild discomfort, and the exam shows slight looseness compared to the uninjured ankle. **Grade 3.** Complete tearing of the ligament, with significant localized pain, bruising, and swelling. Weight-bearing produces substantial pain, and the exam shows pronounced instability. ## Treatment for Ankle Sprains ### Nonsurgical Treatment Nearly all isolated ankle sprains heal without surgery. Even complete ligament tears (Grade 3) heal through proper immobilization and rehabilitation without needing operative repair. Treatment follows a three-phase progression that applies to all sprains: **Phase 1** includes brief immobilization, activity restriction, and ice for swelling.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Treatment follows a three-phase progression that applies to all sprains: **Phase 1** includes brief immobilization, activity restriction, and ice for swelling. Early weight-bearing as comfort allows is the standard approach. Grade 2 sprains benefit from a removable supportive device like a walking boot or inflatable brace. Grade 3 injuries may require a short leg cast or a protective cast-brace for 10 to 14 days. Swelling and discomfort typically last 2 to 3 days, and crutches may be recommended if walking is difficult. **Phase 2** typically starts early and focuses on functional rehabilitation, including: - Motion exercises to improve ankle movement through its available range - Isometric strengthening — contracting muscles without moving the joint - Balance retraining to restore proprioception Immobilization should end during this phase to prevent stiffness from developing. **Phase 3** includes progressively more challenging strengthening and balance exercises alongside gradual return to activity.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Balance retraining to restore proprioception Immobilization should end during this phase to prevent stiffness from developing. **Phase 3** includes progressively more challenging strengthening and balance exercises alongside gradual return to activity. Initially, activities that avoid turning or twisting the ankle are emphasized, progressing later to quick cutting movements typical of sports like tennis, basketball, and football. Early return to sports or work often requires ankle taping or bracing for support. This three-phase progression may take as little as 2 weeks for minor injuries but can extend to 6 to 12 weeks for more serious injuries. ### Home Treatment for Ankle Sprains Milder cases may respond to home care recommended by a doctor. **RICE protocol.** Apply this approach right after the injury: - **Rest.** Avoid walking on the injured ankle and stop participating in sports. - **Ice.** Apply cold therapy immediately to control swelling, using 20- to 30-minute applications three to four times a day.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Rest.** Avoid walking on the injured ankle and stop participating in sports. - **Ice.** Apply cold therapy immediately to control swelling, using 20- to 30-minute applications three to four times a day. Never apply ice directly to the skin; use an ice pack or a towel wrap and monitor the skin. - **Compression.** Compression bandages, wraps, or elastic supports help immobilize and stabilize the ankle and may reduce swelling. Continue wearing compression as long as it's comfortable. - **Elevation.** Keep the ankle above heart level as much as possible during the first 48 hours to manage and minimize swelling. **Physical therapy.** Rehabilitation activities in phases two and three improve flexibility, muscle strength, and balance. - **Early movement.** Exercises involving unrestricted ankle movement without resistance help prevent stiffness. Stretching bands may assist with range-of-motion work.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Physical therapy.** Rehabilitation activities in phases two and three improve flexibility, muscle strength, and balance. - **Early movement.** Exercises involving unrestricted ankle movement without resistance help prevent stiffness. Stretching bands may assist with range-of-motion work. - **Strengthening exercises.** Once swelling and discomfort decrease, exercises targeting the muscles and tendons in the front and back of the lower leg and ankle begin. Water-based exercise may substitute if weight-bearing is too painful. Progressive resistance training is introduced as tolerated. - **Proprioception (balance) training.** Poor balance often precedes repeat injuries and chronic instability. Example exercises include standing on the injured foot with the other foot raised and eyes closed. text: # Ankylosing spondylitis Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a long-term condition in which the spine and other areas of the body become inflamed. It's a type of axial spondyloarthritis and usually first develops in teenagers and young adults. Symptoms tend to develop gradually, usually over several months or years, and may come and go over time. For some people the condition improves with time, but for others it can gradually get worse. ## Symptoms - Back pain and stiffness that gets better with exercise but does not improve, or gets worse, with rest - Pain and stiffness that is worse in the morning and at night, sometimes waking you - Pain in the buttock region - **Arthritis** - pain on moving the affected joint, tenderness when the joint is examined, and swelling and warmth in the affected area (commonly hips and knees)

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: Ankylosing spondylitis is defined within this guideline as "radiographic axial spondyloarthritis." ## 1.1 Recognition and Referral in Non-Specialist Care Settings "Do not rule out the possibility that a person has spondyloarthritis solely on the presence or absence of any individual sign, symptom or test result." Signs and symptoms may be musculoskeletal (inflammatory back pain, enthesitis, dactylitis) or extra-articular (uveitis, psoriasis). Be aware that axial spondyloarthritis affects a similar number of women as men, can occur in people who are HLA-B27 negative, and may be present despite no evidence of sacroiliitis on plain film X-ray. If exactly 3 additional criteria are present, perform an HLA-B27 test and refer if positive.

text: # Osteoarthritis of the Elbow ## Overview Osteoarthritis of the elbow develops when the cartilage surface deteriorates or sustains damage. This commonly results from previous injuries such as elbow dislocation or fracture, though it frequently occurs through normal age-related joint wear from years of activity. While osteoarthritis typically affects weight-bearing joints like hips and knees, the elbow remains relatively resistant due to its well-matched joint surfaces and strong stabilizing ligaments. ## Anatomy The elbow functions as a hinge joint comprising three bones: - The humerus (upper arm bone) - The ulna (forearm bone on the pinky finger side) - The radius (forearm bone on the thumb side) The bone surfaces where they meet are covered with articular cartilage, a smooth substance that protects the bones and enables them to move easily. A synovial membrane covers remaining interior surfaces, producing lubricating fluid that reduces friction during arm movement.

text: # Arthritis of the Foot and Ankle ## Overview Arthritis is inflammation of one or more joints, and it frequently affects the many small joints of the foot and ankle. More than one hundred distinct forms of arthritis exist, and many of them target the foot and ankle region, making routine walking and recreational activities challenging for those affected. While arthritis has no cure, numerous treatment approaches can slow disease progression and relieve discomfort. With appropriate management, most people with arthritis are able to control their symptoms, stay physically active, and maintain a good quality of life. ## Anatomy During standing, walking, and running, the foot and ankle provide support, absorb shock, and help maintain balance. Three bones make up the ankle joint, which allows mostly up-and-down motion. The foot itself contains 28 bones and more than 30 joints, allowing for a wide range of movement.

A membrane called the synovium surrounds each joint and produces fluid that lubricates the joint and nourishes the cartilage. Strong bands of fibrous tissue called ligaments connect bones to each other and stabilize the joints. text: ## Description: Major Types of Arthritis ### Osteoarthritis This "wear-and-tear" type of arthritis commonly affects middle-aged people but can develop earlier. The protective cartilage gradually wears down, becoming rough and thin. As cartilage is lost, joint space narrows, sometimes leading to bone rubbing on bone and the formation of painful bony growths called osteophytes (bone spurs). Contributing factors include advancing age, excess body weight, and a family history of the disease. Symptoms usually develop gradually and worsen over time. ### Rheumatoid Arthritis This chronic, whole-body condition often begins in the foot and ankle and affects multiple joints throughout the body, frequently in a symmetrical pattern (the same joints on both sides of the body). Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease — the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissue. Immune cells invade the synovial membrane lining the joint, causing swelling.

text: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease — the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissue. Immune cells invade the synovial membrane lining the joint, causing swelling. Over time, the inflamed synovium invades and damages bone, cartilage, ligaments, and tendons, which can lead to severe joint deformity and disability. Rheumatoid arthritis is not directly inherited, but a genetic predisposition can make certain people more susceptible. A triggering event — an infection or an environmental factor — activates these susceptibility genes. Following this trigger, immune cells produce substances that attack the joints. ### Posttraumatic Arthritis Injury to the foot or ankle can lead to this form of arthritis. Fractures and dislocations, especially those involving the joint surface, are the most common causes. Like osteoarthritis, cartilage breakdown is the hallmark of this condition, and it can develop years after the original injury.

text: Sometimes more than one surgical approach is needed. ### Arthroscopic Debridement This procedure, used for early-stage arthritis, removes loose fragments of cartilage, inflamed synovial tissue, and bone spurs around the joint. During arthroscopy, surgeons insert a small camera (arthroscope) into the joint and use a video monitor to guide surgical instruments. Because the instruments are thin, only small incisions are needed instead of a large surgical opening. Arthroscopy is most helpful when pain is caused by bone spurs rubbing against each other without significant narrowing of the joint space. However, removing bone spurs may speed up cartilage breakdown by increasing joint motion. ### Arthrodesis (Fusion) This procedure permanently eliminates motion between the bones of a diseased joint by fusing them into one continuous bone.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
condition_display: Arthritis of the Foot and Ankle
text: However, removing bone spurs may speed up cartilage breakdown by increasing joint motion. ### Arthrodesis (Fusion) This procedure permanently eliminates motion between the bones of a diseased joint by fusing them into one continuous bone. After removing the damaged cartilage, the surgeon places hardware — pins, plates, screws, or rods — to hold the joint in the desired position while the bones fuse, similar to how a broken bone heals. Eliminating motion eliminates the pain caused by that motion. Arthrodesis generally produces good results, but complications can include: - Nonunion (failure of the bones to fuse), which can sometimes lead to hardware breakage. A broken piece of metal is not painful by itself, but nonunion causes renewed pain and swelling. Repeat surgery with bone graft and new hardware may be necessary. Repeat fusion attempts have a lower success rate, making strict adherence to post-operative rehabilitation important.

text: Ankle replacement is suited for patients with: - Severe ankle arthritis - Complete destruction of the joint surfaces - Pain that substantially interferes with daily functioning Replacement provides better pain relief and mobility than fusion. Because it preserves joint motion, nearby joints experience less stress, reducing the chance of arthritis developing in those joints later. Implant components can occasionally loosen or wear out over time. If the implant fails severely, revision surgery — replacing the failed implant with new components — may be needed. An alternative is removing the implant and fusing the joint. This is technically more difficult than a primary fusion. Once the implant is removed, the resulting bone gap must be filled with graft material to preserve leg length. Because newly grafted bone may be weaker, the risk of nonunion increases, and subsequent fusion is more complicated than an initial procedure. ## Recovery Surgical treatment typically succeeds in eliminating arthritis pain and restoring the ability to perform daily activities.

Full recovery takes four to nine months, depending on the severity of the condition before surgery and how complex the procedure was. Foot and ankle surgery involves notable discomfort. While some pain is to be expected, advances in pain management have improved doctors' ability to control and minimize it. A cast is typically applied after surgery to restrict foot and ankle movement and prevent the fusion from failing. Keeping the foot elevated above heart level for one to two weeks after surgery helps reduce swelling. text: # Hip Osteoarthritis: Clinical Overview ## Description Osteoarthritis represents a degenerative joint condition affecting individuals primarily over age 50, though younger people may develop it. text: # Arthritis of the Knee ## Overview Arthritis is inflammation of one or more of your joints. Pain, swelling, and stiffness are the primary symptoms of arthritis. text: # Arthritis of the Shoulder ## Overview Arthritis involves inflammation of one or more joints, ultimately causing cartilage loss that enables smooth movement. Muscles and tendons called the rotator cuff maintain proper arm positioning. Your doctor or physical therapist can develop personalized programs. - **Other therapies**: These include "contrast soaks" — alternating warm and cold water soaks — to reduce swelling. DMARDs have risks and benefits, with rheumatologists directing their use.

text: # Baker's Cyst (Popliteal Cyst) ## Overview Baker's cysts, also known as popliteal cysts, represent one of the most common disorders in the knee. These fluid-filled sacs form a lump at the back of the knee, creating stiffness and discomfort. The condition honors Dr. William Morrant Baker, a 19th-century surgeon who first documented it. ## Cause Baker's cysts typically emerge from internal knee problems like osteoarthritis or meniscus tears. These conditions cause the joint to produce excess fluid, which can then go out a one-way valve in the back of the knee, leading to the formation of a cyst. Specific triggering conditions include: - Osteoarthritis - Rheumatoid arthritis - Meniscus tear - Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear - Other tissue-damaging joint conditions In younger patients, cysts often develop without an identifiable cause. ## Symptoms

When symptoms manifest, they may include: - A fullness sensation or lump behind the knee - Knee pain - Stiffness or tightness at the back of the knee - Swelling in the knee and lower leg Large cysts can interfere with blood flow in the veins of your leg. This can cause pain, swelling, weakness, or even numbness if there is nerve compression. Symptoms sometimes mimic deep vein thrombosis, making immediate medical evaluation crucial if you experience increasing calf pain and swelling. ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination

text: # Biceps Tendon Tear at the Shoulder ## Overview Tendons attach muscles to bones. The biceps tendons attach the biceps muscle to bones in the shoulder and elbow. If you tear the biceps tendon at the shoulder, you may lose some strength in your arm and have pain when you forcefully turn your arm from palm down to palm up. Most people need only simple treatments to relieve symptoms and can still function at a high level with a biceps tendon tear around the shoulder. This is because there are two attachments of the biceps tendon in the shoulder and, typically, a tear only involves one. You may benefit from surgery to repair the torn tendon if: - Your symptoms cannot be relieved by nonsurgical treatments - You develop debilitating (unbearable) cramping in the biceps muscle - You develop significant shoulder pain - Your arm weakness prevents you from working or performing daily activities, such as bathing, getting dressed, cooking, cleaning, or shopping

text: # Bunions (Hallux Valgus) ## Overview A bunion is a painful bony bump that forms on the inside of the foot at the base of the big toe. It is associated with hallux valgus, a progressive deformity in which the big toe gradually leans toward the smaller toes while the foot's outer border shifts outward. Pain comes from two sources: friction between the bony bump and footwear, and mechanical changes that alter pressure across the forefoot, which can cause secondary pain in the neighboring toes. The deformity develops gradually over time. Pressure on the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint initially causes the big toe to drift inward. Over time, the bones, tendons, and ligaments rearrange, producing the characteristic deformity. It often progressively worsens, eventually making it difficult to wear shoes comfortably or walk without discomfort.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Over time, the bones, tendons, and ligaments rearrange, producing the characteristic deformity. It often progressively worsens, eventually making it difficult to wear shoes comfortably or walk without discomfort. Bunions are more common in women than men, and most cases develop during adulthood rather than childhood. In many cases, conservative management — wearing properly sized shoes with a roomy toe box and taking steps to reduce pressure — relieves symptoms. If conservative treatment does not help after a reasonable trial, surgery may be considered to correct both the bump and the underlying hallux valgus deformity. ## Anatomy The big toe has two joints. The main one, called the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint, is where the first metatarsal bone meets the base of the big toe's proximal phalanx. Bunions originate specifically at this MTP joint. ## Description

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Bunions originate specifically at this MTP joint. ## Description A bunion forms when the bones of the MTP joint become misaligned: the first metatarsal shifts toward the inner border of the foot, the big toe's bones angle toward the second toe, and the MTP joint enlarges and protrudes on the inner side of the forefoot. The enlarged joint often becomes inflamed through a combination of abnormal joint mechanics and direct friction from shoes. The name "bunion" comes from a Greek word meaning "turnip," since the bump on the side of the foot commonly appears red and swollen, similar to the vegetable. ### Bunion Progression Bunions typically start small, but they tend to enlarge over time. Because the MTP joint bends with every step, an enlarging bunion causes progressively more discomfort and difficulty walking. Severe cases can produce notable cosmetic changes, including the big toe angling completely under or over the second toe.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo

Severe cases can produce notable cosmetic changes, including the big toe angling completely under or over the second toe. Pressure from the big toe may push the second toe out of its normal position, sometimes causing it to contact the third toe and develop a hammer toe deformity. Friction between the toes can create calluses, adding to the discomfort and difficulty walking. ### Related Foot Complications An enlarged MTP joint can lead to bursitis — inflammation of the fluid-filled sac that normally cushions the joint. Ongoing pain and arthritic changes can develop if the smooth cartilage covering the joint is damaged by abnormal joint motion. ### Adolescent Bunion In addition to the typical adult presentation, a variation called "adolescent bunion" mainly affects girls between the ages of 10 and 15.

Nonsurgical care cannot reverse an established deformity, but it can meaningfully reduce pain and help prevent it from getting worse. ### Footwear Changes Pain often improves simply by switching to properly fitted shoes with a roomy toe box that does not compress the toes. Some shoes can be stretched at specific points to relieve pressure over the bunion. Doctors can offer guidance on appropriate shoe selection and fit for individual needs. ### Padding Silicone-based cushioning pads worn inside the shoe can reduce pain over the bunion. text: # Hip Bursitis: Comprehensive Overview ## What Are Bursae? Bursae are small, jelly-like sacs that are located throughout the body, including around the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, and heel. These structures contain fluid and function as cushions between bones and soft tissues, reducing friction during movement. ## Types of Hip Bursitis Two major bursae in the hip can become inflamed: 1. **Trochanteric bursitis**: Affects the bursa covering the greater trochanter (bony hip point), causing lateral hip pain 2. **Iliopsoas bursitis**: Involves the bursa on the groin side of the hip, less common but treated similarly ## Symptoms Patients typically experience sharp, intense pain at the hip point that may extend to the outer thigh. Early-stage symptoms intensify at night, when lying on the affected side, and when rising from seated positions.

text: # Bursitis ## Definition & Overview Bursitis is when the fluid-filled sacs (bursa) that cushion the joints have become painful and swollen (inflamed). The condition typically resolves within weeks with home treatment. ## Symptoms The affected joint may display several indicators: dull, achy pain; tenderness; warmth relative to surrounding skin; swelling; and increased discomfort during movement or pressure. Redness may also appear. Most commonly affects shoulders, hips, elbows, or knees. ## Self-Care Treatment Extra cushioning around the area during sleep provides additional support. ## When to Consult a Doctor Seek GP evaluation if symptoms persist or worsen after 1-2 weeks of self-treatment, when fever or chills develop, if joint movement becomes impossible, or when experiencing severe, sharp, or shooting pain. ## Medical Assessments & Treatments Healthcare providers examine the joint and may extract fluid samples via needle aspiration to check for infection or conditions like gout.

text: # Calcific Tendinitis of the Shoulder ## Overview Shoulder pain affects many adults, with various structures potentially contributing to discomfort. Calcific tendinitis (also called calcific tendinopathy) involves the build-up of calcium deposits within the tendons of the rotator cuff. These deposits trigger inflammation and may cause mechanical impingement on the acromion, the bony shoulder roof. ## Anatomy The shoulder comprises three bones: - The humerus (upper arm bone) - The scapula (shoulder blade) - The clavicle (collarbone) The rotator cuff tendons attach to the top of the humerus (humeral head) and connect the humerus to the shoulder blade's socket (glenoid), enabling shoulder and arm movement. ## Cause and Risk Factors - Adults aged 30-60 face increased risk, though anyone can develop it - Slightly more prevalent in women than men - Can affect one or both shoulders

text: ### Imaging Tests **X-rays**: Cannot visualize soft tissues but reveal calcium deposits around the rotator cuff. **MRI**: Provides soft tissue images showing fluid, inflammation, rotator cuff tears, and calcium buildup within tendons. ## Treatment Treatment aims to reduce pain and restore function, considering age, activity level, and general health. ### Nonsurgical Treatment Many patients experience gradual improvement over weeks to months. - **Rest**: Avoid activities causing or worsening symptoms. - **Physical therapy**: Focus on restoring shoulder motion through stretching, advancing to strengthening exercises as improvement occurs. - **Shock wave therapy**: Shockwaves can be generated by specialized machines to deliver energy to the deep tissues of the shoulder to break up deposits and promote healing. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery becomes an option when nonsurgical treatment fails. text: # Carpal Tunnel Syndrome ## Description & Anatomy Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common condition that causes numbness, tingling, and pain in the hand and forearm. The condition develops when one of the major nerves to the hand -- the median nerve -- is squeezed or compressed as it travels through the wrist. The carpal tunnel itself is a narrow passageway in the wrist, about an inch wide, with floors and sides formed by small wrist bones. The roof of the tunnel is a strong band of connective tissue called the transverse carpal ligament. Because these boundaries are rigid, the carpal tunnel has little capacity to stretch or increase in size. The median nerve originates as a group of nerve roots in the neck and travels down the upper arm, across the elbow, and into the forearm, then passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist on its way to the hand and fingers.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: The median nerve originates as a group of nerve roots in the neck and travels down the upper arm, across the elbow, and into the forearm, then passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist on its way to the hand and fingers. It provides sensation to the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and half of the ring finger, and controls the muscles around the base of the thumb. Nine flexor tendons also travel through the tunnel, enabling finger and thumb bending. Without treatment, in most patients carpal tunnel syndrome gets worse over time, and can lead to permanent dysfunction of the hand, including loss of sensation in the fingers and weakness. ## Cause Most cases result from a combination of factors. Women and older people show higher incidence rates. Risk factors include: - **Heredity**: The carpal tunnel may be naturally smaller in some people, or there may be anatomic differences that change the amount of space for the nerve, and this can run in families.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: Risk factors include: - **Heredity**: The carpal tunnel may be naturally smaller in some people, or there may be anatomic differences that change the amount of space for the nerve, and this can run in families. - **Repetitive hand use**: Repeating the same hand and wrist motions or activities over a prolonged period may aggravate the tendons in the wrist, causing swelling. - **Hand and wrist position**: Extreme flexion or extension of the hand and wrist for a prolonged period increases pressure on the nerve. - **Pregnancy**: Hormonal changes during pregnancy can cause swelling that results in pressure on the nerve. - **Health conditions**: Diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and thyroid gland imbalance are associated with carpal tunnel syndrome. ## Symptoms Symptoms include: - Numbness, tingling, burning, and pain, primarily in the thumb and index, middle, and ring fingers. This often wakes people up at night.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: ## Symptoms Symptoms include: - Numbness, tingling, burning, and pain, primarily in the thumb and index, middle, and ring fingers. This often wakes people up at night. - Occasional shock-like sensations that radiate to the thumb and index, middle, and ring fingers. - Pain or tingling that may travel up the forearm toward the shoulder. - Weakness and clumsiness in the hand -- this may make it difficult to perform fine movements. - Dropping things, due to weakness, numbness, or a loss of proprioception (joint position sense). Onset is typically gradual. Many patients find that their symptoms come and go at first. However, as the condition worsens, symptoms may occur more frequently or persist for longer periods of time. Nighttime symptoms are common because many people sleep with their wrists bent.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: Many patients find that their symptoms come and go at first. However, as the condition worsens, symptoms may occur more frequently or persist for longer periods of time. Nighttime symptoms are common because many people sleep with their wrists bent. Daytime symptoms often occur when holding something for a prolonged period of time with the wrist bent forward or backward, such as when using a phone, driving, or reading a book. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination The doctor will review medical history and perform physical tests, which may include: - Performing "Tinel's sign" by tapping along the median nerve on the palm side of the wrist and hand to see if it causes any tingling into the fingers. - Bending and holding the wrists in a flexed position to test for numbness or tingling. - Testing sensitivity in the fingertips and hands by lightly touching them with a special instrument while the eyes are closed. - Checking for weakness in the muscles around the base of the thumb.

text: - Testing sensitivity in the fingertips and hands by lightly touching them with a special instrument while the eyes are closed. - Checking for weakness in the muscles around the base of the thumb. - Looking for atrophy in the muscles around the base of the thumb; in severe cases, these muscles may become visibly smaller. In many cases, carpal tunnel syndrome can be diagnosed by taking a medical history and performing a physical exam, and no further testing is needed. ### Diagnostic Tests Electrodiagnostic tests may be ordered to measure how well the median nerve is working and help determine whether there is too much pressure on the nerve. These tests help determine the severity of carpal tunnel syndrome, whether compression occurs in other locations, whether other nerves are affected, and whether additional medical conditions affect the nerves. Types include: - **Nerve conduction studies (NCS)**: These tests measure the signals travelling in the nerves of the hand and arm and can detect when a nerve is not conducting its signal effectively.

text: **MRI scans** provide better images of the body's soft tissues than X-rays, to help determine other causes for symptoms or to look for abnormal tissues that could be impacting the median nerve. ## Nonsurgical Treatment For early-stage diagnosis, the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome can often be relieved without surgery. Options include: - **Bracing or splinting**: Wearing a brace or splint at night will keep you from bending your wrist while you sleep. Keeping your wrist in a straight or neutral position reduces pressure on the nerve. Splints may also be worn during aggravating daytime activities. - **Activity changes**: Since symptoms often occur when the hand and wrist are in the same position for too long, modifying activities or workstations can slow or stop progression of the disease. - **Nerve gliding exercises**: Some patients may benefit from exercises that help the median nerve move more freely within the confines of the carpal tunnel. ## Surgical Treatment

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: - **Nerve gliding exercises**: Some patients may benefit from exercises that help the median nerve move more freely within the confines of the carpal tunnel. ## Surgical Treatment Surgery is recommended when nonsurgical treatment does not relieve symptoms or provides only temporary relief. The decision considers symptom severity, physical exam findings, response to non-operative treatment, and testing results. In long-standing cases with constant numbness and wasting of the thumb muscles, surgery may be recommended to prevent irreversible damage. ### Surgical Procedure The procedure is called "carpal tunnel release." The goal is to relieve pressure on the median nerve by cutting the ligament that forms the roof of the tunnel (transverse carpal ligament). Release of this ligament increases the size of the tunnel and decreases pressure on the median nerve, allowing for appropriate blood flow to the nerve and function. In most cases, carpal tunnel surgery is done on an outpatient basis.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: Release of this ligament increases the size of the tunnel and decreases pressure on the median nerve, allowing for appropriate blood flow to the nerve and function. In most cases, carpal tunnel surgery is done on an outpatient basis. The surgery can be done under general anesthesia, which puts you to sleep, or under local anesthesia, which numbs just the hand and arm. **Open carpal tunnel release**: The surgeon makes a small incision in the palm of the hand and views the inside of the hand and wrist through this incision, then divides the transverse carpal ligament (the roof of the carpal tunnel). This increases the size of the tunnel and decreases pressure on the median nerve. After surgery, the ligament may gradually grow back together in a lengthened fashion, but there will be more space in the carpal tunnel.

A special knife is used to divide the transverse carpal ligament, similar to the open carpal tunnel release procedure. The outcomes of open surgery and endoscopic surgery are similar. There are benefits and potential risks associated with both techniques. ### Recovery From Surgery Immediately after surgery, you will be encouraged to elevate your hand above your heart and move your fingers to reduce swelling and prevent stiffness. text: You should expect some pain, swelling, and stiffness after your procedure. Minor soreness in your palm may last several weeks to several months. Nighttime symptoms improve dramatically for most patients in the first week or so after surgery. **Grip and pinch strength** usually return by about 2 to 3 months after surgery. If the condition of the median nerve was poor before surgery, grip and pinch strength may not improve for about 6 to 12 months. **Numbness and tingling** tend to improve over the first several months after surgery. Some patients with mild disease may experience return of sensation right away. Patients with severe disease may not have normal sensation in their fingertips for 6 to 12 months after surgery. You may have to wear a splint or wrist brace for several weeks after surgery. You will be allowed to use your hand for light activities, taking care to avoid significant discomfort.

Driving, self-care activities, and light lifting and gripping may be permitted soon after surgery. ### Complications Common complications include bleeding, infection, wound healing issues, and nerve aggravation or injury. ### Outcomes For most patients, surgery will improve the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome. Recovery, however, may be gradual, and complete recovery may take up to a year. If you have significant pain and weakness for more than 2 months, your doctor may refer you to a hand therapist who can help you maximize your recovery. Additional conditions like arthritis or tendinitis may slow recovery. In long-standing cases of carpal tunnel syndrome with severe loss of feeling and/or muscle wasting around the base of the thumb, recovery will also be slower, and for these patients a complete recovery may not be possible.

text: # Carpal Tunnel Syndrome ## Overview Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is pressure on a nerve in your wrist. text: # Cervical Radiculopathy (Pinched Nerve) ## Overview Cervical radiculopathy, commonly called a "pinched nerve," occurs when a nerve in the neck is compressed or irritated where it branches from the spinal cord. This condition may cause pain radiating into the shoulder and/or arm, along with muscle weakness and numbness. The condition typically stems from degenerative changes in the spine as people age, or from sudden injuries causing herniated disks. ## Anatomy The cervical spine consists of seven small vertebrae forming the neck, part of the spine's 24 stacked bones that create a protective canal for the spinal cord. Key structural components include: - **Spinal cord and nerves**: Electrical pathways carrying signals between brain and muscles, with nerve roots branching through openings (foramen) in vertebrae

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Key structural components include: - **Spinal cord and nerves**: Electrical pathways carrying signals between brain and muscles, with nerve roots branching through openings (foramen) in vertebrae - **Intervertebral disks**: Flexible shock-absorbing structures between vertebrae, approximately half an inch thick, composed of a tough outer ring (annulus fibrosus) and soft, jelly-like center (nucleus pulposus) ## Cause ### Degenerative Changes As spinal disks age, they lose height and water content, becoming stiffer. This causes vertebrae to move closer together. The body responds by forming bone spurs around the disk, which can narrow the foramen and pinch nerve roots. These degenerative changes are called arthritis or spondylosis — normal changes occurring in nearly half of middle-aged and older people, though not all develop symptoms. ### Herniated Disk A disk herniates when its jelly-like center pushes through the outer ring.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Herniated Disk A disk herniates when its jelly-like center pushes through the outer ring. If severely worn or injured, the nucleus may squeeze completely through, bulging toward the spinal canal and compressing the nerve root, causing pain and weakness. Herniated disks often occur with lifting, pulling, bending, or twisting movements. ## Symptoms Pain typically starts at the neck and travels down the arm in the area served by the damaged nerve, described as "burning or sharp" neuropathic pain. Neck movements like extending, straining, or turning the head may increase pain. Additional symptoms include: - Tingling or "pins and needles" in fingers or hand (paresthesia) - Weakness in arm, shoulder, or hand muscles - Loss of sensation or numbness Some patients report pain decreases when placing hands on top of their head, temporarily relieving nerve root pressure. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination Your doctor will: - Discuss your medical history and general health

text: ### Nonsurgical Treatment Initial treatment is nonsurgical, including: - **Soft cervical collar**: A padded ring wrapping around the neck, held with Velcro. text: # Low Back Pain Almost every adult will experience low back pain at some point in their lives. Pain severity ranges from mild to severe, and may be temporary or chronic, sometimes accompanied by leg discomfort. ## Key Causes **Overactivity and muscle strain** Repetitive or unfamiliar activities cause muscle and ligament overstretching. Examples include seasonal sports or excessive yard work. **Disk problems** - Disk tears: small tears in the outer part of the disk occur naturally with aging; some cause no symptoms while others create lasting pain - Disk herniation: the disk's inner material protrudes and puts pressure on the sensitive spinal nerves, causing pain - Disk degeneration: age-related wearing causes disks to shrink and collapse **Structural issues** - Spondylolisthesis (vertebral slippage) - Spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal) - Scoliosis (abnormal spine curvature) - Compression fractures from osteoporosis ## Symptoms

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) — OrthoInfo
text: - Spondylolisthesis (vertebral slippage) - Spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal) - Scoliosis (abnormal spine curvature) - Compression fractures from osteoporosis ## Symptoms Pain characteristics vary: sharp, stabbing, dull, or cramping sensations. Patients often report that reclining or lying down improves their low back pain. Pain typically worsens with bending, lifting, sitting, and standing. Additional symptoms include sciatica (buttock and leg pain extending to the foot). **Red flag symptoms requiring immediate medical attention:** - Leg weakness - Loss of bladder or bowel control - Fever, chills, or unexplained weight loss ## Diagnostic Tests - Physical exam: range-of-motion assessment and nerve function testing - Imaging: X-rays, MRI, CT scans, bone scans, and bone density tests ## Treatment Options **Nonsurgical approaches** - Physical therapy with stretching and strengthening exercises

text: ## Diagnostic Tests - Physical exam: range-of-motion assessment and nerve function testing - Imaging: X-rays, MRI, CT scans, bone scans, and bone density tests ## Treatment Options **Nonsurgical approaches** - Physical therapy with stretching and strengthening exercises - Braces, chiropractic care, yoga, or Pilates **Surgical options** (considered only after 6-12 months of conservative treatment) - Spinal fusion - Disk replacement - Diskectomy (removing herniated disk material) - Laminectomy (removing bone spurs) ## Prevention Strategies - Regular aerobic exercise combined with back-strengthening routines - Proper lifting technique: lift heavy items with your legs, not your back - Maintaining a healthy weight - Avoiding smoking - Using correct posture during standing, sitting, and lifting

text: # Back pain Back pain, particularly lower back pain, is very common. It usually improves within a few weeks, but for some people it can persist or recur. ## Causes Back pain typically stems from injuries such as muscle strains. Medical conditions such as slipped discs, sciatica, or ankylosing spondylitis may also trigger it. Rarely, serious issues like fractures, cancer, or infections are responsible. ## When to seek medical help **See a GP if:** - Pain doesn't improve after a few weeks of home treatment - Pain interferes with daily activities - The pain is causing you concern - Pain is accompanied by unexplained weight loss, a lump or change in shape, symptoms that get worse at night, or pain located in the upper back **Contact NHS 111 or a GP urgently if:** - You have sudden, severe pain, or symptoms such as fever and chills, which warrant prompt attention

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: **Contact NHS 111 or a GP urgently if:** - You have sudden, severe pain, or symptoms such as fever and chills, which warrant prompt attention **Call 999 or go to A&E if you have back pain along with:** - Numbness or tingling around (or loss of feeling in) both legs - Numbness or tingling around (or loss of feeling in) your genitals or bottom (anal area) - Loss of bladder or bowel control (incontinence, or difficulty peeing) - Chest pain - The pain was caused by a serious accident, such as a car crash ## Self-help strategies **Do:** - Stay active and try to continue with your daily activities - Apply ice packs or heat packs to ease pain - Try gentle stretches - Try activities such as walking, swimming, yoga or pilates **Don't:** - Avoid prolonged bed rest ## Professional treatments If self-help measures don't work, a GP may suggest: - Physiotherapy

text: # Claw Toe ## Overview Claw toe is a common foot deformity in which the affected toe curls downward. The curled toe digs into the sole of the shoe, which can create painful thickened areas of skin (calluses). If left untreated, the deformity tends to progress and may eventually become permanent (rigid). ## Anatomy The foot has five toes, and each has three joints except the big toe, which has two. In claw toe, the affected toe bends downward at two locations: the proximal interphalangeal joint (the middle joint) and the distal interphalangeal joint (the joint closest to the toe tip). ## Cause Several factors contribute to this deformity: - **Footwear.** Tight shoes — those that are too short or have high heels — are frequently a cause. - **Nerve damage.** Conditions such as diabetes, stroke, and alcohol use can weaken muscles by damaging nerve function.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Footwear.** Tight shoes — those that are too short or have high heels — are frequently a cause. - **Nerve damage.** Conditions such as diabetes, stroke, and alcohol use can weaken muscles by damaging nerve function. - **Other causes.** Injuries and inflammatory conditions can also produce this foot abnormality. ## Symptoms Signs of claw toe include: - The toe extends upward from the joint where it meets the foot - The toe bends downward at the middle joint, toward the sole - The toe may also bend downward at the joint nearest the tip, curling under the foot - Thickened skin (calluses or corns) may develop on top of the toe or under the ball of the foot ## Doctor Examination A doctor should evaluate the condition and may order tests to rule out nerve conditions causing muscle imbalance. Determining whether the deformity is still flexible or has become fixed (rigid) affects treatment choices.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Doctor Examination A doctor should evaluate the condition and may order tests to rule out nerve conditions causing muscle imbalance. Determining whether the deformity is still flexible or has become fixed (rigid) affects treatment choices. The doctor will also check the skin and any calluses that have formed, which influences the treatment plan. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment (Early Stage) - Splinting or taping the toe to hold it in a better position - Choosing shoes with a roomy toe box and avoiding tight shoes - Manually stretching the toe toward a more normal position - Strengthening exercises such as picking up marbles with the toes and towel curls ### Nonsurgical Treatment (Advanced Stage) - Padding to redistribute pressure and reduce stress on the ball of the foot - "Deep" or extra-depth shoes that provide additional room (about 3/8 inch of extra depth) - Professional shoe modification to create extra room for the toe ## Surgical Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - "Deep" or extra-depth shoes that provide additional room (about 3/8 inch of extra depth) - Professional shoe modification to create extra room for the toe ## Surgical Treatment **Flexible deformities.** Surgeons may release (cut) a tendon on the underside of the toe to prevent or treat sores on the sole of the foot. **Rigid deformities.** Treatment may involve lengthening or cutting a tendon combined with shortening the bone or fusing the joint (arthrodesis), often followed by placement of a pin for 4 to 6 weeks to hold the toe in position while it heals. ## Recovery After surgery, stiffness, swelling, and redness typically last 4 to 6 weeks. Weight-bearing is initially limited to the heel for short distances, and longer walking is restricted during this time. Elevating the foot promotes healing and reduces discomfort.
