text: # Collateral Ligament Injuries ## Overview Collateral ligament injuries involve stretching or tearing the ligaments on the sides of the knee. There are two main collateral ligaments: the medial collateral ligament (MCL), located on the inner side, and the lateral collateral ligament (LCL), located on the outer side. MCL tears account for 43 to 52% of all knee injuries, while LCL injuries represent less than 2% of knee injuries. ## Anatomy of the Knee **Bones** Three bones meet to form your knee joint: the femur (thighbone), the tibia (shinbone), and the patella (kneecap). The femur comes from above the knee and meets the tibia, which is below the knee. The kneecap sits in front of the joint. **Ligaments** Bones are connected to other bones by ligaments. There are four primary ligaments in your knee.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The kneecap sits in front of the joint. **Ligaments** Bones are connected to other bones by ligaments. There are four primary ligaments in your knee. They act like strong ropes to hold the bones together and keep your knee stable. **Collateral ligaments** are found on the sides of your knee. They control the side-to-side motion of your knee and brace it against unusual movement. The medial collateral ligament (MCL) is on the inside and connects the femur to the tibia. The lateral collateral ligament (LCL) is on the outside and connects the femur to the fibula (the smaller bone in the lower leg). **Cruciate Ligaments** are found inside your knee joint. They cross each other to form an X, with the ACL in front and the PCL in back. The cruciate ligaments control the front and back motion of your knee.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Cruciate Ligaments** are found inside your knee joint. They cross each other to form an X, with the ACL in front and the PCL in back. The cruciate ligaments control the front and back motion of your knee. Most severe MCL tears occur at the same time as ACL tears. **Cartilage** Articular cartilage covers the surfaces of the femur, tibia, and patella. It reduces friction and helps your bones glide smoothly against each other as you move your leg. **Meniscus** Your knee cartilage is cushioned by menisci — rubbery, C-shaped disks that act as "shock absorbers" between the thighbone and shinbone, helping to protect and stabilize the knee joints. Each knee has two menisci — one on the outside of the knee (lateral) and one on the inside (medial). People who tear their MCL might suffer a meniscus tear at the same time.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Each knee has two menisci — one on the outside of the knee (lateral) and one on the inside (medial). People who tear their MCL might suffer a meniscus tear at the same time. **Tendons** Tendons connect bone to muscle. They allow for joint movement and provide stability. ## Description The knee is not designed to withstand forces from either side. When you twist too quickly or have a direct impact to the side of your knee, the joint is forced to bend in the wrong direction. This puts enormous strain on the ligaments. An injured collateral ligament often refers to either: - Rupturing the MCL or LCL within the ligament itself - A tear in the bone-ligament connection, meaning the ligament pulls off the bone and may take a small piece of bone with it The MCL is injured more often than the LCL because the outer knee is more exposed to impact.

text: - A tear in the bone-ligament connection, meaning the ligament pulls off the bone and may take a small piece of bone with it The MCL is injured more often than the LCL because the outer knee is more exposed to impact. ## Classification of Collateral Ligament Tears Injured ligaments are classified using a three-grade sprain system based on the degree of injury: - **Grade 1:** The ligament is mildly damaged. It has been slightly stretched but is still able to help keep the knee joint stable. - **Grade 2:** A Grade 2 sprain stretches the ligament to the point where it becomes loose. This is often referred to as a partial tear of the ligament. - **Grade 3:** This type of sprain is most commonly referred to as a complete tear of the ligament. The ligament has been torn in half or pulled directly off the bone. The knee joint is unstable. ## Cause

The knee joint is unstable. ## Cause Injuries to the collateral ligaments are usually caused by a force that pushes the knee sideways and overstresses the ligament. - Medial collateral ligament tears often occur through direct trauma or sudden changes in direction or speed. The stress on the outside of the knee from these events can strain or tear the MCL. - Lateral collateral ligament tears are caused by trauma to the inside of the knee, forcing the knee outward and stressing the ligament. ### Risk Factors - High-contact sports - Sports with high-velocity pivoting - Weak lower body strength - Past knee injuries ## Symptoms When you injure your MCL or LCL, you might hear or feel a "pop" and you may feel your knee give out from under you.

text: ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination and Patient History Your doctor will ask you about the following: - Cause of your injury - Current symptoms (swelling, clicking, etc.) - Any past injuries to the knee - Your baseline level of activity The doctor will check all the structures of your injured knee and compare them to your non-injured knee. Most ligament injuries can be diagnosed with a thorough physical examination of the knee. ### Imaging Tests The doctor will usually order imaging tests to confirm the diagnosis and rule out any additional injuries. These tests may include: **X-rays:** Although X-rays do not explicitly show any injury to your collateral ligaments, they can reveal whether the ligament tore off a piece of bone when it was injured. Stress views (images where the physician applies force to the inside and outside of the knee) are important in younger patients for evaluating whether the growth plate was injured.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Stress views (images where the physician applies force to the inside and outside of the knee) are important in younger patients for evaluating whether the growth plate was injured. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan:** An MRI scan offers the best view of your injured ligaments. It allows the doctor to examine all knee structures (e.g., ligaments, cartilage, meniscus) and offers insight into the severity of the injury. ## Treatment The treatment for collateral ligament injuries depends on the patient's individual needs, severity of injury, and whether there are other injuries. **Medial Collateral Ligament** If you have a low-grade MCL injury and no related injuries, you can manage your injury non-operatively. - You can continue to move around while wearing a hinged knee brace for stability. - You will also work with a physical therapist to prevent stiffness and rebuild strength and confidence in the knee. **Lateral Collateral Ligament**

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - You can continue to move around while wearing a hinged knee brace for stability. - You will also work with a physical therapist to prevent stiffness and rebuild strength and confidence in the knee. **Lateral Collateral Ligament** Similar to MCL tears, LCL tears can often be treated without surgery. If your LCL injury involves other structures in your knee, your treatment will address those as well. Non-operative management is an option for LCL tears that are not severe — Grade I and II — and are stable. The patient typically cannot bear weight for 1 week and will use a hinged knee brace to stabilize the knee during recovery. Physical therapy is also critical to regain mobility and strength. Surgery may be recommended if the ligament has pulled directly off the bone or if you have other injuries along with the LCL tear. ## Return to Sports After a Collateral Ligament Injury

Surgery may be recommended if the ligament has pulled directly off the bone or if you have other injuries along with the LCL tear. ## Return to Sports After a Collateral Ligament Injury After initial management following the injury, the focus of your care will shift to restoring your prior level of activity. This can be achieved by consistently working with a physical therapist. Once you have regained your range of motion and strength, your doctor may allow functional progression. This is a gradual, progressive return to sports activities. Depending on the severity of your sprain, your doctor may suggest wearing a knee brace during sports activities to prevent re-injury.

text: # Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Nerve Entrapment at the Elbow) ## Overview Ulnar nerve entrapment occurs when the ulnar nerve in the arm becomes compressed or irritated. The ulnar nerve travels from the neck down into the hand and can be constricted in several places. The most common compression location is behind the inside part of the elbow, known as cubital tunnel syndrome. Common symptoms include numbness and tingling in the pinky and ring fingers. Most cases respond to nonsurgical treatments like activity modification and bracing, though surgery may be necessary if symptoms persist or nerve damage occurs. ## Anatomy The ulnar nerve travels through the cubital tunnel at the elbow, running under a bump of bone at the inside of the elbow called the medial epicondyle. This "funny bone" location places the nerve close to the skin surface.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The ulnar nerve travels through the cubital tunnel at the elbow, running under a bump of bone at the inside of the elbow called the medial epicondyle. This "funny bone" location places the nerve close to the skin surface. Beyond the elbow, the nerve travels under muscles on the inside of the forearm and into the hand on the side of the palm with the pinky finger. It passes through another tunnel called Guyon's canal upon entering the hand. The ulnar nerve provides sensation to the little finger and half the ring finger. It controls most of the little muscles in the hand that help with fine movements, and some of the bigger muscles in the forearm that help with a strong grip. ## Cause In many cases, the exact cause remains unknown. However, the ulnar nerve is especially vulnerable at the elbow due to its narrow passage with minimal protective soft tissue.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Cause In many cases, the exact cause remains unknown. However, the ulnar nerve is especially vulnerable at the elbow due to its narrow passage with minimal protective soft tissue. Elbow bending compresses and stretches the nerve while reducing blood supply, which explains why symptoms worsen with bent elbows. ### Common Causes of Compression - **Repetitive bending:** Sleeping with bent elbows or regularly bending the elbow irritates the nerve and decreases blood supply, causing numbness, particularly upon waking - **Nerve subluxation:** The nerve may slide out from behind the medial epicondyle when bending; repeated movement irritates it over time - **Pressure from leaning:** Extended pressure on the elbow compresses the nerve - **Fluid buildup:** Swelling in the elbow can compress the nerve - **Direct trauma:** A blow to the inside of the elbow causes pain and electric shock sensations in the ring and pinky fingers ("funny bone" injury)

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Fluid buildup:** Swelling in the elbow can compress the nerve - **Direct trauma:** A blow to the inside of the elbow causes pain and electric shock sensations in the ring and pinky fingers ("funny bone" injury) - **Throwing activities:** Baseball pitching creates significant stress on the elbow's inner side ### Risk Factors - Prior elbow fracture or dislocation - Bone spurs or elbow arthritis - Elbow joint swelling - Elbow joint cysts - Repetitive or prolonged elbow bending or flexing activities - Baseball pitching ## Symptoms Cubital tunnel syndrome causes aching pain on the elbow's inside; however, most symptoms occur in the hand. - **Numbness and tingling:** Numbness and tingling in the ring finger and little finger are common symptoms. These symptoms fluctuate and worsen when the elbow bends during activities like driving or phone use. Some patients experience nighttime numbness.

text: These symptoms fluctuate and worsen when the elbow bends during activities like driving or phone use. source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Avoid leaning on the elbow or resting the arm on open windows while driving - Keep the elbow straight while sleeping using a towel wrap or backward-worn elbow pad ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination Physical examination tests may include: - **Tinel's test:** Tapping over the nerve at the funny bone; if irritated, it causes a shock sensation in the pinky and ring fingers (though this can occur in normal nerves too) - **Subluxation assessment:** Checking whether the ulnar nerve moves abnormally when bending the elbow - **Positional testing:** Moving the neck, shoulder, elbow, and wrist to identify position-related symptoms - **Sensory and strength evaluation:** Testing hand and finger sensation and strength ### Tests **X-rays:** While most ulnar nerve compression cannot be visualized on X-rays, doctors may use them to detect bone spurs, arthritis, or bony nerve compression.

text: ### Tests **X-rays:** While most ulnar nerve compression cannot be visualized on X-rays, doctors may use them to detect bone spurs, arthritis, or bony nerve compression. **Nerve conduction studies:** These tests determine how well the nerve is working and help identify where it is being compressed, by sending electrical current down the arm to detect slowed conduction at compression sites. They help differentiate between elbow, wrist, or neck compression and identify muscle damage through needle electrode examination of muscles the ulnar nerve controls. ## Treatment Unless nerve compression has caused disability or muscle wasting, nonsurgical treatment is typically attempted first. ### Nonsurgical Treatment Occasionally, doctors prescribe oral steroids for short-term inflammation relief. **Bracing or splinting:** A padded brace or splint worn at night maintains straight elbow positioning.

text: ### Nonsurgical Treatment Occasionally, doctors prescribe oral steroids for short-term inflammation relief. **Bracing or splinting:** A padded brace or splint worn at night maintains straight elbow positioning. **Nerve gliding exercises:** Exercises help the ulnar nerve slide through the cubital tunnel and Guyon's canal, potentially improving symptoms while preventing arm and wrist stiffness. Exercises involve wrist and finger curling toward and away from the body, followed by elbow bending, performed with the arm extended. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery is recommended when: - Nonsurgical methods prove ineffective - Severe nerve compression exists - Nerve compression has caused muscle weakness or damage These outpatient procedures include: - **Cubital tunnel release:** The ligament roof of the cubital tunnel is cut and divided to increase tunnel size and reduce nerve pressure. New tissue growth heals the ligament while maintaining expanded space for nerve movement.

text: These outpatient procedures include: - **Cubital tunnel release:** The ligament roof of the cubital tunnel is cut and divided to increase tunnel size and reduce nerve pressure. New tissue growth heals the ligament while maintaining expanded space for nerve movement. This procedure works best for mild to moderate compression when the nerve doesn't subluxate. - **Ulnar nerve transposition:** The nerve is typically moved from behind the medial epicondyle to a new position in front of it. text: # De Quervain's Tenosynovitis ## Overview De Quervain's tenosynovitis is a painful condition affecting thumb tendons. The condition occurs when tendons that control thumb movement become irritated inside the narrow tunnel they pass through to get from the wrist to the thumb. Pain and tenderness typically develop along the thumb side of the wrist, especially when: - Moving the thumb - Making a fist - Grasping or gripping something - Turning the wrist - Lifting objects with arms extended forward and thumbs pointing upward ## Anatomy Tendons are rope-like structures connecting muscle to bone, enabling movement. Two muscles have tendons running together through a narrow tunnel on the thumb side of the wrist: - **Abductor pollicis longus (APL)**: helps move the thumb away from the hand - **Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)**: helps straighten the thumb

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Abductor pollicis longus (APL)**: helps move the thumb away from the hand - **Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)**: helps straighten the thumb These forearm muscles have tendons wrapped in synovium, a slippery soft tissue layer that provides nutrients and allows smooth gliding. The tendons and sheaths sit within a protective tunnel keeping them close to bone as they cross from wrist to hand. In De Quervain's tenosynovitis, these tendons become irritated and the sheath thickens, causing reduced space. The tendons no longer glide freely, resulting in increased friction and pain during thumb and wrist movements. ## Causes The exact cause remains unclear, though wrist and thumb movements like typing, texting, or lifting can worsen symptoms. Potential risk factors include: - Association with pregnancy and postpartum period (symptoms often appear 4-6 weeks after delivery)

text: # NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s — assessment and management NICE does not publish a guideline specifically titled "degenerative disc disease." The full guideline is published by NICE at nice.org.uk/guidance/ng59; this content reflects that guidance as reproduced on the NCBI Bookshelf. ## Self-Management Healthcare professionals should provide people with advice and information, tailored to their needs and capabilities, to help them self-manage their low back pain, at all steps of the treatment pathway. text: # Dupuytren's Disease ## Overview Dupuytren's disease affects the palmar fascia, which is the fibrous layer of tissue that lies underneath the skin in the palm and fingers. The condition causes this tissue to thicken and contract over time, potentially pulling fingers inward toward the palm. This contraction may result in difficulty straightening fingers, known as a Dupuytren's contracture. In some cases, the worsening contracture interferes with hand function and daily activities, prompting treatment through nonsurgical or surgical interventions. ## Description The palmar fascia normally anchors and stabilizes skin on the palm side of the hand. Without it, palm skin would be as loose as skin on the back of the hand. In Dupuytren's disease, this fascia gradually thickens and shortens.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Without it, palm skin would be as loose as skin on the back of the hand. In Dupuytren's disease, this fascia gradually thickens and shortens. The condition typically begins with lumps of tissue (nodules) forming under the palm skin, potentially followed by pitting — deep dents on the palm surface as diseased tissue pulls on overlying skin. As the disease progresses, fascia bands in the palm develop into thick cords that can tether one or more fingers and the thumb into bent positions, creating a contracture. Although these cords may resemble tendons, tendons are not involved in Dupuytren's. Many contractures progress very slowly over years and may remain mild enough to require no treatment. However, moderate or severe cases make straightening fingers difficult, necessitating treatment to reduce contracture and improve motion. Typically, as contractures worsen, fascial involvement becomes more severe, and treatment success decreases. ## Cause

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: However, moderate or severe cases make straightening fingers difficult, necessitating treatment to reduce contracture and improve motion. Typically, as contractures worsen, fascial involvement becomes more severe, and treatment success decreases. ## Cause The complete cause remains unknown, but evidence strongly suggests genetics plays the most important role. Anecdotal reports describe Dupuytren's developing or worsening following hand injury or surgery, though no solid evidence supports this connection. Similarly, no convincing evidence indicates overuse causes the condition. ### Risk Factors Multiple factors contribute to Dupuytren's development or progression: - **Ancestry:** People of northern European (English, Irish, Scottish, French, Dutch) and Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian, Finnish) descent show higher incidence - **Heredity:** The condition frequently runs in families - **Alcohol use:** Drinking alcohol may be associated with Dupuytren's - **Certain medical conditions:** People with diabetes and seizure disorders have higher rates

text: - **Heredity:** The condition frequently runs in families - **Alcohol use:** Drinking alcohol may be associated with Dupuytren's - **Certain medical conditions:** People with diabetes and seizure disorders have higher rates - **Age:** Incidence increases with advancing age - **Trauma:** The disease may appear or worsen following hand trauma, including surgery ## Symptoms Dupuytren's contracture typically progresses very slowly over years. Signs and symptoms include: **Nodules:** One or more small lumps may develop in the palm. These nodules typically attach to overlying skin and initially feel tender, though tenderness usually diminishes over time. Pitting, or deep dents, may appear in skin near nodules. **Cords:** Nodules may thicken and contract, forming dense, tough tissue cords underneath the skin. These cords can limit or prevent finger and thumb straightening or spreading.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Cords:** Nodules may thicken and contract, forming dense, tough tissue cords underneath the skin. These cords can limit or prevent finger and thumb straightening or spreading. **Contractures:** As underlying tissue tightens, one or more fingers may pull toward the palm, with difficulty spreading them apart. The ring and little fingers are most commonly affected, though any finger or the thumb can be involved. When fingers are affected: - The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint — where the finger meets the hand (knuckle) — is most commonly involved - The proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint — the middle finger joint after the MCP — is the next most common. PIP contractures are harder to treat and less likely to completely recover than MCP contractures - The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint — the last finger joint near the fingernail — is less likely to be affected

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: PIP contractures are harder to treat and less likely to completely recover than MCP contractures - The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint — the last finger joint near the fingernail — is less likely to be affected The disease can be progressive, with increasing finger bending making full straightening difficult. Grasping large objects, placing hands in pockets, or performing simple activities may become challenging. Some patients develop thickened tissue on feet (Ledderhose disease) or penis (Peyronie's disease). Symptoms typically do not occur elsewhere on the body. ## Doctor Examination Your doctor will likely discuss your general health, medical history, and symptoms. Since Dupuytren's can run in families, the doctor may ask about relatives with the disease. During the hand examination, your doctor will typically: - Record nodule and cord locations on your palm - Measure finger and thumb range of motion - Test finger and thumb sensation

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: During the hand examination, your doctor will typically: - Record nodule and cord locations on your palm - Measure finger and thumb range of motion - Test finger and thumb sensation - In some cases, document hand appearance with clinical photographs These measurements may be compared with future measurements to determine if the condition is progressing over time. ## Treatment Currently, no cure exists for Dupuytren's; however, it is not life- or limb-threatening and is not cancer. The condition does not spread to vital organs. Although effects vary by patient, Dupuytren's usually progresses very slowly and may not become problematic for many years. For some patients, the condition may never progress beyond palm lumps. If it does progress, doctors typically recommend nonsurgical treatment first to slow disease progression. ### Nonsurgical Treatment Effectiveness varies by patient. **Splinting:** Although patients often request splints to prevent contracture progression, splinting is not proven to prevent finger contracture progression.

text: ### Nonsurgical Treatment Effectiveness varies by patient. **Splinting:** Although patients often request splints to prevent contracture progression, splinting is not proven to prevent finger contracture progression. Forceful finger stretching is unhelpful and potentially injurious. Splinting may protect surgical sites after Dupuytren's surgery; however, it remains unclear whether splinting reduces recurrent contracture risk or wound tightening during healing. Collagenases are enzymes breaking down collagen. A targeted collagenase specifically breaks down collagen in Dupuytren's cords without damaging other hand structures. When properly injected into a cord, collagenase can rupture the cord, allowing improved finger motion. While collagenase does not completely remove the cord, symptoms improve following treatment. Collagenase treatment involves two steps: - Then, at a separate visit, the doctor manipulates the finger until the cord ruptures This non-operative alternative to surgery offers less pain and swelling than major surgery and may suit patients with multiple medical issues unsuitable for surgery. However, disease recurrence is higher with collagenase than surgery. Other potential complications match surgery risks: infection, nerve or blood vessel injury, pain, and stiffness. **Needle aponeurotomy:** This office procedure with local anesthesia breaks up the Dupuytren's cord using a small needle placed into the cord and moved precisely until completely cutting through it. While not removing the cord, the break allows improved finger motion. Rare complications include infection, nerve or blood vessel injury, pain, and stiffness. ### Surgical Treatment If contracture interferes with hand function, your doctor may recommend surgery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: While not removing the cord, the break allows improved finger motion. Rare complications include infection, nerve or blood vessel injury, pain, and stiffness. ### Surgical Treatment If contracture interferes with hand function, your doctor may recommend surgery. The goal is reducing contracture and improving affected finger motion. Although no known cure exists, surgery aims to "set back the clock" by reducing the cord's restricting effects through disruption or removal. Unfortunately, healing tissues form with similar cord development potential — but hand function gains remain significant. The most commonly performed procedures are: - Fasciotomy - Partial palmar fasciectomy **Fasciotomy:** Your doctor makes a palm incision, then divides thickened cord tissue. Although the cord itself remains, division decreases contracture and increases affected finger movement. Fasciotomy typically uses local anesthetic only, without sleep. After the procedure, the wound often remains open and heals gradually, and a splint is typically worn during recovery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Fasciotomy typically uses local anesthetic only, without sleep. After the procedure, the wound often remains open and heals gradually, and a splint is typically worn during recovery. Because diseased tissue remains unremoved, contracture recurrence may be more likely with fasciotomy than partial palmar fasciectomy. **Partial palmar fasciectomy:** Your doctor makes an incision, then removes as much abnormal tissue and cords as possible to straighten fingers. Multiple incision types exist; however, "zig-zag" incisions are typically used, allowing skin healing without additional contracture. Sometimes the wound heals open gradually on its own after fasciectomy; other cases require skin grafts. A splint may be worn during recovery. Partial palmar fasciectomy is more extensive than fasciotomy, generally requiring more wound care, physical therapy, longer healing time, and greater patient recovery effort, but removes maximum diseased tissue, helping prevent disease recurrence.

text: Partial palmar fasciectomy is more extensive than fasciotomy, generally requiring more wound care, physical therapy, longer healing time, and greater patient recovery effort, but removes maximum diseased tissue, helping prevent disease recurrence. In some very severe cases, doctors may apply a device to the affected finger before surgery that gradually stretches the finger and cords over about six weeks, potentially making subsequent surgery easier, safer, and more effective. The device is removed during the partial palmar fasciectomy. **Complications:** Surgery for Dupuytren's contracture carries risks increasing with contracture severity, number of contractures addressed in a single procedure, and presence of other medical conditions. Possible risks include pain, scarring, nerve and/or blood vessel injury, wound infection, stiffness, loss of sensation (temporary loss may result from stretched contracted nerves), and loss of finger viability or finger loss (rare).

Although surgery aims to improve finger straightening ability, sometimes patients lose the ability to bend involved digits due to stiffness. Elevating the hand above the heart and gently moving fingers decrease swelling and improve stiffness. Physical therapy strengthens finger and hand function, reduces swelling, and aids wound care; hand therapists often create splints for recovery wear. **Outcomes:** Most patients show improved finger movement after surgery. However, because surgery does not "cure" the condition, approximately 20% experience meaningful contracture recurrence. Some patients may require additional surgery. ## Summary In general, Dupuytren's disease treatment can be quite successful.

text: # Elbow (Olecranon) Bursitis ## Overview Elbow bursitis affects the olecranon bursa, a thin, fluid-filled sac that is located at the boney tip of the elbow. The body contains many bursae that serve as cushions between bones and soft tissues, containing lubricating fluid. When the olecranon bursa becomes irritated or inflamed, fluid accumulates and bursitis develops. ## Causes **Trauma:** A forceful blow to the elbow tip can trigger excessive fluid production and swelling. **Prolonged Pressure:** Extended leaning on the elbow against hard surfaces (tables, armrests) causes gradual swelling over months. Occupations like plumbing or HVAC work, requiring prolonged kneeling and elbow pressure, increase vulnerability. Athletic activities such as extended plank holds may also trigger this condition.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Occupations like plumbing or HVAC work, requiring prolonged kneeling and elbow pressure, increase vulnerability. Athletic activities such as extended plank holds may also trigger this condition. **Infection:** Breaks in the skin from insect bites, scrapes, or puncture wounds allow bacteria entry into the bursa sac, producing fluid, redness, swelling, and pain. Untreated infections may develop into pus. Occasionally, infection occurs without obvious skin injury. **Medical Conditions:** Rheumatoid arthritis and gout are associated with elbow bursitis development. ## Symptoms **Swelling:** Initial symptom, though loose elbow skin may delay detection of minor swelling. **Pain:** As swelling increases, bursal stretching causes pain that worsens with direct pressure or bending. Swelling may restrict elbow motion. **Redness and Warmth:** Infected bursae display red and warm skin. Untreated infection risks spreading throughout the arm or into the bloodstream.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Swelling may restrict elbow motion. **Redness and Warmth:** Infected bursae display red and warm skin. Untreated infection risks spreading throughout the arm or into the bloodstream. Infected bursae may spontaneously drain pus. ## Doctor Examination After reviewing symptoms and history, physicians examine the affected arm and elbow. **X-rays:** Doctors may order imaging to identify foreign bodies or bone spurs, which are often found on the tip of the elbow bone (ulna) in patients who have had repeated instances of elbow bursitis. **Fluid Testing:** Doctors may extract bursal fluid samples via needle to determine infection or gout involvement. ## Nonsurgical Treatment **For Infected Bursas:** Doctors may aspirate (withdraw) bursal fluid using a needle, typically performed in-office settings. This relieves symptoms and provides laboratory samples for bacterial identification and antibiotic sensitivity testing. Doctors often prescribe broad-spectrum antibiotics preemptively before specific infection identification.

Casts or prolonged immobilization typically aren't necessary. Specific range-of-motion exercises begin within days.

text: # Femoroacetabular Impingement ## Overview Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a condition where extra bone grows along one or both hip joint bones, creating an irregular shape. This abnormal structure causes the bones to rub together during movement, potentially damaging the joint over time and causing pain that limits activity. ## Anatomy The hip is a ball-and-socket joint consisting of: - The socket (acetabulum), part of the pelvis bone - The ball (femoral head), the upper end of the thighbone A slippery tissue called articular cartilage covers both surfaces, enabling smooth, low-friction movement. The acetabulum is ringed by fibrocartilage called the labrum, which forms a gasket-like seal that stabilizes the joint. ## Description

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The acetabulum is ringed by fibrocartilage called the labrum, which forms a gasket-like seal that stabilizes the joint. ## Description In FAI, bony prominences develop on the femoral head and/or acetabulum either from how the hips formed at birth or from bone overgrowth (bone spurs). This extra bone prevents smooth movement and can eventually tear the labrum and break down articular cartilage, leading to osteoarthritis. ### Types of FAI - **Pincer**: Extra bone extends over the acetabulum's normal rim, potentially crushing the labrum underneath. - **Cam**: The femoral head lacks proper roundness, with a bump grinding against cartilage inside the socket. - **Combined**: Both pincer and cam types are present simultaneously. ## Cause FAI develops because hip bones don't form normally during childhood growth.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Combined**: Both pincer and cam types are present simultaneously. ## Cause FAI develops because hip bones don't form normally during childhood growth. When the hip bones are shaped abnormally, there is little that can be done to prevent FAI. Some people never experience problems despite having the condition, though symptoms typically indicate cartilage or labrum damage that may worsen. Athletic individuals may experience pain earlier due to more vigorous hip joint use, though exercise doesn't cause FAI. ## Symptoms Common FAI symptoms include: - Pain (often in the groin or outer hip area) - Stiffness - Limping Turning, twisting, and squatting may trigger sharp pain, though symptoms sometimes appear as a dull ache. ## Home Remedies Initially, identify activities that may have caused pain and modify them while allowing the hip to rest. However, persistent symptoms require medical evaluation, as the longer painful symptoms go untreated, the more damage FAI can cause in the hip.

A positive result reproduces the hip pain. ### Imaging Tests - **X-rays**: Show abnormally shaped bones and signs of arthritis. - **CT scans**: Provide more detailed images of the hip's abnormal shape. - **MRI scans**: Better visualize soft tissue damage to the labrum and cartilage, especially with injected dye. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment - **Activity changes**: Avoid activities causing symptoms. - **Physical therapy**: Specific exercises improve hip range of motion and strengthen supporting muscles, relieving stress on injured structures. ### Surgical Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment - **Activity changes**: Avoid activities causing symptoms. - **Physical therapy**: Specific exercises improve hip range of motion and strengthen supporting muscles, relieving stress on injured structures. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery is recommended when tests show joint damage and nonsurgical treatment fails. Arthroscopic surgery using small incisions allows surgeons to repair labrum and cartilage damage while trimming the acetabulum's bony rim and shaving the femoral head bump. Severe cases may require open surgery with larger incisions. ## Long-Term Outcomes Surgery can successfully reduce impingement symptoms and prevent future joint damage. However, not all of the damage can be completely fixed by surgery, especially if treatment has been put off and the damage is severe. Although surgery offers no guarantee of success, it currently represents the best treatment approach for painful FAI. ## Future Developments Improving surgical results suggest doctors will recommend earlier intervention.

text: # Fibromyalgia Fibromyalgia, also called fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS), is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body. Around 1 in 20 people may be affected by fibromyalgia to some degree, and it's more common in women than men. It usually develops between the ages of 25 and 55, but can also affect children and older people. Diagnosis can be difficult as there's no specific test for it. ## Symptoms The main symptom is widespread pain, which can vary in severity, sometimes depending on the weather, how stressed you are, and how physically active you are that day. - **Widespread pain** - pain felt throughout the body, though it may be worse in particular areas such as the back or neck; described as an ache, a burning sensation, or a sharp, stabbing pain

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: - **Widespread pain** - pain felt throughout the body, though it may be worse in particular areas such as the back or neck; described as an ache, a burning sensation, or a sharp, stabbing pain - **Increased sensitivity to pain** - hyperalgesia (an extreme sensitivity to pain) and allodynia (pain caused by things that should not be painful, such as a light touch); people may also be sensitive to smoke, certain foods, and bright lights - **Stiffness** - may be most severe when you've been in the same position for a long period, such as when you first wake up in the morning - **Fatigue** - can range from a mild, tired feeling to the exhaustion often felt during a flu-like illness, and can come on suddenly - **Poor sleep quality** - the condition can prevent you sleeping deeply enough to feel properly refreshed, even after a full night's sleep

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: - **Poor sleep quality** - the condition can prevent you sleeping deeply enough to feel properly refreshed, even after a full night's sleep - **Cognitive problems ("fibro-fog")** - problems with memory and concentration, and slowed or muddled speech - Headaches - Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) - Feeling dizzy and clumsy - Sensitivity to temperature - Restless legs syndrome - Tingling, numbness, prickling or burning sensations in the hands and feet - Painful periods in women - Anxiety and depression Symptoms can fluctuate depending on time and circumstances, and can sometimes suddenly improve or get worse. ## Causes The exact cause of fibromyalgia isn't known, but it's thought to be related to abnormal levels of certain chemicals in the brain and changes in the way the central nervous system processes pain messages carried around the body. It's also thought some people are more likely to develop fibromyalgia because of genes inherited from their parents.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: It's also thought some people are more likely to develop fibromyalgia because of genes inherited from their parents. In many cases, the condition seems to be triggered by a physically or emotionally stressful event, such as an injury or infection. ## Treatment Treatment for fibromyalgia aims to ease symptoms and improve quality of life. No single treatment works for all symptoms - a combination is often needed. - **Exercise** - regular exercise has been shown to help reduce pain and improve overall quality of life; a GP may be able to refer you to a supervised exercise programme - **Talking therapies:** - Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) - learning to accept what is out of your control and commit to making changes that will improve your life - Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) - a talking therapy that can help you manage your problems by changing the way you think and behave

text: - Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) - a talking therapy that can help you manage your problems by changing the way you think and behave - **Acupuncture** can reduce pain and improve quality of life in some people with long-term pain, though the benefits typically last only up to 3 months

text: # NICE Guideline NG193: Chronic Pain (Primary and Secondary) in Over 16s - Assessment of All Chronic Pain and Management of Chronic Primary Pain (Recommendations) Published: 7 April 2021. Note: this guideline does not use the term "fibromyalgia" as a section heading; instead it defines fibromyalgia as a type of chronic primary pain and gives recommendations for managing chronic primary pain as a category. Per the guideline's own "Terms used in this guideline" section: "Fibromyalgia (chronic widespread pain) is a type of chronic primary pain." The extracts below focus on the definition of chronic primary pain and the management recommendations (section 1.2) most relevant to fibromyalgia/chronic widespread pain. ## 1.1 Assessing All Types of Chronic Pain

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ## 1.1 Assessing All Types of Chronic Pain This guideline covers chronic pain that "persists or recurs for more than 3 months," including chronic primary pain (in which no underlying condition adequately accounts for the pain or its impact) and chronic secondary pain, which can coexist. "Think about a diagnosis of chronic primary pain if there is no clear underlying (secondary) cause or the pain or its impact is out of proportion to any observable injury or disease, particularly when the pain is causing significant distress and disability." Recognise that an initial diagnosis of chronic primary pain may change with time, and re-evaluate if the presentation changes. Offer a person-centred assessment to identify factors contributing to the pain and how it affects the person's life, including lifestyle, day-to-day activities, work and sleep, physical and psychological wellbeing, stressful life events, and social interaction.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: Offer a person-centred assessment to identify factors contributing to the pain and how it affects the person's life, including lifestyle, day-to-day activities, work and sleep, physical and psychological wellbeing, stressful life events, and social interaction. Discuss with the person and their family or carers that symptoms may fluctuate and flare-up, that a reason for the pain may not be identified, that pain may not improve or may need ongoing management, and that quality of life can still improve even if pain remains unchanged. ## 1.2 Managing Chronic Primary Pain ### Exercise Programmes and Physical Activity "Offer a supervised group exercise programme to people aged 16 years and over to manage chronic primary pain. Take people's specific needs, preferences and abilities into account." Encourage people with chronic primary pain "to remain physically active for longer-term general health benefits." ### Psychological Therapy Consider acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for pain, delivered by healthcare professionals with appropriate training.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ### Psychological Therapy Consider acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for pain, delivered by healthcare professionals with appropriate training. "Do not offer biofeedback to people aged 16 years and over to manage chronic primary pain." ### Acupuncture Consider a single course of acupuncture or dry needling (within a traditional Chinese or Western system) only if it is delivered in a community setting, by a band 7 (or lower) healthcare professional with appropriate training, and made up of no more than 5 hours of healthcare professional time (or delivered equivalently for the same or lower cost). ### Electrical Physical Modalities "Do not offer any of the following to people aged 16 years and over to manage chronic primary pain because there is no evidence of benefit: TENS; ultrasound; interferential therapy." ### Pharmacological Management ## Terms Used in This Guideline

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: "Do not offer any of the following to people aged 16 years and over to manage chronic primary pain because there is no evidence of benefit: TENS; ultrasound; interferential therapy." ### Pharmacological Management ## Terms Used in This Guideline **Chronic pain**: Pain that persists or recurs for more than 3 months, including both chronic primary and chronic secondary pain, which can coexist. **Chronic primary pain**: Has no clear underlying condition, or the pain/impact is out of proportion to any observable injury or disease. "The mechanisms underlying chronic primary pain are only partially understood." This guideline is consistent with the ICD-11 definition. "Fibromyalgia (chronic widespread pain) is a type of chronic primary pain." text: # Sprained Finger ## Overview A sprained finger occurs when the ligaments supporting the finger joint(s) are stretched. This commonly happens when a strong force bends the finger backwards, away from the palm, such as: - When falling onto an outstretched hand - When the finger is forced to the side or hit on end (i.e., "jammed"), such as while catching a ball Treatment for a sprained finger may involve a short course of immobilization followed by guided return to motion. For more severe sprains where ligaments holding the joint together are torn, surgery may be needed to restore stability to the joint. ## Anatomy Each finger (not the thumb) has three bones with joints between them: - The distal phalanx is the last bone of the finger at the very tip. It connects to the middle phalanx, the middle bone of the finger, via the DIP joint.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - The distal phalanx is the last bone of the finger at the very tip. It connects to the middle phalanx, the middle bone of the finger, via the DIP joint. - The middle phalanx connects to the proximal phalanx, the bone in the finger closest to the hand, via the PIP joint. - The proximal phalanx connects the finger to the hand (metacarpal) via the MCP joint. While each of these joints is slightly different from the others, they share several similarities: - On the sides of each finger are collateral ligaments. Ligaments are strong, fibrous tissues that typically connect bones to other bones. The ligaments in the finger help keep the bones in proper position while allowing for motion at the joints. - On the palm-side of each finger joint is a strong thick structure called the volar plate. - Surrounding each finger joint is a structure called the joint capsule.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - On the palm-side of each finger joint is a strong thick structure called the volar plate. - Surrounding each finger joint is a structure called the joint capsule. The collateral ligaments, volar plate, and joint capsule work together to allow motion of the finger joints while keeping the joints aligned and stable. Sprains of a finger may affect one or several of these structures. ## Description Most finger sprains involve the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, which is the joint in the middle of the finger. - An injury to this joint typically causes pain and swelling. - In severe cases, it may make the joint unstable. - Following a sprain, the finger typically becomes stiff, and it can be hard to completely flex the finger (i.e., make a fist) and extend the finger (i.e., extend or straighten the finger).

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Following a sprain, the finger typically becomes stiff, and it can be hard to completely flex the finger (i.e., make a fist) and extend the finger (i.e., extend or straighten the finger). Sprains may also involve the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint of the finger, where the finger attaches to the hand, or the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint of the finger, the last joint of the finger closest to the fingertip. Symptoms of these sprains are similar to the symptoms of PIP joint sprains but commonly improve faster. PIP joint sprains may take up to 12 months to fully heal. Swelling may remain for a long time. ## Grades of Finger Sprains Sprains occur when the ligament is stretched, which can also cause small, incomplete tears in the fibers that make up the ligament. Beyond a sprain, ligaments can also be torn completely either:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Grades of Finger Sprains Sprains occur when the ligament is stretched, which can also cause small, incomplete tears in the fibers that make up the ligament. Beyond a sprain, ligaments can also be torn completely either: - In the middle of the ligament, or - At the end(s) of the ligament, where it can pull off of the bone Sprains are graded based on the degree of injury to the ligament: - **Grade 1 sprain (mild).** The ligament is stretched, but not torn. - **Grade 2 sprain (moderate).** The ligament is partially torn. This type of injury may involve some loss of function. - **Grade 3 sprain (severe).** The ligament is completely torn or is pulled off its attachment to the bone. These are significant injuries that require medical or surgical care.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This type of injury may involve some loss of function. - **Grade 3 sprain (severe).** The ligament is completely torn or is pulled off its attachment to the bone. These are significant injuries that require medical or surgical care. If the ligament tears away from the bone, it may take a small chip of the bone with it. This is called an avulsion fracture. ## Cause Any strong force that bends the finger backwards or sideways, or hits the finger on end (i.e., "jams" the finger), can stretch or tear the ligaments of finger joints. This most often occurs by falling onto an outstretched hand. Sprained fingers are common in athletes who participate in sports that involve catching and throwing a ball, such as football, baseball, softball, and basketball. However, they may occur during everyday activities, falls, or other accidental traumas to the hand. ## Symptoms

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: However, they may occur during everyday activities, falls, or other accidental traumas to the hand. ## Symptoms - Depending on the severity of the sprain, pain may or may not occur at the time of the injury. - Bruising, tenderness, and swelling around the affected finger joint may develop. - If a ligament is completely torn, the finger joint may feel loose or unstable. It is important for a doctor to evaluate even a mild finger sprain if it does not improve quickly. - Proper and prompt diagnosis and treatment of a finger injury is necessary to avoid long-term complications, including chronic pain, instability, and arthritis. - In addition, some finger sprains are not sprains at all; they are misdiagnosed fractures or dislocations of the finger, which need to be addressed promptly to avoid permanent dysfunction. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - In addition, some finger sprains are not sprains at all; they are misdiagnosed fractures or dislocations of the finger, which need to be addressed promptly to avoid permanent dysfunction. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination The doctor will ask how and when the injury occurred and ask the patient to describe symptoms, then carefully examine the finger and hand. To help determine if ligaments in the finger are completely torn, the doctor will move the finger in different positions to test the stability of the joint(s). If the joint(s) is loose and unstable, it is an indication that the ligament may be completely torn. ### Imaging Tests **X-rays.** X-rays provide images of dense structures, such as bone. X-rays of the finger and hand may be ordered to ensure there is no avulsion fracture or any broken bones. A special type of X-ray called a stress X-ray may also be ordered.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: X-rays of the finger and hand may be ordered to ensure there is no avulsion fracture or any broken bones. A special type of X-ray called a stress X-ray may also be ordered. During this test, the doctor applies tension to the finger while it is being X-rayed to learn more about the stability of the joint(s). **Other imaging tests.** If more information is needed, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan or an ultrasound may be ordered. These tests can help determine the severity of the injury and inform decisions about treatment and return to activity. ## Treatment Treatment for a sprained finger depends on the severity of the injury. ### Home Care Mild finger sprains will usually improve with home treatment that includes the RICE protocol: - **Rest.** Try not to use the hand strenuously for at least 48 hours. - **Ice.** Apply ice immediately after the injury to keep the swelling down.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Rest.** Try not to use the hand strenuously for at least 48 hours. - **Ice.** Apply ice immediately after the injury to keep the swelling down. Use cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly to the skin. - **Compression.** Wear an elastic compression bandage to reduce swelling. Do not make the bandage too tight, as this could cut off blood flow to the finger. - **Elevation.** As often as possible, rest with the hand raised up higher than the heart. However, if pain and swelling continue for more than 48 hours (2 days), see a doctor. ### Nonsurgical Treatment For a moderate sprain, the doctor may briefly immobilize the finger and then transition to buddy strapping. Buddy straps connect the injured finger to a neighboring finger using the healthy neighbor as a moving splint for the injured finger.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: For a moderate sprain, the doctor may briefly immobilize the finger and then transition to buddy strapping. Buddy straps connect the injured finger to a neighboring finger using the healthy neighbor as a moving splint for the injured finger. This provides support while allowing the injured finger to move to avoid stiffness. To ease pain and swelling, a cold pack can be applied to the finger several times a day for 20 minutes at a time for 2 to 3 days after the injury. Do not apply ice directly to the skin. Depending on the severity of the injury, the buddy straps may need to be worn at all times. It is important to avoid applying any pressure or resistance to the finger until permitted by the doctor. Because immobilization may cause stiffness in an injured finger, the doctor may recommend some stretching exercises to help regain full range of motion when ready. ### Surgical Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: It is important to avoid applying any pressure or resistance to the finger until permitted by the doctor. Because immobilization may cause stiffness in an injured finger, the doctor may recommend some stretching exercises to help regain full range of motion when ready. ### Surgical Treatment For a severe sprain or tear, surgery may be needed to restore the stability of the finger joint and help regain function. Surgery involves: - Reconnecting the ligament to the bone and/or - Repairing the avulsion fracture (ligament with a pulled-off piece of bone attached to it) using a pin, screw, or special bone anchor. After surgery, a short arm cast or a splint may need to be worn for a few weeks to protect the ligament while it heals. Therapy will then likely begin to get the finger moving and avoid stiffness. ## Outcomes When diagnosed and treated properly, most finger sprains will heal well with few complications.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Therapy will then likely begin to get the finger moving and avoid stiffness. ## Outcomes When diagnosed and treated properly, most finger sprains will heal well with few complications. However, ignoring a sprained finger with the hope that it will heal on its own may lead to long-term problems, including chronic instability, weakness, stiffness, and arthritis. In addition, as mentioned above, some finger fractures or dislocations are misdiagnosed as finger sprains. Finger fractures and dislocations may require urgent treatment to avoid permanent dysfunction. It is therefore important to be seen promptly by a doctor for concerning finger injuries. Most finger sprains improve over time. This may take weeks to months. Symptoms of PIP joint sprains — including stiffness, swelling, and pain — may linger for up to 1 year or longer.
