text: # Progressive Collapsing Foot Deformity ## Overview Progressive collapsing foot deformity (PCFD), previously called adult acquired flatfoot (AAF), is a complex foot and ankle condition marked by flattening of the arch along with additional, less obvious structural changes. It is also referred to as posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (PTTD). While several interconnected factors likely contribute, the disorder typically originates from problems with the posterior tibial tendon, a key structure that helps support the arch. When this tendon becomes inflamed or torn, it loses its ability to adequately stabilize the arch, leading to flatfoot. ## Description This condition covers a spectrum of presentations. It may initially appear as a barely noticeable change with minimal discomfort, but it can progress into a severely painful, functionally limiting, and significantly deformed flatfoot. In the earlier stages, most people respond well to conservative treatment involving orthotic devices and supportive braces, without needing surgery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: In the earlier stages, most people respond well to conservative treatment involving orthotic devices and supportive braces, without needing surgery. When conservative measures are not enough, surgery can reduce pain and restore function. Surgical approaches vary widely depending on the disease stage and degree of deformity, ranging from relatively simple procedures — such as removing inflamed tissue or repairing a minor tendon tear — to complex reconstructive surgery. Most patients experience some lasting activity limitations even after surgery. ## Anatomy Several structures work together to maintain the normal arch of the foot, including tendons (which connect muscle to bone) and ligaments (which connect bone to bone). Two structures are particularly important: **Posterior tibial tendon (PTT).** This tendon connects the tibialis posterior calf muscle to bones along the inner arch of the foot. It runs behind the medial malleolus (the bony bump on the inside of the ankle), where it can sometimes be felt or seen.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: It runs behind the medial malleolus (the bony bump on the inside of the ankle), where it can sometimes be felt or seen. Its main jobs are to help raise and support the arch during walking. It also helps lift the toes and rotate the foot and ankle inward. **Spring ligament.** This ligament connects the calcaneus (heel bone) to the navicular bone (a bone on the inner side of the foot) and is an important arch-supporting structure. It is not entirely clear whether damage to these structures causes flatfoot or results from it, though PTT dysfunction is generally considered a key underlying mechanism. Occasionally, injury to the spring ligament happens first. When PCFD develops without a preceding spring ligament injury, that ligament typically becomes torn or significantly stretched as the flatfoot progresses. In addition to the spring ligament, smaller ligaments connecting the bones on the inner side of the foot provide extra arch support.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: In addition to the spring ligament, smaller ligaments connecting the bones on the inner side of the foot provide extra arch support. The deltoid ligament — a large, strong ligament connecting the ankle bones to the heel and inner foot bones — becomes increasingly stretched and weakened as the flatfoot worsens, ultimately contributing to a flatfoot deformity that involves the ankle joint itself. ## Cause There are multiple possible causes of PCFD, and the exact cause likely varies from patient to patient. Potential contributing mechanisms include: - Midfoot arthritis or weakened ligaments can place excessive stress on the posterior tibial tendon, leading to gradual tearing - Traumatic events such as falls can cause sudden tearing or inflammation of the PTT - Overuse can cause tendon tearing; people who take part in demanding sports (basketball, tennis, soccer) may develop tendon tears from repetitive stress, while non-athletic individuals can develop similar problems over time, particularly when regularly wearing unsupportive shoes like sandals

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Overuse can cause tendon tearing; people who take part in demanding sports (basketball, tennis, soccer) may develop tendon tears from repetitive stress, while non-athletic individuals can develop similar problems over time, particularly when regularly wearing unsupportive shoes like sandals - A strong genetic predisposition likely contributes to PCFD Regardless of the initial cause: - Ongoing inflammation and weakness of the PTT reduce its ability to support the arch during walking - The arch begins to sag, transferring excess force to secondary arch-supporting structures, including the spring ligament - Continued stretching and weakening of these structures requires the PTT to work even harder, creating a cycle that worsens over time - Eventually, the tendon and ligaments can tear completely; without their support, the bones of the foot shift substantially, causing pain from bone compression and arthritic changes The literature notes increased prevalence of PCFD in women and in people over the age of 40.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The literature notes increased prevalence of PCFD in women and in people over the age of 40. Other contributing factors include excess body weight, diabetes, and high blood pressure. ## Symptoms - Pain in the arch or along the inner side of the foot and ankle where the PTT is located; swelling may occur along the tendon if it is inflamed or torn; pain often develops before any visible structural changes - Pain and weakness during activity; standing or walking for extended periods becomes difficult for some people; vigorous or high-impact activities like running are especially challenging; unsupportive footwear worsens symptoms; beyond pain, weakness may show up when trying to lift the toes or stand on one foot - Outer (lateral) ankle pain; as the arch flattens further, the heel bone shifts increasingly outward relative to the ankle; enough shift allows the heel bone to press against the outer ankle bone, a process called impingement

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Outer (lateral) ankle pain; as the arch flattens further, the heel bone shifts increasingly outward relative to the ankle; enough shift allows the heel bone to press against the outer ankle bone, a process called impingement The most common location for pain follows the path of the posterior tibial tendon, running along the back and inner side of the foot and ankle. ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination The doctor will take a full medical history and ask about your symptoms. The exam looks for the following signs: - **Posterior tibial tendon swelling and tenderness.** Tenderness and swelling typically localize behind and below the inner ankle bone; the arch itself is often painful. - **Changes in foot shape.** The exam requires the patient to stand.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Changes in foot shape.** The exam requires the patient to stand. Flattening of the arch is usually the first and most noticeable change; as the deformity progresses, additional changes appear, including the heel shifting outward from the ankle and the toes rotating outward relative to the foot and ankle. These changes become visible when viewed from behind. In a healthy foot, the heel lines up straight beneath the calf and only the fourth and fifth toes are visible from behind; a flatfoot shows the heel angled outward relative to the calf and ankle, along with more toes visible from behind — called the "too many toes" sign. - **Reduced ability to rise on one heel.** Successfully standing on one leg and rising onto the toes requires a functioning posterior tibial tendon; inability to do this suggests tendon damage. - **Reduced flexibility.** Doctors check how much the foot can move side to side; flexibility affects treatment planning, since rigid and flexible feet require different approaches.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Reduced flexibility.** Doctors check how much the foot can move side to side; flexibility affects treatment planning, since rigid and flexible feet require different approaches. - **Restricted ankle motion.** Upward movement of the ankle (dorsiflexion) is often limited in flatfoot, usually due to tight calf muscles. ### Imaging **X-rays** provide detailed images of bone that identify arthritic changes and structural misalignments contributing to symptoms. Flatfoot deformity typically shows up on standard X-rays as long as they are taken while the patient is standing. Surgical planning uses measurements taken from X-rays to help determine the best procedure. **CT scan.** CT functions as a three-dimensional X-ray, providing more detailed bone images that can reveal subtle changes not visible on standard X-rays, helping guide surgical planning for deformity correction. Ideally, a weight-bearing CT is used, although this specialized equipment is not always available.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Ideally, a weight-bearing CT is used, although this specialized equipment is not always available. **MRI** shows soft tissue (tendon, ligament) much better than X-ray or CT and can reveal inflammatory or degenerative changes; it is particularly useful when the diagnosis is uncertain. **Ultrasound** uses high-frequency sound waves to create images of structures; it can show the posterior tibial tendon but is generally not needed to confirm a flatfoot diagnosis. ## Nonsurgical Treatment Most symptomatic patients get satisfactory results from appropriate conservative treatment. Pain relief can take more than three months even with early treatment. Longstanding symptoms often require six additional months of treatment before substantial improvement occurs. ### Rest - Reducing or eliminating activities that make pain worse is the foundation of treatment - Low-impact exercise substitutes such as cycling, elliptical machines, and swimming place little stress on the foot, allowing most people to stay active comfortably - Losing weight reduces stress on the arch and its supporting structures

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Low-impact exercise substitutes such as cycling, elliptical machines, and swimming place little stress on the foot, allowing most people to stay active comfortably - Losing weight reduces stress on the arch and its supporting structures ### Ice Applying a cold pack to the area of the posterior tibial tendon with the most pain for 20-minute intervals, three to four times a day, reduces swelling. Ice should never touch the skin directly. Applying cold directly over the tendon after exercise reduces surrounding inflammation. Topical anti-inflammatory preparations applied directly to the affected area may provide additional benefit. ### Orthotic Devices Orthotics are shoe inserts designed to support and position the foot, making walking more comfortable, and are the most common conservative treatment for flatfoot. - Off-the-shelf orthotics are enough for people with mild changes in foot shape; many options on the market target arch support and flatfoot-related pain relief; a doctor's recommendation on specific over-the-counter products can be helpful

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Off-the-shelf orthotics are enough for people with mild changes in foot shape; many options on the market target arch support and flatfoot-related pain relief; a doctor's recommendation on specific over-the-counter products can be helpful - Custom-made orthotics may be needed for moderate-to-severe structural changes; while more expensive, custom versions allow for more precise foot positioning ### Bracing - Simple lace-up ankle braces available commercially may help mild-to-moderate flatfoot by supporting the ankle and back of the foot, reducing stress on the tendon - More advanced flatfoot involving stiffness or arthritis may require larger bracing systems (Arizona braces, Richie braces) that can be customized and often let people with significant deformities avoid surgery ### Immobilization A short leg cast or protective walking boot may be used for six to eight weeks, allowing the tendon to rest and inflammation to settle. Casting causes additional weakening of lower-leg muscles, so it is generally used only when other conservative measures have failed.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: A short leg cast or protective walking boot may be used for six to eight weeks, allowing the tendon to rest and inflammation to settle. Casting causes additional weakening of lower-leg muscles, so it is generally used only when other conservative measures have failed. Doctors may recommend a period of immobilization in a boot or cast followed by bracing once acute pain and swelling have decreased. ### Physical Therapy Programs that strengthen the tendon can benefit people with mild posterior tibial tendon disease. Stretching the calf and Achilles tendon to address ankle tightness is an essential part of any flatfoot treatment program. Cortisone, a powerful anti-inflammatory, may be injected into painful areas. ## Surgical Treatment Surgery may be considered when pain persists despite months of appropriate nonsurgical treatment. The choice of procedure depends on how severe the deformity is, whether arthritis is present, and how much motion remains in the foot.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Surgical Treatment Surgery may be considered when pain persists despite months of appropriate nonsurgical treatment. The choice of procedure depends on how severe the deformity is, whether arthritis is present, and how much motion remains in the foot. Reconstructive surgery can be quite complex; there are many procedures, and combining several is often necessary to address the different components of PCFD: ### Tenosynovectomy (Cleaning the Posterior Tibial Tendon) Used for less advanced disease — with tendon pain and swelling but without major changes in foot shape. Surgically, the doctor removes inflamed tissue surrounding the tendon and repairs any minor tears present at the same time. This procedure can be done alone or alongside other procedures; the main risk is continued tendon deterioration and recurring symptoms. ### Gastrocnemius Recession or Achilles Lengthening These procedures lengthen the calf muscle or Achilles tendon, benefiting people with tightness and limited upward ankle motion.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Gastrocnemius Recession or Achilles Lengthening These procedures lengthen the calf muscle or Achilles tendon, benefiting people with tightness and limited upward ankle motion. They help prevent the flatfoot from recurring but may cause weakness when pushing off the foot or climbing stairs. Small incisions behind the calf allow the procedure to be performed; complication rates are low but include nerve damage and muscle weakness. These operations are frequently combined with other flatfoot correction procedures. ### Tendon Transfer For flexible flatfoot, tendon transfer reconstructs the function of a damaged posterior tibial tendon. This involves either removing the diseased tendon and replacing it with another foot tendon, or — when PTT disease is less severe — attaching a transferred tendon to the remaining tendon.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This involves either removing the diseased tendon and replacing it with another foot tendon, or — when PTT disease is less severe — attaching a transferred tendon to the remaining tendon. Commonly transferred tendons include the flexor digitorum longus (which flexes the smaller toes) and occasionally the flexor hallucis longus (which flexes the big toe); toe motion continues after transfer and gait changes typically go unnoticed. Although a transferred tendon functionally replaces the damaged PTT, the shape of the foot is not fully normalized. Additional procedures to correct foot shape are usually needed; without correcting the shape, ongoing stress leads to re-tearing. ### Ligament Repair Arch-supporting ligaments often become torn or, at minimum, stretched and weakened. In flexible arch presentations, the surgeon may repair a ligament (particularly the spring ligament) as part of the surgery. - If the ligament is substantially healthy, it may be repaired using native tissue alone

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: In flexible arch presentations, the surgeon may repair a ligament (particularly the spring ligament) as part of the surgery. - If the ligament is substantially healthy, it may be repaired using native tissue alone - Most cases require additional reinforcing material to reconstruct the ligament, including strong sutures Similar to tendon transfer, ligament repair typically has to be combined with other procedures because continued stretching and tearing recur without correcting the shape of the foot. ### Osteotomy (Reshaping the Bone) Osteotomies reshape the bones of a flexible flatfoot, creating a more normal arch. Shape correction is important because it reduces the ongoing stress on the posterior tibial tendon, spring ligament, and other arch-supporting structures. - A common calcaneal osteotomy involves cutting the heel bone and repositioning it from its outward position back beneath the center of the ankle

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - A common calcaneal osteotomy involves cutting the heel bone and repositioning it from its outward position back beneath the center of the ankle - Other calcaneal osteotomy techniques involve lengthening the outer side of the heel to help centralize the toes and correct the "too many toes" deformity - Additional osteotomies of the foot and toe bones may be necessary to fully restore the arch shape Some osteotomies require bone grafting material to fill gaps and help the bone heal; the bone fragments are held in place with screws or metal plates. ### Arthrodesis (Bone Fusion) Stiff flatfoot or significant arthritic changes in key foot joints call for a different approach, since the foot is not flexible enough for successful osteotomy and tendon-transfer methods. Joint fusion realigns the foot's structure and eliminates arthritis.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Stiff flatfoot or significant arthritic changes in key foot joints call for a different approach, since the foot is not flexible enough for successful osteotomy and tendon-transfer methods. Joint fusion realigns the foot's structure and eliminates arthritis. The cartilage is removed and the bone fragments are fixed in a corrected position; the bones eventually fuse into a single continuous structure, eliminating joint-related pain. Screws and metal plates hold the fragments in place while they fuse. A rigid flatfoot may require fusing the heel bone and ankle bone in a realigned position; restoring the arch may also require fusing bones in the middle of the foot. Although fusion eliminates motion between the fused bones, people who need this surgery typically already have a rigid deformity with little remaining motion; walking and pain — particularly outer ankle pain from arthritis and impingement — should improve substantially. Motion above and below the ankle typically shows minimal impairment.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Motion above and below the ankle typically shows minimal impairment. With any fusion, complete healing of the bone sometimes fails (nonunion), which may require repeat surgery. ### Ankle-Specific Flatfoot Surgery Severe, advanced flatfoot occasionally progresses to involve the ankle joint, causing instability or arthritis. - Simple ankle joint instability without arthritis may prompt repair of the deltoid ligament (the main ligament on the inner side of the ankle) - Arthritic or stiff ankle joints may need more extensive procedures, including ankle replacement or fusion, to address both deformity and pain ### Complication Considerations - Incomplete pain relief is the most common post-operative complaint; some people are unsatisfied with the appearance of the foot after surgery, expecting it to look completely "normal." It's important to understand that surgery often focuses on preventing worsening deformity and pain, rather than eliminating all pain and restoring a perfect appearance; discussing realistic expectations with the surgeon beforehand is valuable

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Incomplete pain relief is the most common post-operative complaint; some people are unsatisfied with the appearance of the foot after surgery, expecting it to look completely "normal." It's important to understand that surgery often focuses on preventing worsening deformity and pain, rather than eliminating all pain and restoring a perfect appearance; discussing realistic expectations with the surgeon beforehand is valuable - Nonunion (failure of the bone to fuse) can complicate both osteotomies and fusions, sometimes requiring additional procedures to achieve bone healing - Infection at the surgical site is another possible complication People with diabetes and those who use tobacco have a higher risk of complications. ### Surgical Outcomes Most people achieve satisfactory results from surgery; motion capacity and flatfoot severity before surgery are important factors in the outcome — greater severity correlates with a longer recovery and a lower likelihood of returning to sports. Most people need at least six months for healing and substantial pain improvement. Getting the best surgical outcome requires:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Most people need at least six months for healing and substantial pain improvement. Getting the best surgical outcome requires: - Following the surgeon's instructions after surgery (critically, avoiding weight-bearing until cleared) - Reducing stress on the foot (weight loss, avoiding high-impact activity) - Using supportive footwear - Reducing risk factors for complications (quitting smoking, managing diabetes)

text: # Frozen Shoulder (Adhesive Capsulitis) ## Overview Frozen shoulder, also called adhesive capsulitis, causes pain and stiffness in the shoulder. Over time, the shoulder becomes very hard to move. After a period of worsening symptoms, a frozen shoulder tends to get better, although full recovery may take up to 3 years. Physical therapy, with a focus on shoulder flexibility, is the primary treatment recommendation. Frozen shoulder most commonly affects people between the ages of 40 and 60, and occurs in women more often than men. People with diabetes and thyroid conditions are at an increased risk for developing frozen shoulder, though it can happen to anyone at any time, sometimes after an injury or surgery. ## Anatomy The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint made up of the humerus (upper arm bone), scapula (shoulder blade), and clavicle (collarbone). The head of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow socket in the shoulder blade.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The head of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow socket in the shoulder blade. Strong connective tissue called the shoulder capsule surrounds the joint, and synovial fluid lubricates the capsule and joint to help it move easily. ## Description In frozen shoulder, the shoulder capsule thickens and becomes stiff and tight. Thick bands of tissue — called adhesions — develop, and in many cases there is less synovial fluid in the joint. The hallmark signs are severe pain and being unable to move the shoulder, either on your own or with help. It develops in three stages: - **Stage 1 — Freezing**: Pain slowly worsens, and as it worsens the shoulder loses range of motion. This stage typically lasts 6 weeks to 9 months. - **Stage 2 — Frozen**: Pain may actually improve, but stiffness remains. Daily activities may be very difficult during the 4-to-6-month "frozen" stage.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This stage typically lasts 6 weeks to 9 months. - **Stage 2 — Frozen**: Pain may actually improve, but stiffness remains. Daily activities may be very difficult during the 4-to-6-month "frozen" stage. - **Stage 3 — Thawing**: Shoulder motion slowly improves. Complete return to normal or close to normal strength and motion typically takes 6 months to 2 years. ## Cause The causes of frozen shoulder are not fully understood, and there is no clear connection to arm dominance or occupation. Risk factors include: - **Diabetes**: Frozen shoulder occurs much more often in people with diabetes, and diabetic patients tend to have greater stiffness that lasts longer before "thawing." - **Other diseases**: Hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Parkinson's disease, and cardiac disease are associated with frozen shoulder.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Other diseases**: Hypothyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Parkinson's disease, and cardiac disease are associated with frozen shoulder. - **Immobilization**: Frozen shoulder can develop after a shoulder has been held in one position without moving for a period of time due to surgery, a fracture, or other injury. Moving the shoulder soon after injury or surgery is one measure used to help prevent it. ## Symptoms Pain from frozen shoulder is usually dull or aching, is typically worse early in the disease and when moving the arm, and is usually located over the outer shoulder and sometimes the upper arm. ## Doctor Examination After discussing symptoms and medical history, the doctor examines the shoulder by moving it in all directions to check "passive range of motion" (when someone else moves the shoulder) and comparing this to "active range of motion" (moving it yourself). People with frozen shoulder have limited range of motion both actively and passively.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: People with frozen shoulder have limited range of motion both actively and passively. Imaging tests may help rule out other causes of stiffness and pain: - **X-rays**: May show other problems such as arthritis. - **MRI and ultrasound**: Not required to diagnose frozen shoulder, but may help identify other soft-tissue injuries such as a rotator cuff tear. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Frozen shoulder generally gets better over time without surgery, although it may take up to 3 years. Most people improve with relatively simple treatments to control pain and restore motion. - Optimizing other health conditions (for example, improving glucose control in diabetes) can help speed recovery. - Hydrodilatation — gently injecting a large volume of sterile fluid into the shoulder joint under imaging guidance to expand and stretch the capsule — may be recommended if other nonsurgical methods do not relieve symptoms. - Physical therapy with stretching and range-of-motion exercises, sometimes preceded by heat, helps restore motion. Example exercises include:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Physical therapy with stretching and range-of-motion exercises, sometimes preceded by heat, helps restore motion. Example exercises include: - **External rotation — passive stretch**: standing in a doorway, bending the affected elbow to 90 degrees against the door jamb, and rotating the body to stretch, holding 30 seconds. - **Forward flexion — supine position**: lying on the back and using the unaffected arm to lift the affected arm overhead until a gentle stretch is felt, holding 15 seconds. - **Crossover arm stretch**: gently pulling one arm across the chest just below the chin, holding 30 seconds. ### Surgical Treatment If symptoms are not relieved by therapy and other conservative methods, surgery may be discussed, typically offered during the "frozen" stage. The goal is to stretch and release the stiffened joint capsule.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Surgical Treatment If symptoms are not relieved by therapy and other conservative methods, surgery may be discussed, typically offered during the "frozen" stage. The goal is to stretch and release the stiffened joint capsule. - **Manipulation under anesthesia**: The patient is put to sleep and the doctor forces the shoulder to move, causing the capsule and scar tissue to stretch or tear, releasing tightness and increasing range of motion. - **Shoulder arthroscopy**: Tight portions of the joint capsule are cut using pencil-sized instruments inserted through small incisions. Manipulation and arthroscopy are often combined for maximum results, and most patients have good outcomes. ### Recovery Physical therapy after surgery is necessary to maintain the motion achieved, with recovery times ranging from 6 weeks to 3 months. Long-term outcomes are generally good, with most patients having reduced or no pain and improved range of motion, though in some cases some stiffness remains even after several years — diabetic patients especially often retain some stiffness.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Long-term outcomes are generally good, with most patients having reduced or no pain and improved range of motion, though in some cases some stiffness remains even after several years — diabetic patients especially often retain some stiffness. Frozen shoulder can recur, especially if a contributing factor like diabetes is still present, though this is uncommon.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: # Frozen shoulder Frozen shoulder means your shoulder is painful and stiff for months, sometimes years. It can be treated with shoulder exercises and painkillers. The pain and stiffness will usually go away eventually, though recovery time varies significantly between people. ## Symptoms - shoulder pain, which can be worse at night - shoulder stiffness that limits how much you can move your arm ## Causes Often there's no clear explanation, but frozen shoulder involves inflammation and tightening of the tissue around the shoulder joint. Risk factors include a previous injury or surgery that has limited arm movement, and diabetes. ## When to see a GP See a GP if you have shoulder pain and stiffness that's not improving with self-care, or pain that's so bad it's stopping you moving your arm. ## Self-care **Do:** - follow any exercises given to you by a GP or physiotherapist - keep moving your shoulder as much as you can

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: ## Self-care **Do:** - follow any exercises given to you by a GP or physiotherapist - keep moving your shoulder as much as you can - put a heat pack (or a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel) on your shoulder for up to 20 minutes at a time **Don't:** - do not make up your own strenuous exercises or use gym equipment without advice ## Treatment The NHS describes a step-by-step approach: 3. **Restoring movement** - gentle exercises to do at home, with a possible referral to physiotherapy if pain persists Many physiotherapists work directly within GP surgeries.

condition_display: Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand
text: # Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand ## Overview Ganglion cysts represent the most prevalent mass or lump in the hand. They are benign and typically harmless. These fluid-filled cysts can develop in various locations, though they most frequently occur on the back of the wrist. They may appear and disappear rapidly while changing in size. Many require no intervention, but treatment options exist if the cyst causes discomfort, functional limitations, or aesthetic concerns. ## Description A ganglion emerges from a joint like a balloon attached to a stalk. It develops from tissues surrounding joints, including ligaments, tendon sheaths, and joint linings. The interior contains thick, slippery fluid similar to joint lubricant. The back of the wrist is the most common location for ganglion cysts. Ganglion cysts can develop in several hand and wrist joints: - Both the top and underside of the wrist - The end joint of a finger - The base of a finger

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
condition_display: Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand
text: Ganglion cysts can develop in several hand and wrist joints: - Both the top and underside of the wrist - The end joint of a finger - The base of a finger These vary in size and typically enlarge with increased activity. Rest usually causes the lump to reduce in size. ## Cause The trigger for ganglion formation remains unknown. - They occur most frequently in younger individuals between ages 15 and 40 - Women experience them more often than men - They are prevalent among gymnasts who repeatedly stress the wrist - Mucous cysts, developing at the end joint on the nail side of a finger, typically associate with finger joint arthritis and occur more commonly in women aged 40 to 70 ## Symptoms Most ganglions present as a visible lump; smaller ganglions may remain hidden beneath the skin (occult ganglions). While many produce no symptoms beyond the mass appearance, pressure on nerves crossing the joint can cause pain, tingling, and muscle weakness.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
condition_display: Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand
text: While many produce no symptoms beyond the mass appearance, pressure on nerves crossing the joint can cause pain, tingling, and muscle weakness. Large cysts may generate anxiety or dissatisfaction regarding appearance, even without pain. ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination Your doctor will review your medical history and symptoms, potentially asking: - Duration of ganglion presence - Whether it changes in size - Whether it causes pain Your doctor may apply pressure to test tenderness. Since ganglions contain fluid, they are translucent. A penlight may be held against the cyst to verify light passes through, confirming it is a cyst rather than a solid tumor. ### Imaging Tests **X-rays.** X-rays create clear pictures of dense structures like bone. Although X-rays won't show ganglion cysts, they eliminate other conditions such as hand arthritis, wrist arthritis, or bone tumors.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
condition_display: Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand
text: ### Imaging Tests **X-rays.** X-rays create clear pictures of dense structures like bone. Although X-rays won't show ganglion cysts, they eliminate other conditions such as hand arthritis, wrist arthritis, or bone tumors. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans or ultrasounds.** These better visualize soft tissues like ganglions compared to X-rays. MRI or ultrasound may locate occult ganglions not visible externally or distinguish cysts from other tumors. However, further imaging often isn't necessary before treatment. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Initial ganglion cyst treatment is nonsurgical. **Observation.** Without pain or other symptoms, monitoring may be recommended to ensure no unusual changes occur. This remains safe because ganglions are benign and may self-resolve over time. **Immobilization.** Activity often causes ganglion enlargement, increasing pressure on surrounding nerves and causing pain. A wrist brace or splint may relieve symptoms and reduce ganglion size.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
condition_display: Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand
text: **Immobilization.** Activity often causes ganglion enlargement, increasing pressure on surrounding nerves and causing pain. A wrist brace or splint may relieve symptoms and reduce ganglion size. As pain decreases, strengthening exercises and range-of-motion work may be prescribed. **Aspiration.** If the ganglion causes significant pain or substantially limits activities, fluid may be drained through aspiration. The area surrounding the ganglion is numbed and punctured with a needle to withdraw fluid. Unfortunately, aspiration frequently fails to eliminate the ganglion permanently because the root or connection to the joint or tendon sheath remains. Like a weed, the ganglion may regrow if the root persists. Therefore, ganglion cysts often return after aspiration. Aspirations are most often performed on ganglions on the wrist's top. Palm-side wrist ganglions can be problematic to aspirate due to proximity to major vessels and nerves. ### Surgical Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
condition_display: Ganglion Cyst of the Wrist and Hand
text: Aspirations are most often performed on ganglions on the wrist's top. Palm-side wrist ganglions can be problematic to aspirate due to proximity to major vessels and nerves. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery may be recommended if nonsurgical methods don't relieve symptoms or if the ganglion returns after aspiration. The removal procedure is called excision. Surgery removes the cyst and addresses the stalk from which it arises. This may involve removing part of the involved joint capsule or tendon sheath to ensure complete root removal. Even after excision, a small possibility exists that the ganglion will return. Excision is typically an outpatient procedure with patients discharged the same day following recovery observation. Some tenderness, discomfort, and swelling may occur post-surgery. Normal activities can usually resume 2 to 6 weeks after the procedure. ## Outcomes Ganglion cysts rarely cause permanent disability. Cysts that don't self-resolve and produce symptoms typically respond well to surgery.

text: # Physical activity (WHO Fact Sheet) This fact sheet summarizes the key content of the WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour (2020), published at https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240015128 (ISBN 9789240015128, released 25 November 2020). The full guideline document provides evidence-based public health recommendations for children, adolescents, adults, older adults, pregnant and postpartum women, and people living with chronic conditions or disability on the amount of physical activity (frequency, intensity and duration) required to offer significant health benefits and mitigate health risks. For the first time, the guideline also addresses associations between sedentary behaviour and health outcomes. ## Key Facts Regular physical activity provides significant physical and mental health benefits. Globally, 31% of adults and 80% of adolescents do not currently meet the recommended levels of physical activity.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: ## Key Facts Regular physical activity provides significant physical and mental health benefits. Globally, 31% of adults and 80% of adolescents do not currently meet the recommended levels of physical activity. The global cost of physical inactivity to health systems is estimated at approximately USD 27 billion annually through 2030 if trends do not improve. ## Definition and Scope WHO defines physical activity as "any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure." This includes activity undertaken while working, playing, carrying out household chores, travelling, and engaging in recreational pursuits, at any level of skill. ## Health Benefits **Children and adolescents:** Physical activity promotes bone health, healthy growth, and improved development of muscle and cardiorespiratory fitness, and improves cognitive outcomes (such as academic performance) and mental health (reduced symptoms of depression).

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: ## Health Benefits **Children and adolescents:** Physical activity promotes bone health, healthy growth, and improved development of muscle and cardiorespiratory fitness, and improves cognitive outcomes (such as academic performance) and mental health (reduced symptoms of depression). **Adults and older adults:** Regular physical activity is associated with reduced risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease mortality, incident hypertension, site-specific cancers, type 2 diabetes, and improved mental health, cognitive function, and sleep. For older adults, activity also helps prevent falls and bone-density related injuries and supports healthy bone and functional health. **Pregnant and postpartum women:** Physical activity provides significant benefits with minimal risk, decreasing the risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, and delivery complications, and helps decrease postpartum depression, with no evidence of harm to fetal outcomes.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: **Pregnant and postpartum women:** Physical activity provides significant benefits with minimal risk, decreasing the risk of pre-eclampsia, gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, excessive weight gain during pregnancy, and delivery complications, and helps decrease postpartum depression, with no evidence of harm to fetal outcomes. **People living with chronic conditions or disability:** The guidelines note that adults and older adults living with chronic conditions (including hypertension, type 2 diabetes and HIV) or disability should follow the same overall physical activity patterns as the general population, with activity providing similar or greater health benefits than for the general population, and should consult a health professional to determine the type and amount of activity appropriate for their particular condition. ## Activity Recommendations (summary) - Any amount of physical activity is better than none. If people are currently doing no physical activity, starting with small amounts and gradually increasing frequency, intensity and duration is a good way to begin.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: ## Activity Recommendations (summary) - Any amount of physical activity is better than none. If people are currently doing no physical activity, starting with small amounts and gradually increasing frequency, intensity and duration is a good way to begin. - Adults should do at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity, or at least 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity, or an equivalent combination, throughout the week. - Adults should also do muscle-strengthening activities at moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week, as these provide additional health benefits. - Older adults should, as part of their weekly physical activity, do varied multicomponent physical activity that emphasizes functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity on 3 or more days a week, to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. - All adults, including older adults, should limit the amount of time spent being sedentary.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: - All adults, including older adults, should limit the amount of time spent being sedentary. Replacing sedentary time with physical activity of any intensity (including light intensity) provides health benefits, and to help reduce the detrimental effects of high levels of sedentary behaviour on health, all adults and older adults should aim to do more than the recommended levels of moderate-to-vigorous intensity physical activity. - For children and adolescents (5–17 years), an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous intensity, mostly aerobic, physical activity across the week provides health benefits, and vigorous-intensity aerobic activities and those that strengthen muscle and bone should be incorporated at least 3 days a week. ## Global Trends Approximately 1.8 billion adults worldwide are currently at risk of disease from not doing enough physical activity.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: ## Global Trends Approximately 1.8 billion adults worldwide are currently at risk of disease from not doing enough physical activity. Levels of insufficient physical activity are roughly twice as high in high-income countries (26%) compared with low-income countries (16%), and women are generally less active than men, with an average gap of 5 percentage points globally. If current trends continue, the global target of a 15% relative reduction in insufficient physical activity by 2030 will not be met. ## Policy / Member State Response WHO's Global Action Plan on Physical Activity 2018–2030 calls on countries and communities to increase levels of physical activity in all age groups through measures that: create a more active society by changing social norms; create active environments with safe spaces and infrastructure; encourage active people through community-based programmes across multiple settings; and establish active systems through governance, leadership, multisectoral partnerships and workforce capacity building.

text: # Package of Interventions for Rehabilitation, Module 2: Musculoskeletal Conditions (WHO) Published: 5 July 2023 (Geneva: World Health Organization; 2023). ISBN 978-92-4-007110-0 (electronic version). Licence: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO. This module is part of WHO's 8-module "Package of interventions for rehabilitation" series and covers six musculoskeletal conditions: low back pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcopenia, fractures, and amputation. It is intended as "an indispensable resource for countries when planning for and budgeting the integration of rehabilitation services into their health systems," setting out for each condition the recommended assessments, interventions, required assistive products/equipment/consumables, and the rehabilitation workforce needed to deliver them. ## About Low Back Pain

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: ## About Low Back Pain "Low back pain is a condition that many people experience during their lifetime and is the leading cause of years lived with disability." Prevalence accelerates from about 15 years of age and peaks in older age (80-89 years). Low back pain is defined as primary when persistent or recurrent pain is not reliably attributed to an underlying disease process (such as ankylosing spondylitis) or structural pathology. Most people experience a short-term episode, but in about a third it extends to 12 months or more, or recurs across the life course. It is estimated that in 2019, 568 million people worldwide were living with low back pain and associated problems in functioning that could benefit from rehabilitation.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: It is estimated that in 2019, 568 million people worldwide were living with low back pain and associated problems in functioning that could benefit from rehabilitation. "For people with chronic low back pain, multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation, including both physical exercise programmes to restore motor functions, and psychological approaches to enable people with low back pain to cope better with pain, are more effective in improving physical tolerances towards daily activities and general well-being than physical treatment alone." ## About Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is "a chronic condition and the most common form of arthritis," influenced by an interaction between genetic, biomechanical, metabolic, and biochemical responses. It is characterized by joint pain, stiffness and swelling, most commonly in weight-bearing sites (knees, hips, feet, spine) and sites subject to repetitive stress (hands, shoulders). Risk factors include joint injury, being overweight or obese, being female, and older age.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: Risk factors include joint injury, being overweight or obese, being female, and older age. In 2019, an estimated 344 million people worldwide were living with osteoarthritis and associated functioning problems that could benefit from rehabilitation. Rehabilitation targets joint function, pain and swelling, and mobility-related functions such as muscle strength, and promotes self-management skills and psychological health to support continued participation in work and social life. ## About Rheumatoid Arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis is "an autoimmune inflammatory disease that primarily affects synovial joints," particularly the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet, though any synovial joint may be affected. Systemic inflammation can lead to joint swelling and degradation of articular and periarticular tissues, alongside extra-articular conditions such as cardiovascular disease. Risk factors include age, female gender, smoking and obesity.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: Systemic inflammation can lead to joint swelling and degradation of articular and periarticular tissues, alongside extra-articular conditions such as cardiovascular disease. Risk factors include age, female gender, smoking and obesity. In 2019, an estimated 13 million people worldwide were living with rheumatoid arthritis and associated functioning problems that could benefit from rehabilitation. "Interventions for rehabilitation address both the symptoms related to the disease, such as pain, stiffness, or fatigue, as well as the factors that impact the disease activity and comorbidities, such as nutrition or lack of physical activity," in addition to helping people develop self-management and coping strategies. ## About Sarcopenia

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: ## About Sarcopenia Sarcopenia is "a progressive and generalized skeletal muscle condition involving the accelerated loss of muscle mass and function." It occurs commonly as an age-related process but can also occur in mid-life in association with other conditions; it is termed "secondary" when causal factors other than ageing (for example inflammatory processes, malignancy or organ failure) are evident. Prevalence is estimated at approximately 6-22% of adults aged 65 and over. Physical activity and nutrition are protective factors for both prevention and management; rehabilitation targets loss of muscle function itself, its consequences (reduced activity, increased fall risk), and the associated risk of secondary conditions such as fall-related fractures. ## About Fractures

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: Physical activity and nutrition are protective factors for both prevention and management; rehabilitation targets loss of muscle function itself, its consequences (reduced activity, increased fall risk), and the associated risk of secondary conditions such as fall-related fractures. ## About Fractures A fracture is "a break in the continuity of a bone that can occur in any body part and at any age." The top three anatomical sites by years lived with disability are the lower limb, pelvis, and hip, and falls are the leading cause of fracture-related disability. Fractures may result from physical trauma, overuse, or conditions associated with loss of bone strength such as osteoporosis or cancer. In 2019, an estimated 436 million people worldwide were living with fractures and associated functioning problems that could benefit from rehabilitation.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: In 2019, an estimated 436 million people worldwide were living with fractures and associated functioning problems that could benefit from rehabilitation. Rehabilitation should start immediately following acute treatment and continue until optimal functioning is achieved, supporting bone healing, preventing deterioration of function, and helping to prevent secondary conditions such as deep venous thromboembolism and pneumonia. ## About Amputation An amputation is the removal of a limb or body part due to trauma or surgery (for causes such as cancer, diabetes, infection or pain). Symptoms range from physical impairments to phantom limb sensations and pain. In 2019, an estimated 176 million people worldwide were living with amputation and associated functioning problems that could benefit from rehabilitation.

source_note: World Health Organization (WHO)
text: Symptoms range from physical impairments to phantom limb sensations and pain. In 2019, an estimated 176 million people worldwide were living with amputation and associated functioning problems that could benefit from rehabilitation. Rehabilitation should start in the acute phase and continue until optimal functioning is achieved; preparation for, selection, fitting and training in the use of prosthesis is a core component, alongside psychosocial care supporting return to daily life, work, and community and social participation. ## Common Rehabilitation Intervention Framework Across all six conditions, the module organizes rehabilitation into a consistent "assessment leads to intervention" structure grouped by functional target area, typically including: - **Exercise and fitness**: assessment of exercise capacity, paired with fitness/aerobic training using equipment such as cycle ergometers, resistance bands, weights and exercise mats.

text: # Medial Epicondylitis (Golfer's Elbow) ## Overview Medial epicondylitis is a painful condition of the elbow that can be caused by overuse or through overexertion. While commonly affecting golfers, it can result from overhead throwing, tennis, and weightlifting, or develop without specific injury. The condition involves tendons in the forearm that partially tear and wear down over time due to repetitive motions. Most cases respond well to nonsurgical treatment, with surgery considered only after several months without improvement. ## Anatomy The elbow comprises three bones: the humerus (upper arm), radius (outer forearm), and ulna (inner forearm). Muscles controlling forearm rotation and wrist/finger flexion attach via tendons to the medial epicondyle, a bony prominence on the elbow's inner side. Key muscles involved include: - Pronator teres (most commonly injured) - Flexor carpi radialis - Palmaris longus

Risk factors include improper golf swing technique, inadequate equipment, age (typically 40-60), and repetitive activities of daily living, like doing certain household chores. ## Symptoms Symptoms typically develop gradually over weeks to months and include: - Pain or burning in the inner part of the elbow, with occasional shooting pain - Weak grip strength - Decreased wrist and elbow range of motion Some patients develop ulnar neuritis, causing numbness and tingling in ring and pinky fingers. ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination

text: # Gout: Causes and Treatments ## Overview Gout is characterized by sudden attacks of intense pain, swelling, and redness in the joints or soft tissues. The big toe joints are commonly affected first, though gout can develop in multiple joints. The condition develops when uric acid crystals accumulate in joints and soft tissues, triggering an inflammatory response similar to an infection. ## What Gout Affects Gout impacts several tissue types: - **Joints**: Most commonly the big toe, but also fingers, knees, shoulders, elbows, and hips. - **Bursae**: Fluid-filled sacs that cushion bones and soft tissues, particularly at the elbow and kneecap. - **Tendon sheaths**: Protective tunnels in the hands and feet. - **Kidneys**: Elevated uric acid can cause kidney stones (affecting approximately 15% of gout patients). ## Progression Following the initial attack, subsequent episodes may occur within 2 years for untreated individuals.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: - **Kidneys**: Elevated uric acid can cause kidney stones (affecting approximately 15% of gout patients). ## Progression Following the initial attack, subsequent episodes may occur within 2 years for untreated individuals. Over time, attacks become more frequent and severe, potentially affecting multiple joints simultaneously. Chronic cases can produce chalky deposits called tophi and cause permanent joint damage resembling arthritis. ## Causes and Risk Factors Gout develops when the body produces excessive uric acid or fails to eliminate sufficient quantities. Approximately two-thirds of people with elevated uric acid levels never have gout attacks. Key risk factors include: - **Gender/age**: Men typically develop gout between ages 30-45; women after menopause (55-70). - **Family history**: Genetic predisposition increases risk. - **Medical conditions**: High blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease, and certain anemias elevate uric acid.

The affected joint appears red and swollen and may feel hot. Fever warrants immediate medical attention, as infection may be present. ## Diagnosis **Blood tests** measure uric acid levels; however, levels may test normal during acute attacks, as crystals have already moved into tissues. **Synovial fluid analysis** provides a more definitive diagnosis by extracting joint fluid and examining it microscopically for uric acid crystals and white blood cells. ## Treatment ### Acute Attack Management ### Long-Term Management

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: **Synovial fluid analysis** provides a more definitive diagnosis by extracting joint fluid and examining it microscopically for uric acid crystals and white blood cells. ## Treatment ### Acute Attack Management ### Long-Term Management Lifestyle modifications include maintaining a healthy weight through exercise and diet, drinking abundant water, limiting calories (especially from fat), avoiding sugary beverages, consuming complex carbohydrates and low-fat proteins, and eliminating alcohol. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery is considered when tophi removal is needed for persistently inflamed or infected deposits, when joint fusion would provide pain relief in smaller joints with permanent damage, or when joint replacement is needed to address end-stage arthritis (the knee being the most commonly replaced joint). Acute attacks themselves do not require surgery unless a concurrent bacterial infection necessitates urgent joint irrigation.

text: # Hallux Rigidus (Stiff Big Toe) ## Overview Hallux rigidus is a condition in which the joint at the base of the big toe becomes progressively stiff. It is the most common arthritic condition of the foot and can significantly limit comfortable walking. It typically develops in middle-aged adults, most often between ages 30 and 60. ## Anatomy The big toe has two joints. The metatarsophalangeal joint (MTP) is the larger of the two, formed where the first metatarsal bone (the long bone of the foot) meets the first phalanx (the toe bone). This joint allows the toe to bend and grip the ground while accommodating the flexibility the foot needs during walking. Beneath the MTP joint sit two small bones called sesamoid bones. These bones help create a stable pivot point that supports the push-off motion during walking. ## Why Hallux Rigidus Develops

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Beneath the MTP joint sit two small bones called sesamoid bones. These bones help create a stable pivot point that supports the push-off motion during walking. ## Why Hallux Rigidus Develops Normally, the ends of bones in a joint are covered by a smooth layer of articular cartilage. When this cartilage is damaged, the underlying bone surfaces can start to rub against one another. In response, bony growths (spurs) may form on the top of the base of the big toe. These spurs can limit how far the toe can bend — often not enough for normal walking — which causes pain. As the condition advances to later stages, the cartilage wears away completely, resulting in bone-on-bone contact and arthritis within the joint. ## Cause Several factors contribute to the development of hallux rigidus: - Ordinary wear and tear, or repeated injuries to the big toe, that gradually damage the protective cartilage over time

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Cause Several factors contribute to the development of hallux rigidus: - Ordinary wear and tear, or repeated injuries to the big toe, that gradually damage the protective cartilage over time - Biomechanical foot problems, such as flatfoot or bunions, which place excess stress on the MTP joint and can trigger hallux rigidus - An inherited predisposition that makes some people more likely to develop the condition ## Symptoms Symptoms of hallux rigidus vary and may include one or several of the following: - Pain in the big toe joint during walking or other activities; this is often felt on top of the joint but can also feel like a deeper pain within the joint; many people notice difficulty pushing off normally while walking, or pain spread across the top of the foot - Swelling and thickening of tissue around the joint, which may require changes in shoe size or style

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Swelling and thickening of tissue around the joint, which may require changes in shoe size or style - A bump on top of the foot resembling a bunion or callus; this may be accompanied by redness - Reduced ability to bend or straighten the big toe through its normal range ## Diagnosing Hallux Rigidus ### Physical Examination The doctor examines the foot for visible bone spurs and moves the big toe in different directions to measure how much motion is available and to see where pain occurs. This movement testing helps determine whether the pain is coming from deep within the joint or from the bump on top, which guides treatment recommendations. ### Imaging Tests **X-rays** show the location and size of any bone spurs, the extent of arthritic damage within the joint, and how much cartilage has been lost. **CT scan.** Doctors may selectively order a CT scan to evaluate the alignment of the foot's structure.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **CT scan.** Doctors may selectively order a CT scan to evaluate the alignment of the foot's structure. **MRI scan.** An MRI may be ordered to get a better look at the joint cartilage, fluid within the bone, and the ligaments around the joint. It can also help with surgical planning in certain cases. ### Importance of Early Diagnosis Recognizing hallux rigidus early makes treatment simpler. If diagnosis is delayed, bone spurs can grow, arthritis can set in, and the joint can deteriorate further, potentially requiring more complex treatment. ## Treatment of a Stiff Big Toe ### Nonsurgical Treatment **Ice.** Applying an ice pack to the affected area can temporarily reduce inflammation and manage symptoms. Ice should never touch skin directly; use an ice pack or wrap it in a cloth or towel to prevent skin injury. **Shoe changes.** Choosing shoes with a roomy toe box reduces pressure on top of the toe. High heels should be avoided.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Shoe changes.** Choosing shoes with a roomy toe box reduces pressure on top of the toe. High heels should be avoided. Doctors often recommend shoes with stiff soles and a rocker- or roller-shaped bottom. Many patients get relief from regular shoes fitted with stiff carbon-fiber inserts (Morton's extension inserts) or metal plates built into the sole. These modifications support the foot during walking and limit how far the big toe bends, reducing pain and inflammation. - They can sometimes help confirm the diagnosis of hallux rigidus - They can provide pain relief for patients who have tried other nonsurgical options without success but are not good candidates for surgery ### Surgical Treatment **Cheilectomy.** This is the typical recommendation for patients with mild to moderate hallux rigidus. The procedure involves removing bone spurs and shaving away a portion of bone from the big toe to create more room for it to bend.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Cheilectomy.** This is the typical recommendation for patients with mild to moderate hallux rigidus. The procedure involves removing bone spurs and shaving away a portion of bone from the big toe to create more room for it to bend. The procedure can be done through either a traditional open incision or minimally invasive techniques, both of which produce good results. Minimally invasive approaches use smaller incisions, which may allow earlier weight-bearing and a faster initial recovery. Open approaches give the surgeon a complete direct view of the joint throughout the procedure. **Arthrodesis.** Permanently fusing the bones is typically recommended when cartilage damage is severe. In arthrodesis, the surgeon removes the damaged cartilage and uses pins, screws, or metal plates to hold the joint permanently in place. This allows comfortable walking and may allow low-heeled shoes to be worn. Over time the bones fuse together, eliminating the toe joint entirely.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This allows comfortable walking and may allow low-heeled shoes to be worn. Over time the bones fuse together, eliminating the toe joint entirely. Because the toe loses all bending ability after fusion, this procedure is reserved for more severe cases, but it is more reliable at reducing pain in patients with severe hallux rigidus or when cheilectomy has failed. **Resection arthroplasty.** Surgeons may choose to remove part of the joint surface in elderly patients with low functional demands. This procedure is used less often in more active patients. **Arthroplasty (total joint replacement).** Older patients with modest activity demands may be candidates for joint replacement. The surgeon removes the surfaces of the MTP joint and implants an artificial joint, which may relieve pain while preserving some motion. **Hemiarthroplasty (partial joint replacement).** This procedure replaces only one side of the joint and may benefit patients who still have good cartilage on the other side.

text: **Hemiarthroplasty (partial joint replacement).** This procedure replaces only one side of the joint and may benefit patients who still have good cartilage on the other side. It is used less often today than total joint replacement or fusion. **Note on arthroplasty options.** Arthroplasty and hemiarthroplasty are used less often because of the likelihood of needing revision surgery if the implant loosens. Removing the implant during a later procedure risks significant bone loss and may lead to functional problems. ## Surgical Recovery Patients whose pain has not improved substantially several days after surgery should contact their doctor. **Recovery after cheilectomy.** Most patients experience long-lasting pain relief. However, moving the toe soon after surgery is important to prevent scar tissue from making the toe stiff again.

text: # Hammer Toe ## Overview A hammer toe is a deformity of the second, third, or fourth toe, in which the toe is bent at the middle joint, giving it a hammer-like appearance. In its early stages, a hammer toe is flexible and can often be corrected with simple measures, but if left untreated it can become fixed and may require surgery. ## Anatomy The forefoot has five toes, and each has three joints (the big toe usually has two). In hammer toe, the affected toe bends at the middle joint, known as the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint. ## Cause Hammer toe results from a muscle imbalance that puts pressure on the toe's tendons and joints. Muscles work in pairs to straighten and bend the toes; when a toe is held bent for a prolonged period, its muscles and joints can tighten irreversibly. Poorly fitting shoes commonly cause this condition.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Muscles work in pairs to straighten and bend the toes; when a toe is held bent for a prolonged period, its muscles and joints can tighten irreversibly. Poorly fitting shoes commonly cause this condition. A narrow toe box forces the smaller toes into a bent position, and the resulting rubbing can produce corns and calluses. Higher heels increase the downward pressure on the foot and increase toe bending. Over time, weakened small foot muscles create a permanent imbalance. ## Symptoms Hammer toe causes pain during movement and when wearing shoes. Additional symptoms include: - Swelling or redness - Inability to straighten the toe - Difficulty walking - A corn or callus on top of the middle joint or at the tip of the toe ## Doctor Examination **Physical examination.** Doctors determine whether the toe joint is flexible or rigid, which guides treatment selection. **Tests.** X-rays confirm the diagnosis by showing the underlying bone structure.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Doctor Examination **Physical examination.** Doctors determine whether the toe joint is flexible or rigid, which guides treatment selection. **Tests.** X-rays confirm the diagnosis by showing the underlying bone structure. Patients with diabetes or decreased sensation in the foot may need additional testing to identify a neurological cause of the tendon imbalance. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Early-stage, flexible hammer toe typically responds to simple interventions. **Footwear changes.** Avoid tight, narrow, high-heeled shoes. Proper shoes should be about one-half inch longer than your longest toe and have a soft, roomy toe box. Deep-toe-box shoes or a stretched shoe repair may help accommodate the deformity. **Exercises.** Stretching and strengthening exercises help restore muscle balance, including manually stretching the toe, picking up small objects with the toes, and "towel curls" (scrunching a towel under the foot using the toes).

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Exercises.** Stretching and strengthening exercises help restore muscle balance, including manually stretching the toe, picking up small objects with the toes, and "towel curls" (scrunching a towel under the foot using the toes). **Over-the-counter remedies.** Commercial straps, cushions, and nonmedicated corn pads can provide pain relief. People with diabetes, poor circulation, or numbness in the feet should consult their doctor before self-treating. ### Surgical Treatment Rigid joints that do not respond to nonsurgical treatment may require surgery, typically performed as an outpatient procedure with local anesthesia. **Tendon lengthening.** For flexible toe joints, lengthening a tightened tendon corrects the joint imbalance. **Tendon transfer.** Some flexible-joint cases benefit from transferring a tendon from the bottom of the toe to the top to restore a straighter position.

text: **Tendon transfer.** Some flexible-joint cases benefit from transferring a tendon from the bottom of the toe to the top to restore a straighter position. **Arthrodesis (joint fusion).** For rigid joints, the doctor removes a small portion of bone from the PIP joint and inserts external wires/pins or an internal plate to hold the bones together while they fuse. ## Recovery Stiffness, swelling, and redness may persist for 4 to 6 weeks after surgery. Weight-bearing is possible right away, but activity should be limited and the foot elevated to aid healing. text: # Hamstring Muscle Injuries ## Overview Hamstring injuries, commonly called "pulled hamstrings," frequently affect athletes participating in sprinting sports like track, soccer, basketball, and waterskiing. Most injuries occur in the muscle belly or where muscle fibers connect to tendons. Severe injuries may cause avulsion — where the tendon completely detaches from bone, sometimes pulling bone fragments away. ## Cause

text: # Heel Pain ## Overview Walking places substantial cumulative stress on the feet — each mile walked generates roughly 60 tons of pressure on each foot. While the feet are structurally capable of managing significant load, excessive stress can exceed their tolerance, frequently resulting in heel pain, which is the most common problem affecting the foot. ## Anatomy The foot's skeleton is typically divided into three regions: the rear section (hindfoot), the middle section (midfoot), and the front section (forefoot). The heel bone (calcaneus) is the largest bone in the foot and sits in the hindfoot. Two important soft-tissue attachments connect to the heel: - The Achilles tendon comes down from the calf muscle and attaches to the back of the heel - The plantar fascia, a thick fibrous band that runs along the sole of the foot, also attaches to the heel bone Both attachment points, where soft tissue connects to bone, are prone to inflammation and are common sources of pain.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - The plantar fascia, a thick fibrous band that runs along the sole of the foot, also attaches to the heel bone Both attachment points, where soft tissue connects to bone, are prone to inflammation and are common sources of pain. ## Cause Heel pain has various sources, generally grouped into two main locations: **Pain under the heel:** - **Stone bruise.** Directly stepping on a hard object (a rock or stone) can bruise the fat pad under the heel, sometimes causing visible discoloration. - **Plantar fasciitis.** Excessive running or jumping inflames the fibrous band connecting the heel bone to the base of the toes, and this is often made worse by worn-out athletic shoes. - **Heel spur.** Untreated plantar fasciitis can lead to a calcium deposit where the fascia attaches to the heel bone; this is a result of the underlying problem rather than the cause of it.

text: - **Heel spur.** Untreated plantar fasciitis can lead to a calcium deposit where the fascia attaches to the heel bone; this is a result of the underlying problem rather than the cause of it. - **Calcaneus stress fracture.** Repeated high-impact activity can gradually damage and eventually fracture the heel bone. - **Nerve entrapment.** Impact activities can cause swelling and inflammation of nerves under the heel bone. - **Calcaneus fracture.** Falls from a height or car accidents can fracture the heel bone; these injuries are less common but can be severe, often requiring surgical reconstruction. **Pain at the back of the heel:** - **Retrocalcaneal bursitis.** The area where the Achilles tendon attaches to the heel bone becomes inflamed, often from excessive running or friction from footwear.

text: ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Conservative management includes: - **Rest.** Minimizing weight-bearing until symptoms improve; pain from a stone bruise naturally settles down with reduced activity. - **Ice.** Applying ice to the back of the heel reduces inflammation in 20-minute applications separated by equal rest periods (never applying ice directly to the skin — use a protective barrier). - **Taping.** Wrapping the heel can reduce discomfort and support healing in cases of fasciitis. - **Orthotic inserts.** Heel pads or cups provide support; open-backed shoes benefit people with tendon problems at the back of the heel. - **Night splinting.** Devices worn overnight significantly reduce pain that occurs first thing in the morning. - **Rehabilitation exercises.** Programs that emphasize stretching the Achilles tendon and calf are critical for resolving symptoms and preventing recurrence. Long-standing heel pain requires an extended treatment period — typically several months — often combining multiple interventions.

text: # Herniated Disk in the Lower Back ## What Is It? A herniated disk occurs when the soft, jelly-like center of the disk pushes through the tough outer ring. This condition most frequently affects the lower back and can result from age-related wear (disk degeneration) or a traumatic injury. ## Common Symptoms Patients typically experience lower back pain initially, which may improve after several days. Additional symptoms include: - Sharp, often shooting pain that travels from the buttock down the back of one leg (sciatica) - Leg numbness or tingling - Leg weakness - Rarely, loss of bladder or bowel control, which indicates cauda equina syndrome — a medical emergency ## Risk Factors Contributing risk factors include: being male, aged 20-50; improper lifting technique; excess body weight; repetitive activities that strain the spine; prolonged sitting or a sedentary lifestyle; and smoking. ## Treatment Approaches **Nonsurgical options (typically attempted first):**

text: ## Treatment Approaches **Nonsurgical options (typically attempted first):** - Brief bed rest (1-2 days maximum) - Physical therapy **Surgical procedures (for persistent symptoms or neurological deficits):** - Microdiskectomy — the most common surgical approach - Endoscopic diskectomy — a newer, minimally invasive alternative ## Prognosis Most people feel better within a few weeks or months without surgery, with typical recovery occurring within 3-4 months. text: # Slipped disc A slipped disc, also called a prolapsed or herniated disc, is when a soft cushion of tissue between the bones (vertebrae) in your spine bulges outwards. ## Symptoms Common signs include: - Lower back pain - Neck pain/discomfort - Numbness or tingling in the arms, legs, hands or feet - Muscle weakness - Sciatic pain that travels from the lower back down the leg (sciatica) Not all slipped discs cause symptoms. ## Self-management strategies **Activity:** Gradual, gentle exercise such as walking, swimming and yoga helps recovery better than prolonged rest. **Professional advice:** A pharmacist can recommend suitable pain management options. ## When to see a GP Seek GP care if: - Painkillers aren't helping - Pain persists beyond a few weeks - You develop a fever - You have unexplained weight loss - There's swelling in your back - Pain worsens at night ## Emergency care (call 999)
