text: # Hip Bursitis ## Overview Bursae are small, fluid-filled sacs located throughout the body between bones and soft tissues, functioning as cushions to reduce friction during joint motion. Hip bursitis involves inflammation of these structures. ## Types of Hip Bursae Two major bursae in the hip commonly become irritated: - **Trochanteric bursa**: Covers the bony point of the hip bone (greater trochanter); inflammation is called trochanteric bursitis. - **Iliopsoas bursa**: Located on the inside/groin side of the hip; when inflamed, causes groin area pain and is less common than trochanteric bursitis. ## Symptoms The primary symptom is pain at the hip point, typically extending to the outer thigh. Early pain is usually sharp and intense, later becoming an ache across a larger area.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Symptoms The primary symptom is pain at the hip point, typically extending to the outer thigh. Early pain is usually sharp and intense, later becoming an ache across a larger area. Pain worsens at night, when lying on the affected hip, after prolonged sitting, and during prolonged walking, stair climbing, or squatting. ## Risk Factors Hip bursitis is more common in women and middle-aged or elderly people. Associated risk factors include: - Repetitive stress injuries from running, stair climbing, bicycling, or prolonged standing - Hip injuries from falls or extended pressure on one side - Spine diseases including scoliosis and lumbar arthritis - Tight iliotibial band - Leg-length inequality - Rheumatoid arthritis - Previous hip surgery or prosthetic implants - Bone spurs or calcium deposits in tendons ## Doctor Examination Diagnosis involves comprehensive physical examination checking for tenderness over the hip bone point.

Soreness usually resolves within days. ## Prevention While hip bursitis cannot always be prevented, these measures help reduce inflammation severity: - Avoid repetitive hip-stress activities - Maintain healthy weight - Use properly fitting shoe inserts for leg-length differences - Maintain hip muscle strength and flexibility

text: # Hip Strains ## Overview A hip strain occurs when muscles supporting the hip joint are stretched beyond their limit or torn. These injuries range from mild to severe and can significantly limit hip mobility. While many strains improve with home care, severe cases may need physical therapy or medical intervention. ## Description The hip joint is anchored by large bones — the femur and pelvis — that support several muscle groups: - Muscles crossing the abdomen and buttocks (hip flexors, gluteals) - Muscles extending down the thigh (tensor fasciae latae, adductors, quadriceps, hamstrings) Strains involve injured muscles and tendons, with injury occurring where muscles connect to tendons. Damage can range from simple stretches to partial or complete tears. text: # Iliotibial Band (IT Band) Syndrome ## Anatomy The iliotibial (IT) band is a thick band of connective tissue fibers (fascia) that runs along the outside of the thigh between the hip and the knee. The main function of the IT band is to help stabilize the hip and knee joint while walking or running. ## Description IT band syndrome occurs when the IT band becomes irritated, usually due to excessive friction between the IT band and the outside (lateral side) of the knee. As a result, the slippery fluid-filled sac (bursa) that helps the IT band glide over the bony prominence (bump) at the outside of the knee becomes inflamed, causing pain. The IT band can also rub on the outside of the hip at the greater trochanter, which results in trochanteric bursitis, or inflammation of the bursa at the side of the hip bone. ## Cause

During arthroscopy, your doctor will make tiny incisions to insert a small camera and instruments into the joint or surrounding area. During this procedure, your doctor will make a small incision, typically over the skin of the hip. After identifying the IT band, they will make a z-shaped incision near the middle of the band. text: # Kienböck's Disease ## Overview Kienböck's disease is a condition where the blood supply to one of the small bones in the wrist, the lunate, is interrupted. The lunate is a carpal bone. Bone is living tissue that requires a regular supply of blood for nourishment. If the blood supply to a bone stops, the bone or parts of the bone can die. This is called osteonecrosis. A loss of blood supply to the lunate causes the bone to lose its structural support, and it will collapse, causing a painful, stiff wrist. Over time, these changes can lead to arthritis of the surrounding bones in the wrist. ## Cause The cause of Kienböck's disease is not known. There may be one or more factors that cause a disruption of blood flow to the bone. Many people with Kienböck's disease think they have a sprained wrist at first.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: There may be one or more factors that cause a disruption of blood flow to the bone. Many people with Kienböck's disease think they have a sprained wrist at first. They may have experienced some form of trauma to the wrist, such as a fall. This type of trauma can injure the blood vessels that supply the lunate. Some things may put a person more at risk for the disease. For instance: - Some people may have fewer blood vessels that supply the lunate; most people have two arteries that supply blood to the lunate, but in some people there is only one source. - Forces acting on the lunate may be different depending on the relative lengths of the two bones in the forearm (the radius and the ulna). If the radius and ulna are different lengths, extra pressure can be put on the lunate during some wrist motions and when pressure is applied to the wrist during activity, such as when doing a push-up.

Over time, this extra pressure may lead to a compromise of blood flow to the lunate and cause Kienböck's disease. ## Symptoms The most common symptoms of Kienböck's disease include: - Wrist pain - Wrist swelling - Limited range of motion in the affected wrist/wrist stiffness - Decreased grip strength - Tenderness directly over the bone (on the top of the hand at about the middle of the wrist) ## Doctor Examination Kienböck's disease is a condition that progresses slowly, often over many months or years. Many people do not decide to see a doctor until they have lived with symptoms for several months, or perhaps longer.

text: ## Doctor Examination Kienböck's disease is a condition that progresses slowly, often over many months or years. Many people do not decide to see a doctor until they have lived with symptoms for several months, or perhaps longer. During the first appointment, the doctor will discuss symptoms and medical history, then examine the hand and wrist. In its early stages, Kienböck's disease may be difficult to diagnose because the symptoms are so similar to those of a sprained wrist. Imaging tests, such as X-rays and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, are used to make a diagnosis. Even with special imaging studies, however, the early diagnosis of Kienböck's disease is not always clear or able to be confirmed. Kienböck's disease progresses through four stages of severity, and treatment is planned based on several factors, most important, the stage of progression. ### Stage I - Symptoms are similar to those of a wrist sprain.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Kienböck's disease progresses through four stages of severity, and treatment is planned based on several factors, most important, the stage of progression. ### Stage I - Symptoms are similar to those of a wrist sprain. - Although the blood supply to the lunate has been disrupted, X-rays may still appear normal or suggest a possible fracture. - An MRI scan can better detect the effects of abnormal blood flow and is helpful in making the diagnosis in this early stage. ### Stage II - The lunate bone begins to harden due to the lack of blood supply. This hardening process is called sclerosis and is an abnormal increase in bone density. - The lunate will appear brighter or whiter in areas on X-rays, indicating denser bone. - To better assess the condition of the lunate, an MRI scan or a computed tomography (CT) scan may be ordered.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - The lunate will appear brighter or whiter in areas on X-rays, indicating denser bone. - To better assess the condition of the lunate, an MRI scan or a computed tomography (CT) scan may be ordered. - The most common symptoms during this stage include wrist swelling and intermittent pain, particularly when force is applied to the wrist, such as with weightbearing. ### Stage III - The necrotic or dead lunate bone begins to collapse and fragment (break) into pieces (Stage IIIA). As the bone begins to collapse or break apart, the surrounding bones become affected and may begin to shift position (Stage IIIB). - During this stage, patients typically experience increasing pain, weakness in gripping, and limited wrist motion. ### Stage IV - The abnormal forces through the wrist due to the collapse of the lunate and shifted position of the other carpal bones result in arthritis of the wrist.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Stage IV - The abnormal forces through the wrist due to the collapse of the lunate and shifted position of the other carpal bones result in arthritis of the wrist. - Similar to Stage III, patients typically experience wrist pain, weakness in gripping, and limited wrist motion. ## Treatment Although there is no complete cure for Kienböck's disease, there are several nonsurgical and surgical options for treating it. Treatment strategies consider the stage of the condition and the patient's symptoms. The goals of treatment are to relieve the pressure on the lunate and to try to restore blood flow within the bone. ### Nonsurgical Treatment In the very early stage of the disease: - Immobilizing the wrist for a period of time can help relieve pressure on the lunate. - A short period of splinting or casting may be recommended. It is important to monitor any changes in symptoms during the early stage of Kienböck's disease.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - A short period of splinting or casting may be recommended. It is important to monitor any changes in symptoms during the early stage of Kienböck's disease. If the pain is not relieved with simple treatments or it returns, surgery may be recommended. Occasionally, if the diagnosis is not certain, imaging studies may be repeated after this period of initial treatment. ### Surgical Treatment There are several surgical options for treating Kienböck's disease. The choice of procedure depends on several factors, in particular how far the disease has progressed. The key factors in decision-making include: - The presence or absence of lunate collapse or fragmentation - Joint arthritis Additional factors to consider include: - The patient's activity level - The patient's personal goals - The patient's symptom tolerance - The surgeon's experience with the procedures **Revascularization.** In some cases, it may be possible to restore the blood supply to the lunate bone. This procedure is called revascularization.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - The patient's symptom tolerance - The surgeon's experience with the procedures **Revascularization.** In some cases, it may be possible to restore the blood supply to the lunate bone. This procedure is called revascularization. It is more successful during early phases of the disease — stages 1 and 2 — before the lunate has collapsed or fragmented. Revascularization involves removing a portion of bone with attached blood vessels from another bone — most often a forearm bone (radius) or an adjacent bone in the hand. This piece of bone with its blood supply is called a vascularized graft. It is moved carefully, preserving the feeder blood vessel, and inserted into the lunate bone. To help the bones stay in place and to reduce pressure on the lunate bone during healing, an external fixator or a plate may be temporarily applied, spanning the forearm to the hand.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: To help the bones stay in place and to reduce pressure on the lunate bone during healing, an external fixator or a plate may be temporarily applied, spanning the forearm to the hand. - This external fixator is a metal device that is attached to the outside of the wrist with pins that insert into the bones. - A plate is placed below the skin directly against the forearm bone (radius), crossing the wrist joint and attaching to the metacarpal bone in the hand. Both devices can relieve pressure on the lunate while the graft is healing and restoring a blood supply. **Joint leveling.** If the two bones of the lower arm are not the same length, a joint leveling procedure may be recommended. Bones can be made longer using bone grafts or shortened by removing a section of the bone. This leveling procedure reduces the forces that compress the lunate and often stops the progression of the disease.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Bones can be made longer using bone grafts or shortened by removing a section of the bone. This leveling procedure reduces the forces that compress the lunate and often stops the progression of the disease. **Proximal row carpectomy.** If the lunate is severely collapsed or broken into pieces, it can be removed. In this procedure, the two bones on either side of the lunate are also removed. This procedure will relieve pain while maintaining partial wrist motion. **Fusion (arthrodesis).** To reduce pressure on the lunate, nearby wrist bones can be fused together to make one, solid bone. A fusion can be partial, in which just some of the wrist bones are fused together. This procedure relieves pain and retains some wrist motion. If the disease has progressed to severe arthritis of the wrist, fusing all of the bones of the wrist to the radius will relieve pain and improve hand function.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This procedure relieves pain and retains some wrist motion. If the disease has progressed to severe arthritis of the wrist, fusing all of the bones of the wrist to the radius will relieve pain and improve hand function. Although all wrist motion is eliminated in a complete fusion, forearm rotation is preserved. ## Outcomes Kienböck's disease varies considerably in its severity, as well as in its rate of progression. Each patient's response to treatment depends on the degree of damage to the lunate and surrounding wrist bones. Some patients may require more than one procedure over time if the disease continues to progress. ## Summary Kienböck's disease is a challenging condition to both diagnose and treat. Often, the progression of the disease is slow, and typically the condition is not discovered until the wrist becomes painful or problematic. Treatment is based on the severity and stage of the condition.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Often, the progression of the disease is slow, and typically the condition is not discovered until the wrist becomes painful or problematic. Treatment is based on the severity and stage of the condition. The condition of the lunate bone (collapse, fragmentation) and surrounding joint surfaces (arthritis) will determine treatment options. While patients should not expect to ever return to normal wrist function, appropriate treatment gives the best opportunity for long-term pain relief and preservation of function.

text: # Meniscus Tears ## Anatomy Two bones meet to form the knee joint: the femur and the tibia. The kneecap (patella) sits in front of the joint to provide some protection. Two wedge-shaped pieces of fibrocartilage act as shock absorbers between the femur and tibia. These are the menisci. The menisci help to transmit weight from one bone to another and play an important role in knee stability. ## Description The meniscus can tear from acute trauma or as the result of degenerative changes that happen over time. Tears are noted by how they look, as well as where the tear occurs in the meniscus. Common types of meniscus tears include bucket handle, flap, and radial. Sports-related meniscus injuries often occur along with other knee injuries, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears. ## Cause Acute meniscus tears often happen during sports.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Sports-related meniscus injuries often occur along with other knee injuries, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears. ## Cause Acute meniscus tears often happen during sports. These can occur through either a contact or non-contact injury — for example, a pivoting or cutting injury. As people age, they are more likely to have degenerative meniscus tears. Aged, worn tissue is more prone to tears. An awkward twist when getting up from a chair may be enough to cause a tear in an aging meniscus. ## Symptoms You might feel a pop when you tear the meniscus. Most people can still walk on their injured knee, and many athletes are able to keep playing with a tear. Over 2 to 3 days, however, the knee will gradually become stiffer and more swollen. The most common symptoms of a meniscus tear are: - Pain - Stiffness and swelling - Catching or locking of your knee

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Over 2 to 3 days, however, the knee will gradually become stiffer and more swollen. The most common symptoms of a meniscus tear are: - Pain - Stiffness and swelling - Catching or locking of your knee - The sensation of your knee giving way - Inability to move your knee through its full range of motion ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination After discussing your symptoms and medical history, your doctor will examine your knee. They will check for tenderness along the joint line where the meniscus sits. This often indicates a tear. One of the main tests for meniscus tears is the McMurray test. Your doctor will bend your knee, then straighten and rotate it. This puts tension on a torn meniscus. If you have a meniscus tear, this movement may cause pain, clicking, or a clunking sensation within the joint. ### Imaging Tests

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This puts tension on a torn meniscus. If you have a meniscus tear, this movement may cause pain, clicking, or a clunking sensation within the joint. ### Imaging Tests Because other knee injuries can cause similar symptoms, your doctor may order imaging tests to help confirm the diagnosis. **X-rays.** X-rays provide images of dense structures, such as bone. Although an X-ray will not show a meniscus tear, your doctor may order one to look for other causes of knee pain, such as osteoarthritis. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans.** An MRI assesses the soft tissues in your knee joint, including the menisci, cartilage, tendons, and ligaments. MRI is the preferred method of diagnosing acute meniscus tears (tears that occur due to injury) because of its high level of accuracy.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: MRI is the preferred method of diagnosing acute meniscus tears (tears that occur due to injury) because of its high level of accuracy. If MRI is not available or you cannot have one for another reason, your doctor may order a computed tomography (CT) arthrogram (a CT scan where dye is injected) or ultrasound. ## Treatment The treatment your doctor recommends will depend on a number of factors, including your age, symptoms, and activity level. The doctor will also consider the type, size, and location of the injury. The outer one-third of the meniscus has a rich blood supply. A tear in this "red" zone may heal on its own or can often be repaired with surgery. A longitudinal tear is an example of this kind of tear. In contrast, the inner two-thirds of the meniscus lacks a significant blood supply. Without nutrients from blood, tears in this "white" zone with limited blood flow cannot heal.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: A longitudinal tear is an example of this kind of tear. In contrast, the inner two-thirds of the meniscus lacks a significant blood supply. Without nutrients from blood, tears in this "white" zone with limited blood flow cannot heal. Because the pieces cannot grow back together, symptomatic tears in this zone that do not respond to conservative treatment are usually trimmed surgically. ### Nonsurgical Treatment Many meniscus tears will not need immediate surgery. If your symptoms do not persist and you have no locking or swelling of the knee, your doctor may recommend nonsurgical treatment. **RICE.** The RICE protocol is effective for most sports-related injuries. RICE stands for: - **Rest.** Take a break from the activity that caused the injury. Your doctor may recommend that you use crutches to avoid putting weight on your leg. - **Ice.** Use cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Your doctor may recommend that you use crutches to avoid putting weight on your leg. - **Ice.** Use cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly to the skin. - **Compression.** To prevent additional swelling and blood loss, wear an elastic compression bandage. - **Elevation.** To reduce swelling, recline when you rest, and put your leg up higher than your heart. ### Surgical Treatment If your symptoms persist with nonsurgical treatment, your doctor may suggest arthroscopic surgery. **Procedure.** Knee arthroscopy is one of the most commonly performed surgical procedures. In this procedure, the surgeon inserts a miniature camera through a small incision (portal) in the knee. This provides a clear view of the inside of the knee. The surgeon then inserts surgical instruments through two or three other small portals to trim or repair the tear.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This provides a clear view of the inside of the knee. The surgeon then inserts surgical instruments through two or three other small portals to trim or repair the tear. - **Partial meniscectomy.** In this procedure, the damaged meniscus tissue is trimmed away. This procedure typically allows for immediate weight bearing, and full range of motion soon after surgery. - **Meniscus transplant.** When the meniscus is largely gone, you may experience ongoing pain, and osteoarthritis may develop. For younger, active people who do not want to undergo partial or total knee replacement, a meniscus transplant may be a good alternative. A meniscus transplant replaces the damaged meniscus with donor tissue matched for size. - **Meniscus repair.** Some meniscus tears can be repaired by suturing (stitching) the torn pieces together.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: A meniscus transplant replaces the damaged meniscus with donor tissue matched for size. - **Meniscus repair.** Some meniscus tears can be repaired by suturing (stitching) the torn pieces together. Whether a tear can be successfully repaired depends upon the type of tear, as well as the overall condition of the injured meniscus. Because the meniscus must heal back together, recovery time for a repair is longer than for a meniscectomy. Once the initial healing is complete, your doctor will prescribe rehabilitation exercises. Regular exercise to restore your knee mobility and strength is necessary. You will start with exercises to improve your range of motion. Strengthening exercises will gradually be added to your rehabilitation plan. Participating in physical therapy after surgery is important to have a good recovery. Rehabilitation time for a meniscus repair is about 3 to 6 months.

With proper diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation, patients often return to their pre-injury abilities.

text: # Burning Thigh Pain (Meralgia Paresthetica) ## Overview A painful burning sensation on the outer thigh may indicate compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN), a condition called meralgia paresthetica. The nerves in your body transmit sensory information to the brain and motor messages from the brain to muscles. When swelling, trauma, or pressure narrows the openings through which nerves pass, nerve compression can occur. ## Symptoms Symptoms typically appear on one side of the body and include: - Pain on the outer thigh, sometimes extending to the outer knee - A burning sensation, tingling, or numbness in the same area - Possible aching in the groin or pain across the buttocks - Greater sensitivity to light touch than firm pressure in affected areas ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination - Your doctor will check for sensory differences between the affected and unaffected leg - The doctor will apply pressure on the nerve to reproduce the burning sensation

text: # Morton's Neuroma ## Overview People who feel like they are walking on a stone and have persistent discomfort in the forefoot may be dealing with Morton's neuroma. Despite the name, it is not truly a tumor but rather a thickening of the tissue surrounding one of the small nerves leading to the toes. This tissue thickening produces pain, tingling, or forefoot discomfort that can limit participation in various activities. ## Anatomy of the Forefoot The forefoot contains 14 phalanges (toe bones) and five metatarsal bones connecting the forefoot to the midfoot. Between the metatarsal bases lie four web spaces: - The first web space is between the big toe and second toe - The second web space lies between the second and third toes - The third web space lies between the third and fourth toes - The fourth web space lies between the fourth and fifth toes

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - The first web space is between the big toe and second toe - The second web space lies between the second and third toes - The third web space lies between the third and fourth toes - The fourth web space lies between the fourth and fifth toes Sensation in the toes comes from the medial and lateral plantar nerves, which run along the sole of the foot and branch toward the toes. These branching nerves at the web-space level are called common digital plantar nerves. The transverse metatarsal ligaments connect the rounded ends of the metatarsals, and the common digital plantar nerves pass beneath these ligaments in the web space. ## Description Other names for this condition include interdigital neuroma, degenerative compression neuropathy, and plantar neuroma. It occurs about eight times more often in women than men, typically in people between the ages of 30 and 60, though it can occur outside that range.

text: It occurs about eight times more often in women than men, typically in people between the ages of 30 and 60, though it can occur outside that range. The third web space (between the third and fourth toes) is the most common location, typically developing after irritation, trauma, or excessive pressure. The second web space, between the second and third toes, is occasionally affected but less commonly. The primary symptom is pain or discomfort in the ball of the foot. ## Cause Research suggests the underlying mechanism likely involves entrapment or compression of the common digital plantar nerve. Compression of the nerve within the web space may cause swelling and abnormal tissue growth around the nerve, though the exact cause is not fully understood. ## Symptoms Visible signs like a lump or skin discoloration typically do not accompany Morton's neuroma. Common symptoms include:

Common symptoms include: - Persistent burning or sharp pain in the forefoot that may extend into the toes, especially with weight-bearing activities like walking or running (night pain is uncommon) - A sensation of a pebble or marble under the ball of the foot while walking - Pain typically in the third web space, occasionally in the second web space - Possible numbness or unpleasant tingling in the toes - Increased pain with activities requiring forefoot push-off, such as sprinting - Aggravation from footwear: high heels (which position the foot similarly to sprinting) and tight, narrow shoes (which compress the toe bones and pinch the nerve) ## Diagnosis ### Medical History and Physical Examination The doctor will ask about your overall health, medical history, and symptoms (location, nature, severity, duration), the specific activities that trigger pain, and what relieves it. The physical examination includes:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Diagnosis ### Medical History and Physical Examination The doctor will ask about your overall health, medical history, and symptoms (location, nature, severity, duration), the specific activities that trigger pain, and what relieves it. The physical examination includes: - Checking the skin of the foot and ankle for signs of excessive pressure - Inspecting the toes and foot for any deformity that could contribute to forefoot pain - Applying pressure to the web spaces to identify exactly where the pain is located - Checking the range of motion of the toes and other joints to look for arthritis or inflammation - Squeezing the foot to check for a "Mulder's click," which is sometimes present with Morton's neuroma - Compressing the web space to try to reproduce the neuroma pain - Injecting local anesthetic into the affected web space — pain relief afterward supports the diagnosis and also provides symptom relief ### Imaging Tests X-rays may be used to rule out a stress fracture or arthritis in the toe joints.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Injecting local anesthetic into the affected web space — pain relief afterward supports the diagnosis and also provides symptom relief ### Imaging Tests X-rays may be used to rule out a stress fracture or arthritis in the toe joints. MRI is generally not needed but may be considered in certain situations. ## Nonsurgical Treatment Initial management typically includes one or more of the following: - **Footwear changes.** Replacing high heels and tight, narrow shoes with wider shoes that have a roomier toe box, lower heels, and soft soles allows the metatarsal bones to spread and reduces pressure on the nerve. - **Orthotics.** Custom shoe inserts and metatarsal pads or bars redistribute pressure in the forefoot and help separate the metatarsal bones, reducing pressure and irritation on the neuroma. ## Surgical Treatment When nonsurgical treatment fails after 3 to 6 months or symptoms come back, surgery may be recommended. Several surgical techniques produce similar success rates.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Surgical Treatment When nonsurgical treatment fails after 3 to 6 months or symptoms come back, surgery may be recommended. Several surgical techniques produce similar success rates. The surgeon accesses the nerve through an incision on the top or bottom of the foot over the web space, then chooses between: - **Decompression.** Releasing the surrounding tissue to relieve pressure on the nerve. This may preserve sensation but has slightly less predictable outcomes than removing the nerve. This approach has gained favor among surgeons since it preserves nerve function and limits post-surgical sensation problems. - **Neurectomy.** Removing the diseased portion of the nerve. This provides high rates of pain relief but carries risks including permanent numbness and the formation of a "stump neuroma" — a new neuroma forming from the remaining end of the nerve. Increasingly, surgeons use minimally invasive dorsal approaches with smaller incisions, which may reduce soft-tissue disruption and speed recovery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Increasingly, surgeons use minimally invasive dorsal approaches with smaller incisions, which may reduce soft-tissue disruption and speed recovery. The specific approach depends on multiple factors that should be discussed with the surgeon. ## Recovery After Surgery Post-operative protocols vary by surgeon, but generally: - Patients may walk in a stiff-soled post-operative shoe, though weight-bearing may be limited to the heel if the incision was made on the bottom of the foot - High-impact activities (running, jumping) and submerging the foot in water should be avoided until the surgical wound has fully healed — typically at least 2 to 3 weeks after surgery - Return to normal footwear commonly occurs by about four weeks after the procedure Surgery is the most reliable treatment, with numerous studies reporting 80% to 95% long-term success rates. ## Treatment Outcomes - Conservative measures (shoe changes, activity modification, orthotics) provide relief in roughly 50% of patients

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Treatment Outcomes - Conservative measures (shoe changes, activity modification, orthotics) provide relief in roughly 50% of patients - Chemical and radiofrequency ablation achieve good success, with 70% to 80% of patients improving - Neurectomy or decompression has the highest success rate, with most studies reporting 80% to 95% success Possible complications after otherwise successful treatment include: - Ongoing mechanical overload after decompression, causing incomplete relief and continuing symptoms - A risk of permanent numbness after neurectomy - A risk of stump neuroma formation, which can produce similar symptoms without being a true recurrence About 5% to 20% of patients experience recurrence of symptoms requiring further treatment. Repeat surgery for recurrence achieves similar success rates (80% to 95%) as initial surgery.

text: # Muscle Cramps ## Overview A muscle cramp is an involuntary contraction of a muscle that occurs suddenly and does not relax. These involuntary spasms can affect any skeletal muscle under voluntary control, involving part or all of a muscle, or several muscles in a group. ## Most Commonly Affected Areas - Back of the lower leg/calf (gastrocnemius) - Back of the thigh (hamstrings) - Front of the thigh (quadriceps) - Feet, hands, arms, abdomen, and along the rib cage ## Cause Although the exact cause remains unknown, researchers believe inadequate stretching and muscle fatigue lead to abnormalities in the mechanisms that control muscle contraction. ### Contributing Factors - Poor conditioning - Exercising or working in intense heat - Dehydration - Depletion of salt and minerals (electrolytes) ### Inadequate Stretching and Muscle Fatigue When poorly conditioned, muscle fatigue can alter spinal neural reflex activity.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Exercising or working in intense heat - Dehydration - Depletion of salt and minerals (electrolytes) ### Inadequate Stretching and Muscle Fatigue When poorly conditioned, muscle fatigue can alter spinal neural reflex activity. Overexertion depletes oxygen supply, causing waste buildup and spasm. ### Heat, Dehydration, and Electrolyte Depletion Sweat drains the body's fluids, salt, and minerals (potassium, magnesium, calcium), potentially causing muscle spasms. ### Risk Factors - Infants, young children, and people over age 65 - Being ill or overweight - Overexerting during work or exercise - Endurance athletes and older people performing strenuous activities ## Symptoms - Range from slight twitching to agonizing pain - Cramping muscles may feel hard and appear visibly distorted - Duration: a few seconds to 15 minutes or longer; may recur multiple times ## Home Remedies - Stop the triggering activity

Examples include slowly running in place or walking briskly for a few minutes. ### Calf Muscle Stretch - Lean forward against a wall with one leg in front of the other - Straighten your back leg and press your heel into the floor; front knee is bent - Hold for 15 to 30 seconds - Keep both heels flat on the floor; point back foot toes toward front foot heel ### Hamstring Muscle Stretch

text: # Neck Pain ## Description The neck has significant mobility and supports the weight of the head. Because it has less protection than other regions of the spine, it remains vulnerable to injury and to disorders that cause pain and restricted motion. For many people, neck pain is temporary and resolves naturally; others require medical diagnosis and treatment for symptom relief. ## Anatomy The spine consists of 24 stacked bones called vertebrae. Seven small cervical vertebrae begin at the base of the skull and form the neck. Vertebrae, ligaments, and muscles provide spinal stability and enable movement. The spinal cord extends from the base of the skull to the lower back through the spinal canal, and nerve roots branch from the spinal cord through openings in the vertebrae (foramina), transmitting messages between the brain and muscles. Flexible intervertebral disks between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers during activities like walking or running. ## Cause

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Flexible intervertebral disks between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers during activities like walking or running. ## Cause Neck pain can stem from soft-tissue issues (muscles, ligaments, nerves) or from skeletal and disk problems. Common causes include: - **Soft-tissue injuries**: Strains or sprains affecting muscles and ligaments. - **Prolonged wear and tear**: Cervical spondylosis (arthritis of the neck), which can potentially lead to cervical spondylotic myelopathy (spinal cord compression) or cervical radiculopathy (a pinched neck nerve). Rarely, infections or tumors cause neck pain, and neck problems can sometimes generate pain in the upper back, shoulder, or arm. ### Cervical Disk Degeneration (Spondylosis / Arthritis) Cervical disks act as shock absorbers between the neck bones.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Cervical Disk Degeneration (Spondylosis / Arthritis) Cervical disks act as shock absorbers between the neck bones. Degeneration typically occurs in people age 40 and older — as spinal disks age they lose height and begin to bulge, and their water content decreases, causing drying and weakening, which reduces cushioning capacity. When the outer rim of a disk weakens, it may bulge outward and press on the spinal cord or nerve roots — a herniated cervical disk — which can cause arm and leg pain, numbness, tingling, and weakness. Cervical spondylosis is extremely common: more than 85% of people over the age of 60 are affected. ### Injury The neck's flexibility and its role in supporting the head make it extremely vulnerable to injury from motor vehicle accidents, diving mishaps, contact sports, and falls.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Injury The neck's flexibility and its role in supporting the head make it extremely vulnerable to injury from motor vehicle accidents, diving mishaps, contact sports, and falls. Rear-end automobile collisions may produce hyperextension or hyperflexion of the neck beyond normal limits — commonly called whiplash. Regular seatbelt use helps prevent or minimize neck injury. Common neck injuries include sprains and strains of muscles and ligaments, pinched nerves (cervical radiculopathy), and — in severe cases — fractures or dislocations that can damage the spinal cord and cause paralysis. ## When to Seek Medical Care After severe neck pain from an injury (motor vehicle accident, diving accident, or fall), a trained professional such as a paramedic should immobilize the patient to prevent further injury and reduce the risk of paralysis — immediate medical care is essential, and time is most critical following trauma. Seek immediate medical care when an injury causes radiating neck pain down the arms and legs.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Seek immediate medical care when an injury causes radiating neck pain down the arms and legs. Seek evaluation from a medical professional for radiating pain or numbness in the arms or legs causing weakness, even without significant neck pain — subtle signs of a serious spine problem include difficulty with fine motor skills such as changes in handwriting, trouble fastening buttons, and dropping keys or cups. Regardless of cause, seek medical care when neck pain is: - Continuous and persistent (not resolving over time) - Severe - Accompanied by radiating pain or numbness down the arms or legs - Accompanied by headaches, numbness, tingling, or weakness

Note: "KEEP A HIGH THRESHOLD FOR INVASIVE PROCEDURES" ## History to Take - Acute or chronic - Severity of pain - Site and onset of pain - Radiation of pain - Associated features such as fever, trauma, weight lifting, associated tingling or numbness - Anticonvulsants and steroids intake ## Red Flag Signs (consider referral to a higher center for evaluation) - Features of neurological deficit including sudden onset of loss of bladder/bowel control, numbness/paresthesias/weakness of upper limbs or lower limbs - Severe worsening pain, especially at night or when moving the neck - Significant history of trauma - Weight loss, fever, history of cancer

source_note: Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India
text: - Severe worsening pain, especially at night or when moving the neck - Significant history of trauma - Weight loss, fever, history of cancer - First episode of severe pain in a patient over 50 years of age ## Assessment Conduct a full assessment including: - History taking - Physical and neurological examination - Evaluation of red flags - Psychosocial risk factors If red flag signs are present: refer to a higher centre for evaluation. If no red flag signs: proceed to lab test and imaging based on provisional diagnosis, and manage according to duration (acute/sub-acute vs chronic). **Lab and imaging tests (based on provisional diagnosis):** - Lab tests: Hemogram with ESR and CRP - Imaging: X-rays of the Cervical Spine - Anteroposterior (AP) and lateral views; MRI of the Cervical spine ## Acute and Sub-acute Neck Pain (duration less than 12 weeks) - Immobilize neck in acute stage.

source_note: Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Department of Health Research, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India
text: ## Acute and Sub-acute Neck Pain (duration less than 12 weeks) - Immobilize neck in acute stage. Once pain subsides, start neck strengthening exercises and/or physical activity - Recommend neck strengthening exercises and/or physical activity (when pain becomes bearable) - Avoid lifting heavy weights - Prescribe self-care strategies: alternating cold and heat therapy; continuation of Activities of Daily Living as tolerated - Encourage early return to work - Educate the patient that neck pain usually resolves with time - Re-assess at 2-6 weeks (including red flags) if the patient is not returning to normal function or symptoms are worsening - If not improving, consider lab test and imaging, and consider referral to: a physical therapist; an orthopaedic surgeon (for unresolving radicular symptoms); or a multidisciplinary pain program (if not returning to work) ## Chronic Neck Pain (duration greater than 12 weeks) - Consider lab test and imaging (X-rays)

text: # Neck pain and stiff neck Most neck pain only lasts a few weeks and can often be managed with self-care, but it's worth seeing a GP if it doesn't improve. ## Causes - sleeping in an awkward position - poor posture, for example spending long periods sitting at a desk - a pinched nerve - an injury, such as whiplash ## Self-care **Do:** - use a low, firm pillow to support your neck while sleeping - put a heat or cold pack on your neck - try gentle neck-flexibility exercises **Heat/cold application:** - a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel, applied for about 5 minutes, up to 3 times a day - a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel, applied for up to 20 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day **Don't:** - do not wear a neck collar or brace - try to keep your neck moving unless advised otherwise

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: - a hot water bottle wrapped in a towel, applied for up to 20 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day **Don't:** - do not wear a neck collar or brace - try to keep your neck moving unless advised otherwise - do not do activities that need a lot of neck movement, such as driving or cycling, if your neck movement is limited ## When to see a GP See a GP if: - the pain doesn't improve after a few weeks - painkillers aren't helping - you're worried about the pain - you also have other symptoms, such as pins and needles or a cold arm ## Prevention **Do:** - try to keep your head level with your body when sleeping - use a firm mattress - sit upright with your shoulders back and relaxed **Don't:** - do not stay in the same position for long periods - do not sleep on your front - do not twist your neck awkwardly in bed

text: # Osteoporosis Osteoporosis is a health condition that weakens bones, making them fragile and more likely to break. It develops slowly over several years and is often only diagnosed when a fall or sudden impact causes a bone to break (fracture). The most common injuries in people with osteoporosis are broken wrist, broken hip, and broken spinal bones (vertebrae). Breaks can also happen in other bones, such as the arm, pelvis and ribs. ## Symptoms Osteoporosis is not usually painful until a bone is broken, but broken bones in the spine are a common cause of long-term pain. Osteoporosis in the spine can cause the bones that make up the spine to weaken, so they crush or fracture, which can result in a stooped posture in older people as the curvature of the spine increases. ### Osteopenia

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: Osteoporosis in the spine can cause the bones that make up the spine to weaken, so they crush or fracture, which can result in a stooped posture in older people as the curvature of the spine increases. ### Osteopenia Osteopenia is when a bone density scan shows that your bone density is lower than average for your age, but not low enough to be classed as osteoporosis. Osteopenia does not always lead to osteoporosis - whether it progresses depends on a number of factors. ## Causes Losing bone density is a normal part of ageing, but some people lose bone density much faster than normal, leading to osteoporosis and an increased risk of fractures. Things that can increase the risk include: - taking high-dose steroid tablets for more than 3 months - other medical conditions, such as inflammatory conditions, hormone-related conditions, or malabsorption problems - a family history of osteoporosis

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: Things that can increase the risk include: - taking high-dose steroid tablets for more than 3 months - other medical conditions, such as inflammatory conditions, hormone-related conditions, or malabsorption problems - a family history of osteoporosis - having or having had an eating disorder such as anorexia or bulimia - a low body mass index (BMI) - not doing much physical activity, or being unable to move around much - heavy drinking and smoking Women are also at increased risk after the menopause, when levels of the hormone oestrogen (which helps keep bones healthy) drop, particularly if the menopause happens before age 45. ## Diagnosis A FRAX or Q-Fracture online assessment tool may be used to estimate your risk of a fracture over the next 10 years. A DEXA scan is a painless scan that measures bone density and usually takes 10 to 20 minutes. - T score above -1 SD: normal

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: A DEXA scan is a painless scan that measures bone density and usually takes 10 to 20 minutes. - T score above -1 SD: normal - T score -1 to -2.5 SD: osteopenia - T score below -2.5 SD: osteoporosis ## Treatment ### Bisphosphonates Slow the rate at which bone is broken down in the body. Options include alendronic acid, ibandronic acid, risedronate and zoledronic acid. They're usually taken on an empty stomach with water, and you need to remain upright for 30 minutes afterwards. Bisphosphonates usually take 6 to 12 months to work, and you may need to take them for 5 years or longer. Side effects can include irritation of the food pipe, difficulty swallowing and stomach pain. ### SERMs Raloxifene is only recommended for women after the menopause.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: Side effects can include irritation of the food pipe, difficulty swallowing and stomach pain. ### SERMs Raloxifene is only recommended for women after the menopause. It's a daily tablet that can help maintain bone density and reduce the risk of fracture, particularly of the spine. ### Parathyroid hormone ### Supplements All adults should have 10 micrograms of vitamin D a day, and about 700mg of calcium a day. ## Prevention Regular exercise, eating a healthy diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, taking a daily vitamin D supplement, stopping smoking, and cutting down on alcohol can all help keep bones strong and reduce your risk of osteoporosis. ## Living with osteoporosis - Remove hazards at home that could cause a fall - Have regular vision and hearing checks - Manage pain with painkillers, heat or cold treatment, and relaxation techniques - Counselling can help if you're finding it difficult to cope

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)

text: # NICE Guideline NG259: Osteoporosis - Risk Assessment (Recommendations) Published: 29 July 2026. This guideline replaces the fracture-risk-assessment content of the 2012 NICE guideline on osteoporosis (CG146) and covers assessing fragility fracture risk, bone density assessment, deciding whether pharmacological treatment is appropriate, and follow-up. Note: content sourced from the guideline's separate chapter pages — "Fragility fracture risk assessment" (sections 1.1-1.4), "Identifying vertebral fragility fractures" (section 1.5), "Deciding whether pharmacological treatment is appropriate" (section 1.7), and "Follow-up for people not having treatment" (sections 1.8-1.10). ## 1.1 Risk Factors for Fragility Fractures

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ## 1.1 Risk Factors for Fragility Fractures "Assess fragility fracture risk in all people aged 50 and over and women who have experienced menopause with either of the following risk factors: a previous fragility fracture; current or frequent use of systemic glucocorticoids (for example, 5 mg or more prednisolone daily or equivalent for over 3 months, or intermittent use of higher doses)" unless this is a replacement dose for adrenal insufficiency. For men and women under 50 who have not experienced menopause, assess fragility fracture risk only if they have had a previous hip or vertebral fragility fracture, or 2 or more major osteoporotic fractures; consider assessment for a previous non-hip non-vertebral fracture, current/frequent glucocorticoid use, or untreated early menopause/premature ovarian insufficiency. ## 1.3 Risk Prediction Tools

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ## 1.3 Risk Prediction Tools "Complete a full clinical risk assessment alongside a risk prediction tool to determine the 10-year risk of major osteoporotic fracture using either FRAX or QFracture for people aged between 40 and 90," or QFracture for people aged 30-39. Use the same risk prediction tool throughout a person's care, since FRAX and QFracture assess risk differently. Take into account that fragility fracture risk is decreased while taking systemic hormone replacement therapy (HRT). Seek advice from a specialist when assessing fragility fracture risk in people aged under 30, or with rare forms of osteoporosis or bone disease (for example suspected idiopathic osteoporosis, pregnancy-associated osteoporosis, osteogenesis imperfecta, osteomalacia or hypophosphatasia). ## 1.4 Bone Density Assessment

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ## 1.4 Bone Density Assessment "Offer a DXA scan to measure BMD (with or without completing a risk prediction tool) when assessing fragility fracture risk in people aged 30 and over who have had: a previous hip or vertebral fragility fracture; a single major osteoporotic fragility fracture in the last 2 years; or 2 or more fragility fractures." Consider BMD measurement with a DXA scan to help guide treatment decisions for people with a 10-year risk of major osteoporotic fracture of 10% or more. Do a baseline BMD measurement with a DXA scan when starting treatment, unless not tolerated, not technically feasible, or not needed for treatment/monitoring decisions. If there is likely to be a significant delay before a DXA scan, consider fast-tracking within 6 weeks for people likely to need anabolic treatment, or starting antiresorptive treatment while waiting if anabolic treatment is unlikely to be needed.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: If there is likely to be a significant delay before a DXA scan, consider fast-tracking within 6 weeks for people likely to need anabolic treatment, or starting antiresorptive treatment while waiting if anabolic treatment is unlikely to be needed. ## 1.5 DXA-Based Vertebral Fracture Assessment (VFA) Consider doing a VFA when doing a DXA scan for men aged 70 and over, women aged 60 and over, or younger people with a previous major osteoporotic fracture, signs/symptoms of vertebral fracture (for example unexplained back or radiating rib pain, height loss over 4cm, or spinal deformity), suspicion of vertebral fracture from the DXA scan, current/frequent glucocorticoid use, or exceptionally low BMD for age (Z-score less than -2). ## 1.7 Criteria for Pharmacological Treatment

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ## 1.7 Criteria for Pharmacological Treatment "Make a shared decision with the person about whether to start pharmacological treatment based on the following: 10-year risk of major osteoporotic fracture obtained from FRAX or QFracture (if available); BMD from a DXA scan (if available); the number, timing and skeletal sites of previous fragility fractures (especially hip or vertebral fractures); a clinical assessment of risk factors." The guideline notes that "the World Health Organization use BMD T-score to define osteoporosis and osteopenia (T-score of -2.5 or less for osteoporosis, and between -2.5 and -1 for osteopenia)," while acknowledging there is no single BMD threshold below which treatment becomes effective.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: The guideline notes that "the World Health Organization use BMD T-score to define osteoporosis and osteopenia (T-score of -2.5 or less for osteoporosis, and between -2.5 and -1 for osteopenia)," while acknowledging there is no single BMD threshold below which treatment becomes effective. If a DXA scan is not tolerated, not technically feasible, or not needed to inform treatment or monitoring decisions (for example for older people living with frailty), make a shared decision about treatment based on the other listed factors without a DXA scan. Seek specialist advice on treatment options for younger people with fractures or idiopathic osteoporosis, for suspected rare forms of osteoporosis, or for other rare bone diseases associated with fragility fractures. ## 1.8-1.9 Follow-Up for People Not Having Treatment Advise people who have declined or delayed treatment when and how to re-access the service and to contact their GP if their circumstances change.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: ## 1.8-1.9 Follow-Up for People Not Having Treatment Advise people who have declined or delayed treatment when and how to re-access the service and to contact their GP if their circumstances change. For people with a 10-year risk of major osteoporotic fracture below 10%, consider reassessing risk using the same tool used at baseline when there is a change in clinical circumstances, or at 5 years if there is no change. For people with a 10-year risk of 10% or more, or who had a DXA scan but whose condition did not meet treatment criteria, consider reassessing BMD with a DXA scan within 2 to 3 years if their condition was close to meeting treatment criteria (especially with risk of accelerated bone loss), or at 5 years otherwise. ## 1.10 Timing of Follow-Up DXA Scans

text: # Paget's disease of bone Paget's disease of bone disrupts the normal cycle of bone renewal, causing bones to become weakened and possibly deformed. It's fairly common in the UK, particularly in older people, and is rare in people under 50. There's currently no cure, but treatment can help relieve symptoms. Paget's disease of bone can affect 1 bone or several bones. The most commonly affected areas are the pelvis, spine and skull. ## Symptoms Many people with Paget's disease of bone have no symptoms, and it's only found during tests carried out for another reason. When symptoms do occur, they can include: - bone or joint pain - a warm sensation over the affected bone - changes in the shape of a bone - a shooting pain that travels along or across the body, numbness and tingling (peripheral neuropathy), or balance problems, if a bone is pressing on a nerve ## Causes

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: - changes in the shape of a bone - a shooting pain that travels along or across the body, numbness and tingling (peripheral neuropathy), or balance problems, if a bone is pressing on a nerve ## Causes Bone is constantly being renewed - old bone is broken down by cells called osteoclasts, and replaced with new bone by cells called osteoblasts. In Paget's disease of bone, the osteoclasts break down bone too quickly, and the new bone that's produced is larger but weaker than normal bone. It's not clear what triggers this, but you're at a higher risk if you have a family history of Paget's disease of bone - you may inherit a genetic fault that means you're much more likely to develop the condition. ## When to see a GP

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: ## When to see a GP See a GP if you have persistent bone or joint pain, notice a change in the shape of a bone, or have numbness, tingling or balance problems that could suggest a bone is pressing on a nerve. ## Treatment - **Supportive therapies** - including physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and devices such as walking sticks or shoe inserts - **Surgery** - may be needed if further problems develop, such as fractures, deformities or severe joint damage - Getting enough calcium and vitamin D is also recommended ## Complications Possible complications of Paget's disease of bone include fragile bones that are more likely to fracture, osteoarthritis, bone deformities, hearing loss (if the skull is affected), heart problems, and, rarely, bone cancer.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: # Patellofemoral Arthritis ## Anatomy The patella is a small bone located in front of the knee joint — where the femur (thighbone) and tibia (shinbone) meet. It protects your knee and connects the muscles in the front of your thigh to your tibia. The patella rests in a groove on top of the femur called the trochlear groove. When you bend and straighten your knee, the patella moves back and forth inside this groove. A slippery substance called articular cartilage covers the ends of the femur, trochlear groove, and underside of the patella. Articular cartilage helps your bones glide smoothly against each other as you move your leg. ## Description Patellofemoral arthritis occurs when the articular cartilage along the trochlear groove and on the underside of the patella wears down and becomes inflamed. When cartilage wears away, it becomes frayed.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Description Patellofemoral arthritis occurs when the articular cartilage along the trochlear groove and on the underside of the patella wears down and becomes inflamed. When cartilage wears away, it becomes frayed. When the wear is severe, the underlying bone may become exposed. Moving the bones along this rough surface may be painful. ## Cause ### Dysplasia Dysplasia occurs when the patella does not fit properly in the trochlear groove of the femur. Because of this, when the knee moves, there are increased stresses on the cartilage. This begins to wear the cartilage down. ### Kneecap Fracture Patellar (kneecap) fractures often damage the articular cartilage that covers and protects the underside of the bone. Even though the broken bone heals, the joint surface may no longer be smooth. There is friction when the patella moves against the joint surface of the femur.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Even though the broken bone heals, the joint surface may no longer be smooth. There is friction when the patella moves against the joint surface of the femur. Over time, this can lead to arthritis. ## Symptoms The main symptom of patellofemoral arthritis is pain. Typically, the pain is on the front of the knee, behind the kneecap (also known as anterior knee pain). The pain can be present at rest or with no activity at all. Most of the time, however, it is brought on by activities that put pressure on the kneecap, such as: - Going up and down stairs - Sitting with the knees bent - Rising from a chair - Kneeling or squatting In addition, you may experience a crackling sensation called crepitus when you move your knee. Crepitus is sometimes painful and can be loud enough for other people to hear.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Rising from a chair - Kneeling or squatting In addition, you may experience a crackling sensation called crepitus when you move your knee. Crepitus is sometimes painful and can be loud enough for other people to hear. When the disease is advanced, your kneecap may get stuck, or catch, when you straighten your knee. ## Doctor Examination When you visit the doctor, they will do a complete medical history and physical examination, as well as order imaging tests. ### Medical History Your doctor will ask you several questions about your general health, your knee pain, and your ability to function. It is important for your doctor to determine the exact location of your pain so they can determine whether you have patellofemoral arthritis or another condition. ### Physical Exam Your doctor will examine the affected knee in various positions to see if there is pain or restricted motion.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Physical Exam Your doctor will examine the affected knee in various positions to see if there is pain or restricted motion. They will look for creaking or grinding noises (crepitus) that indicate bone-on-bone friction, muscle loss (atrophy), and signs of injury to muscles, tendons, and ligaments. During the exam, the doctor will: - Inspect your knee to determine the overall alignment of the joint - Palpate (feel) around your knee to see if your pain can be reproduced - Test range of motion to determine if you have knee stiffness or problems with patellar tracking (the kneecap moves out of place when the knee straightens or bends) - Assess the quality of the ligaments around the joint and the overall stability of your knee ### Imaging Tests **X-rays.** X-rays provide images of dense structures, such as bone.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Assess the quality of the ligaments around the joint and the overall stability of your knee ### Imaging Tests **X-rays.** X-rays provide images of dense structures, such as bone. Your doctor will order X-rays from several different angles to ensure that your arthritis is limited to the space between the kneecap and the femur, and to assess the overall alignment of your knee. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans.** MRI scans provide images of the soft tissues in your knee. Your doctor may order an MRI to better evaluate the cartilage in your knee. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Treatment of patellofemoral arthritis is similar to the treatment of knee arthritis in general. Most cases can be treated without surgery. Nonsurgical options include: **Exercise.** Regular exercise can decrease stiffness and strengthen the muscles that support your knee.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Most cases can be treated without surgery. Nonsurgical options include: **Exercise.** Regular exercise can decrease stiffness and strengthen the muscles that support your knee. Patients who have patellofemoral arthritis should try to avoid activities that put stress on the front of the knee, such as squatting. If you regularly do high-impact exercise, switching to low-impact activities will put less stress on your knee. Walking and swimming are good low-impact options. **Activity modification.** In many cases, avoiding activities that bring on symptoms — such as climbing stairs — will help relieve pain. **Weight loss.** If you are overweight, losing just a few pounds can make a big difference in the amount of stress you place on your knee. Losing weight can also make it easier to move and maintain independence. **Physical therapy.** Specific exercises can improve range-of-motion in your knee and help with patellar tracking, including:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Losing weight can also make it easier to move and maintain independence. **Physical therapy.** Specific exercises can improve range-of-motion in your knee and help with patellar tracking, including: - Exercises to strengthen the quadriceps muscles and remove some of the load from the patella - Stretching the external rotator muscles around the hip joint If an exercise causes pain, stop the exercise and talk to your doctor or physical therapist. **Viscosupplementation.** In this procedure, a substance is injected into the joint to improve the quality of the joint fluid. The effectiveness of viscosupplementation in treating arthritis is unclear and continues to be studied by researchers. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery is an option when nonsurgical treatment has failed. Several types of surgical procedures are available. **Chondroplasty.** This procedure is done with arthroscopy — inserting thin surgical instruments into small incisions around your knee.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Surgery is an option when nonsurgical treatment has failed. Several types of surgical procedures are available. **Chondroplasty.** This procedure is done with arthroscopy — inserting thin surgical instruments into small incisions around your knee. During a chondroplasty, your surgeon trims and smooths roughened arthritic joint surfaces. Chondroplasty is an option in cases of mild to moderate cartilage wear. **Realignment.** The soft tissues on either side of the kneecap are tightened or released to change the position of the kneecap in the trochlear groove. **Cartilage grafting.** Normal healthy cartilage may be taken from another part of the knee or from a tissue bank to fill a hole in the articular cartilage. This procedure is typically considered only for younger patients who have small areas of cartilage damage.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This procedure is typically considered only for younger patients who have small areas of cartilage damage. **Tibial tuberosity transfer.** This procedure can help relieve pain in patients with arthritis in specific portions of the patella. The patellar tendon below the kneecap attaches to a bump on the front of the knee called the tibial tuberosity. Shifting the bump in any direction will change the position of the kneecap. After the procedure, the patella should move more smoothly in the trochlear groove, reducing pressure on the arthritic areas and relieving pain. **Patellofemoral replacement.** During this partial knee replacement, the surgeon uses special tools to remove damaged cartilage and a small amount of bone from the patellofemoral compartment. A plastic button, or cover, is used to resurface the backside of the patella.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: A plastic button, or cover, is used to resurface the backside of the patella. This button will line up with a thin metal component that is used to resurface the trochlear groove at the end of the femur. These parts are typically secured to the bone with cement. Patellofemoral replacement surgery cannot be performed if there is arthritis involving other parts of the knee. If this is the case, your doctor may recommend a total knee replacement. **Total knee replacement.** In a total knee replacement, all the cartilage surfaces of the knee are resurfaced. The end of the femur and the top of the tibia are capped with a metal prosthesis. A plastic spacer is placed in between these components to create a smooth gliding surface. Additionally, the patella itself is usually resurfaced with a plastic button. ## Outcomes

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: A plastic spacer is placed in between these components to create a smooth gliding surface. Additionally, the patella itself is usually resurfaced with a plastic button. ## Outcomes For most patients, treatment for patellofemoral arthritis is successful in relieving pain and improving function. Outcomes vary, however, depending on patient-specific factors and the type of treatment. Your doctor will talk with you about the expected outcome of treatment in your specific situation.

text: # Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome ## Description Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) is a broad term used to describe pain in the front of the knee and around the patella, or kneecap. Also known as "runner's knee," it affects athletes and non-athletes alike, with particular prevalence among females and young adults. The condition can impair everyday activities like stair climbing and kneeling. ## Anatomy of the Knee The knee comprises the femur's lower end, tibia's upper end, and patella. Ligaments and tendons connect these bones. Key structures include: - **Quadriceps tendon**: Connects thigh muscles to the patella - **Patellar retinacula**: Stabilize the patella by attaching to the tibia - **Patellar tendon**: Stretches from patella to tibia - **Trochlear groove**: A groove where the patella rests and moves

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Patellar tendon**: Stretches from patella to tibia - **Trochlear groove**: A groove where the patella rests and moves - **Articular cartilage**: Enables smooth bone gliding - **Menisci**: Rubbery, C-shaped shock-absorbing disks - **Synovium**: Tissue lining that produces lubricating fluid - **Fat pad**: Cushions the kneecap ## Why PFPS Occurs PFPS develops when nerves sense pain in the soft tissues and bone around the kneecap. Chondromalacia patella — softening of undersurface cartilage — may accompany this condition, causing inflammation and bone pain despite cartilage lacking nerves. ## Cause **Overuse**: Repetitive stress from jogging, squatting, or stair climbing; sudden activity increases in frequency, duration, or intensity; improper training techniques; equipment changes; footwear or playing surface modifications.

Contributing factors include: - Leg alignment problems (hip to ankle) - Patella alta (riding too high) - Muscular imbalances or weakness in quadriceps and hip muscles ## Symptoms The most common symptom of PFPS is a dull, aching pain in the front of the knee. Additional symptoms include: - Pain during knee-bending activities - Pain after prolonged sitting with bent knees - Pain related to activity changes - Popping or crackling sounds ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination Doctor assesses pain location, activity triggers, knee/core strength through squatting and lunging. Evaluation includes: - Lower leg and kneecap alignment - Knee stability and hip rotation
