text: # Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) Injuries ## Anatomy Three bones meet to form your knee joint: the femur (thighbone), the tibia (shinbone), and the patella (kneecap). The kneecap sits in front of the joint to provide some protection. Bones are connected to other bones by ligaments. There are four primary ligaments in your knee. They act like strong ropes to hold the bones together and keep your knee stable. **Collateral ligaments.** These are found on the sides of your knee. The medial collateral ligament is on the inside, and the lateral collateral ligament is on the outside. They control the side-to-side motion of your knee and brace it against unusual movement. **Cruciate ligaments.** These are found inside your knee joint.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: They control the side-to-side motion of your knee and brace it against unusual movement. **Cruciate ligaments.** These are found inside your knee joint. They cross each other to form an X (or cross), with the anterior cruciate ligament in front and the posterior cruciate ligament in back. The cruciate ligaments control the front and back motion of your knee. The posterior cruciate ligament keeps the shinbone from moving backward too far. It is stronger than the anterior cruciate ligament and is injured far less often. The posterior cruciate ligament has two parts, which blend into one structure about the size of a person's little finger. ## Description Injuries to the posterior cruciate ligament are not as common as other knee ligament injuries. In fact, they are often subtle and more difficult to evaluate than other ligament injuries in the knee.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Description Injuries to the posterior cruciate ligament are not as common as other knee ligament injuries. In fact, they are often subtle and more difficult to evaluate than other ligament injuries in the knee. Often, a posterior cruciate ligament injury occurs along with injuries to other structures in the knee, such as cartilage, other ligaments, and bone. Many posterior cruciate ligament tears are partial tears with the potential to heal on their own. People who have injured only their posterior cruciate ligaments may be able to return to sports without experiencing knee stability problems. ## Cause An injury to the posterior cruciate ligament can happen many ways. It typically requires a powerful force. - A direct blow to the front of the knee (such as a bent knee hitting a dashboard in a car crash, or a fall onto a bent knee in sports) - Pulling or stretching the ligament (such as in a twisting or hyperextension injury)

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Pulling or stretching the ligament (such as in a twisting or hyperextension injury) PCL injuries are rarely caused by a simple misstep. ## Symptoms The typical symptoms of a posterior cruciate ligament injury are: - Pain with swelling that occurs steadily and quickly after the injury - Swelling that makes the knee stiff and may cause a limp - Difficulty walking - The knee feels unstable, like it may "give out" ## Doctor Examination During your first visit, your doctor will talk to you about your symptoms and medical history. ### Physical Examination During the physical examination, your doctor will check all the structures of your injured knee, and compare them to your non-injured knee. Your injured knee may appear to sag backwards when bent. It might slide backwards too far, particularly when it is bent beyond a 90-degree angle. ### Imaging Tests Other tests that may help your doctor confirm your diagnosis include X-rays and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: It might slide backwards too far, particularly when it is bent beyond a 90-degree angle. ### Imaging Tests Other tests that may help your doctor confirm your diagnosis include X-rays and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. It is possible, however, for these images to appear normal, especially if the injury occurred more than 3 months before the tests. **X-rays.** Although they will not show any injury to your posterior cruciate ligament, X-rays can show whether the ligament tore off a piece of bone when it was injured. This is called an avulsion fracture. Your doctor may also order stress views, in which the doctor can assess just how far back the shin bone can move. **Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).** MRI scans create better images of soft tissues, like the posterior cruciate ligament, than X-rays. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment If you have injured only your posterior cruciate ligament, your injury may heal quite well without surgery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment If you have injured only your posterior cruciate ligament, your injury may heal quite well without surgery. Your doctor may recommend nonsurgical treatment options: **RICE.** When you are first injured, the RICE method — rest, ice, gentle compression, and elevation — can help speed your recovery. **Immobilization.** Your doctor may recommend a special brace to prevent the tibia bone from sagging backward (gravity tends to pull the bone backward when you are lying down). To further protect your knee, you may be given crutches to keep you from putting weight on your leg. **Physical therapy.** As the swelling goes down, you will start a careful rehabilitation program. Specific exercises will restore function to your knee and strengthen the leg muscles that support it. Strengthening the muscles in the front of your thigh (quadriceps) has been shown to be a key factor in a successful recovery. ### Surgical Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Specific exercises will restore function to your knee and strengthen the leg muscles that support it. Strengthening the muscles in the front of your thigh (quadriceps) has been shown to be a key factor in a successful recovery. ### Surgical Treatment Your doctor may recommend surgery if you have combined injuries. For example, if you have dislocated your knee and torn multiple ligaments including the posterior cruciate ligament, surgery is almost always necessary. Additionally, patients with an isolated PCL tear may benefit from reconstruction if they have persistent instability or pain that is not improving with non-operative treatment. **Rebuilding the ligament.** Because sewing the ligament ends back together does not usually heal, a torn posterior cruciate ligament is typically reconstructed, or rebuilt. Your doctor will replace your torn ligament with a tissue graft. This graft is most often taken from another part of your body, or from another human donor (cadaver).

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Your doctor will replace your torn ligament with a tissue graft. This graft is most often taken from another part of your body, or from another human donor (cadaver). It can take several months for the graft to heal into your bone. Surgery to rebuild a posterior cruciate ligament is typically performed with an arthroscope using small incisions; however, some surgeons will still make an additional incision on the side of the knee. Arthroscopic surgery is less invasive than traditional open surgery. The benefits of less invasive techniques include less pain from surgery and quicker recovery times. Surgical procedures to repair posterior cruciate ligaments continue to improve. More advanced techniques help patients resume a wider range of activities after rehabilitation. ## Rehabilitation Whether or not your treatment involves surgery, rehabilitation plays a vital role in getting you back to your daily activities. A physical therapy program will help you regain knee strength and motion.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Rehabilitation Whether or not your treatment involves surgery, rehabilitation plays a vital role in getting you back to your daily activities. A physical therapy program will help you regain knee strength and motion. If you had surgery, physical therapy will begin 1 to 4 weeks after your procedure. How long it takes you to recover from a posterior cruciate ligament injury will depend on the severity of your injury. Combined injuries often have a slow recovery, but most patients do well over time. If your injury requires surgery, it may be several weeks before you return to a desk job — and possibly months if your job requires a lot of activity. Full recovery typically requires 6 to 12 months. Although rehabilitation is a slow process, your commitment to therapy is the most important factor in returning to activities you enjoy.

text: # Pes Anserine (Knee Tendon) Bursitis ## Description Bursae are small, jelly-like sacs distributed throughout the body, including around the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, and heel. They contain a small amount of fluid and are positioned between bones and soft tissues, acting as cushions to help reduce friction during movement. Pes anserine bursitis is an inflammation of the bursa located between the tibia (shinbone) and three tendons of the hamstring muscle (sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus) on the inner/medial side of the knee. The condition occurs when the bursa becomes irritated and produces extra fluid, which causes it to swell and put pressure on the nearby parts of the knee.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The condition occurs when the bursa becomes irritated and produces extra fluid, which causes it to swell and put pressure on the nearby parts of the knee. Pain and tenderness on the inner/medial side of your knee, about 2 to 3 inches below the joint, are common symptoms of pes anserine bursitis. ## Cause Bursitis is usually caused by overuse, or constant friction and stress on the bursa. Pes anserine bursitis is common in athletes who: - Put extra strain on their hamstrings or inner knee through repetitive motion, such as runners, swimmers, or cyclists - Play sports with lateral (side-to-side) movements or sudden changes in direction, such as soccer, tennis, or basketball People with osteoarthritis of the knee are also at risk. To see whether you have pes anserine bursitis or a different condition, your doctor will examine your knee and talk to you about your symptoms. ## Treatment Treatment of pes anserine bursitis is almost entirely non-operative. text: # Plantar Fasciitis and Bone Spurs ## Overview Plantar fasciitis is one of the most common causes of pain on the bottom of the foot at the heel. Approximately 2 million patients are treated for this condition every year. Heel pain commonly affects athletes due to overuse, overweight individuals due to overload, and people whose work requires extended periods of standing. ## Anatomy The plantar fascia is a long, thin ligament beneath the skin on the bottom of the foot. It connects the heel to the front of the foot and supports the arch. ## Cause The plantar fascia absorbs high stresses from walking, running, and sports activities. Excessive pressure can damage or tear the tissue, triggering the body's inflammatory response, which produces heel pain and soreness. Risk factors include: - New or increased activity - Repetitive high-impact activity (running, dancing, sports) - Prolonged standing on hard surfaces

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Risk factors include: - New or increased activity - Repetitive high-impact activity (running, dancing, sports) - Prolonged standing on hard surfaces - Foot anatomy — flat feet or a high arch - Tight calf muscles - Obesity - Age — most common between 40 and 60 ## Symptoms - Pain on the bottom of the foot near the heel - Pain during the first steps after waking or after periods of rest, which typically subsides within minutes - Increased pain after (not during) exercise or activity ## Doctor Examination The doctor checks for a high arch or flat foot, the area of maximum tenderness on the bottom of the foot just forward of the heel bone, limited upward motion of the ankle, and rules out other conditions such as Achilles tendinitis, a heel stress fracture, or nerve entrapment.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The doctor checks for a high arch or flat foot, the area of maximum tenderness on the bottom of the foot just forward of the heel bone, limited upward motion of the ankle, and rules out other conditions such as Achilles tendinitis, a heel stress fracture, or nerve entrapment. X-rays help rule out other causes of heel pain such as fractures or arthritis, and can show a heel spur, which can result from longstanding tension on the plantar fascia where it attaches to the heel. Notably, most people who have bone spurs on their heels do not have heel pain, so heel spurs are not the cause of plantar fasciitis pain and it can be treated without removing the spur. MRI and ultrasound are not routinely used to diagnose plantar fasciitis and are rarely ordered. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment More than 90% of patients with plantar fasciitis improve within 10 months of starting simple treatment.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: MRI and ultrasound are not routinely used to diagnose plantar fasciitis and are rarely ordered. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment More than 90% of patients with plantar fasciitis improve within 10 months of starting simple treatment. - **Rest**: Reducing or stopping activities that worsen pain; a walking boot and crutches may be used temporarily. - **Changing activity**: Substituting low-impact exercise such as cycling or swimming. - **Stretching**: Plantar fasciitis is aggravated by tight muscles in the feet and calves, and stretching the calves and plantar fascia is the most effective way to relieve pain. - **Calf stretch**: Lean forward against a wall with one knee straight and heel on the ground, the other leg forward with a bent knee, pushing the hips toward the wall; hold 10 seconds, repeat 20 times per foot.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Calf stretch**: Lean forward against a wall with one knee straight and heel on the ground, the other leg forward with a bent knee, pushing the hips toward the wall; hold 10 seconds, repeat 20 times per foot. - **Plantar fascia stretch**: Seated, cross the affected foot over the opposite knee, grasp the toes and slowly pull them toward you (using a towel if needed), holding 10 seconds and repeating 20 times per foot — best done in the morning before standing or walking. - **Ice**: Rolling the foot over cold water or ice for 20 minutes, three to four times daily. - **Physical therapy**: Stretching exercises for the calf muscles and plantar fascia, sometimes with specialized ice treatments, massage, and other inflammation-reducing therapies.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Physical therapy**: Stretching exercises for the calf muscles and plantar fascia, sometimes with specialized ice treatments, massage, and other inflammation-reducing therapies. - **Supportive shoes and orthotics**: Shoes with thick soles and extra cushioning reduce pain with standing and walking; soft silicone heel pads, and pre-made or custom orthotics, can help. Worn athletic shoes should be replaced. - **Night splints**: Most people sleep with their feet pointed down, which relaxes the plantar fascia and contributes to morning heel pain; a night splint stretches the fascia during sleep. Other nonsurgical options if symptoms persist after several months: - **Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)**: High-energy shockwave impulses meant to stimulate healing; results are mixed and it is uncommon, but is noninvasive and low risk, so it is sometimes tried before surgery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT)**: High-energy shockwave impulses meant to stimulate healing; results are mixed and it is uncommon, but is noninvasive and low risk, so it is sometimes tried before surgery. - **Ultrasonic tissue repair**: A minimally invasive, ultrasound-guided probe used to break up and remove damaged fascia tissue. ### Surgical Treatment Because more than 90% of patients recover with nonsurgical treatment, surgery is generally reserved for people who have not improved after 12 months of aggressive nonsurgical treatment. - **Partial plantar fascia release**: Performed via an open approach (larger incision) or endoscopic approach (small incision with a camera) to partially cut the fascia at its heel attachment and relieve tension. Large bone spurs are rarely removed since spurs don't cause the pain. Protected weightbearing is recommended afterward.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Large bone spurs are rarely removed since spurs don't cause the pain. Protected weightbearing is recommended afterward. - **Gastrocnemius recession**: Lengthens a calf muscle for patients who still have difficulty flexing the foot despite extensive calf stretching, since tight calf muscles place added stress on the plantar fascia. Performed via traditional open incision or a smaller incision with an endoscope. Complication rates are low but may include sural nerve damage or calf weakness. Most patients have good results with surgery, but because it can result in chronic pain and dissatisfaction, it is recommended only after trying all nonsurgical treatments.

text: # Polymyalgia rheumatica Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a condition that causes pain, stiffness and inflammation in the muscles around the shoulders, neck and hips. It's an age-related condition, mainly affecting people over 65, and rarely occurs in people under 50. It's more common in women. ## Symptoms - muscle stiffness, especially in the morning, that usually lasts longer than 45 minutes - extreme tiredness - loss of appetite - weight loss - depression ## Causes The exact cause of PMR is not known, but a combination of genetic and environmental factors is thought to be responsible. ## Treatment You'll usually be started on a moderate dose, which is then gradually reduced over time. Most people need a course of steroid treatment that lasts for 12 months to 2 years to prevent their symptoms returning. ## When to see a GP See a GP if you have pain and stiffness that lasts for more than a week.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)

text: # Prepatellar (Kneecap) Bursitis ## Overview Bursae are small, fluid-filled sacs located throughout the body, including around the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, and heel. They function as cushions to help reduce friction between bones and soft tissues. Prepatellar bursitis involves inflammation of the bursa at the patella (front of the kneecap). The condition develops when the bursa becomes irritated and produces too much fluid, which causes it to swell and put pressure on the nearby parts of the knee. ## Cause Prepatellar bursitis frequently results from pressure due to constant kneeling. Workers in plumbing, roofing, carpet laying, coal mining, and gardening face elevated risk. A direct blow to the knee's front can also trigger the condition. Athletes in contact sports — football, wrestling, basketball — face greater risk. Individuals with rheumatoid arthritis or gout are more vulnerable.

This infectious form is less common, but more serious and must be treated more urgently. ## Symptoms - Pain with activity, typically not occurring at night - Rapid swelling on the kneecap's front - Tenderness and warmth to the touch - Infection-related bursitis may produce fluid, redness, fever, and chills ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination Your physician will inquire about symptom severity, symptom duration, and risk factors. text: # Repetitive strain injury (RSI) Repetitive strain injury (RSI) is a term used for pain caused by repeated movement of part of the body. It generally gets better on its own, though recovery can be helped along with appropriate self-care. RSI can affect the shoulders, elbows, forearms, wrists, hands, and fingers, and symptoms usually develop gradually. ## Symptoms - pain, which may feel like burning, aching or throbbing - stiffness - weakness - tingling, pins-and-needles, or numbness - cramp - swelling ## Causes - repetitive activities, such as hairdressing, decorating, typing, or working on an assembly line - sports involving repetitive movements, such as golf or tennis - poor posture, for example while working - regular use of hand-held power tools Repetitive or strenuous work does not always cause RSI. ## Self-care **Do:** - try to keep active and gradually increase how much activity you do

text: - poor posture, for example while working - regular use of hand-held power tools Repetitive or strenuous work does not always cause RSI. ## Self-care **Do:** - try to keep active and gradually increase how much activity you do - put a cold pack on the affected area for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours - talk to your employer about making changes to your workspace or work pattern **Don't:** - avoid resting completely for more than a few days, as this can weaken the affected area ## When to see a GP See a GP if you have symptoms of RSI and they are not going away or are getting worse. ## Treatment - **Physiotherapy** - exercises, massage, and posture advice; free physiotherapy is available through the NHS - **Occupational therapy** - to identify underlying causes and suggest changes to your workspace

text: # Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition that causes pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints. It usually affects the hands, feet and wrists, and symptoms can flare up unpredictably. Some people also experience tiredness and weight loss. ## Symptoms The main symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis are joint pain, swelling and stiffness. - **Pain** - a throbbing and aching pain, often worse in the mornings and after a period of inactivity - **Stiffness** - reduced mobility in the affected joints; morning stiffness from rheumatoid arthritis often lasts longer than the 30 minutes typical of osteoarthritis - **Swelling, warmth and redness** - the lining of joints affected by rheumatoid arthritis becomes inflamed, causing them to swell and feel hot; firm swellings called rheumatoid nodules may develop under the skin around joints General symptoms can include: - tiredness and reduced energy - a high temperature - sweating

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: General symptoms can include: - tiredness and reduced energy - a high temperature - sweating - a poor appetite - weight loss Inflammation can also affect other parts of the body, for example causing dry eyes if the eyes are affected, or chest pain if the heart or lungs are affected. Symptoms may develop gradually over weeks, or progress rapidly over just a few days, and vary considerably between individuals. ## When to see a GP See a GP if you have persistent pain, swelling or stiffness in your joints, even if a diagnosis hasn't been made. Early diagnosis and treatment helps prevent joint damage and reduces the risk of the condition getting worse. ## Causes Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease, where the immune system mistakenly attacks the cells that line joints, causing them to become swollen, stiff and painful. Over time this can damage the joint itself, as well as nearby cartilage and bone. Risk factors include: - being female - having a family history of rheumatoid arthritis

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: Over time this can damage the joint itself, as well as nearby cartilage and bone. Risk factors include: - being female - having a family history of rheumatoid arthritis - smoking The exact trigger for the immune system attack is not known. ## Treatment DMARDs ease symptoms and slow the progression of the condition by blocking the effects of the chemicals released when the immune system attacks joints. A combination of DMARDs is usually given as initial treatment. Side effects can include feeling sick, loss of appetite, a sore mouth, diarrhoea, headaches and hair loss. Regular blood tests are needed to monitor effects on blood cells and the liver. ### JAK inhibitors Usually used in combination with methotrexate. ### Painkillers They provide short-term relief, but long-term use carries risks including weight gain, osteoporosis, easy bruising, muscle weakness and thinning of the skin. ### Supportive treatments

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: ### Painkillers They provide short-term relief, but long-term use carries risks including weight gain, osteoporosis, easy bruising, muscle weakness and thinning of the skin. ### Supportive treatments - **Physiotherapy** can help improve fitness and muscle strength and make joints more flexible, including heat/ice packs and TENS. - **Occupational therapy** provides training and advice to help protect your joints, including splints or other aids. - **Podiatry** can help with foot problems, including joint support or shoe insoles to ease pain. ### Surgery Options include carpal tunnel release, tendon repair, removal of inflamed tissue, arthroscopy, or joint replacement (which typically involves several days in hospital followed by months of rehabilitation; prosthetic joints usually last 10 to 20 years). ### Diet There's no strong evidence that specific diets help, though some people find their symptoms worsen after certain foods.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: ### Diet There's no strong evidence that specific diets help, though some people find their symptoms worsen after certain foods. A Mediterranean-style diet - based on vegetables, fruit, legumes, nuts, beans, cereals, grains, fish and unsaturated fats - is often recommended. ## Complications Possible complications of rheumatoid arthritis include carpal tunnel syndrome, inflammation of other parts of the body (such as the lungs, heart or eyes), and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Proper management of the condition can help reduce the risk of these complications.

text: # NICE Guideline NG100: Rheumatoid Arthritis in Adults - Management (Recommendations) Published: 11 July 2018. Last updated: 12 October 2020 (with further amendments dated 2024). ## 1.1 Referral, Diagnosis and Investigations **Referral from primary care**: "Refer for specialist opinion any adult with suspected persistent synovitis of undetermined cause." Refer urgently (even with a normal acute-phase response, negative anti-CCP antibodies or rheumatoid factor) if the small joints of the hands or feet are affected, more than one joint is affected, or there has been a delay of 3 months or longer between symptom onset and seeking medical advice. **Investigations for diagnosis**: Offer a blood test for rheumatoid factor in adults with suspected RA who have synovitis on clinical examination. Consider measuring anti-CCP antibodies if rheumatoid factor is negative.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: **Investigations for diagnosis**: Offer a blood test for rheumatoid factor in adults with suspected RA who have synovitis on clinical examination. Consider measuring anti-CCP antibodies if rheumatoid factor is negative. X-ray the hands and feet in adults with suspected RA and persistent synovitis. **Investigations following diagnosis**: As soon as possible after diagnosis, measure anti-CCP antibodies (if not already done), X-ray the hands and feet for erosions (if not already done), and measure functional ability (for example using the Health Assessment Questionnaire, HAQ) as a baseline. ## 1.2 Treat-to-Target Strategy Consider a target of remission rather than low disease activity for people at increased risk of radiological progression. Measure CRP and disease activity (for example DAS28) monthly in specialist care until the target is achieved. ## 1.3 Communication and Education

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: Measure CRP and disease activity (for example DAS28) monthly in specialist care until the target is achieved. ## 1.3 Communication and Education Explain the risks and benefits of treatment options in ways that can be easily understood, and offer people the opportunity to talk about and agree all aspects of their care. Offer verbal and written information to improve understanding of the condition and counter misconceptions. Offer the opportunity to take part in educational activities, including self-management programmes. ## 1.4 Initial Pharmacological Management For adults with newly diagnosed active RA: offer first-line treatment with cDMARD monotherapy (oral methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine) as soon as possible, ideally within 3 months of onset of persistent symptoms, escalating dose as tolerated. Consider hydroxychloroquine as an alternative first-line option for mild or palindromic disease.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: Consider hydroxychloroquine as an alternative first-line option for mild or palindromic disease. Consider short-term bridging treatment with glucocorticoids when starting a new cDMARD. Offer additional cDMARDs in combination (step-up strategy) when the treatment target has not been achieved despite dose escalation. ## 1.5 Further Pharmacological Management "Anakinra is not recommended for the treatment of RA, except in the context of a controlled, long-term clinical study," and the combination of TNF inhibitor therapy with anakinra should not be offered. **Glucocorticoids**: Offer short-term glucocorticoid treatment for managing flares to rapidly decrease inflammation. In established RA, only continue long-term glucocorticoid treatment when the long-term complications have been fully discussed and all other treatment options have been offered. ## 1.6 Symptom Control ## 1.7 The Multidisciplinary Team

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: In established RA, only continue long-term glucocorticoid treatment when the long-term complications have been fully discussed and all other treatment options have been offered. ## 1.6 Symptom Control ## 1.7 The Multidisciplinary Team Adults with RA should have ongoing access to a multidisciplinary team, providing periodic assessment of the effect of the disease on their lives (pain, fatigue, everyday activities, mobility, work, social/leisure activities, quality of life, mood, sexual relationships), and access to a named coordinating team member such as a specialist nurse. ## 1.8 Non-Pharmacological Management **Physiotherapy**: Adults with RA should have access to specialist physiotherapy, with periodic review, to improve general fitness and encourage regular exercise, learn exercises for joint flexibility and muscle strength, and learn about short-term pain relief methods such as TENS and wax baths.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: **Physiotherapy**: Adults with RA should have access to specialist physiotherapy, with periodic review, to improve general fitness and encourage regular exercise, learn exercises for joint flexibility and muscle strength, and learn about short-term pain relief methods such as TENS and wax baths. **Occupational therapy**: Access to specialist occupational therapy if there are difficulties with everyday activities or problems with hand function. **Hand exercise programmes**: Consider a tailored strengthening and stretching hand exercise programme for adults with RA who have pain and dysfunction of the hands or wrists, delivered by a practitioner with training and skills in this area. **Podiatry**: All adults with RA and foot problems should have access to a podiatrist, and functional insoles/therapeutic footwear should be available if indicated. **Psychological interventions**: Offer psychological interventions (for example relaxation, stress management, cognitive coping skills) to help adults adjust to living with RA.

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: **Psychological interventions**: Offer psychological interventions (for example relaxation, stress management, cognitive coping skills) to help adults adjust to living with RA. **Diet and complementary therapies**: There is no strong evidence that dietary changes benefit arthritis, though a Mediterranean diet can be encouraged. Complementary therapies may provide short-term symptomatic benefit for some but there is little evidence for long-term efficacy; they should not replace conventional treatment. ## 1.9 Monitoring Consider a review appointment 6 months after achieving the treatment target to confirm it has been maintained. Offer all adults with RA, including those who have achieved the treatment target, an annual review to assess disease activity and damage, measure functional ability, check for comorbidities (including hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, osteoporosis and depression), assess complications, and assess the need for surgical referral. "Do not use ultrasound for routine monitoring of disease activity in adults with RA." ## 1.10 Timing and Referral for Surgery

source_note: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
text: "Do not use ultrasound for routine monitoring of disease activity in adults with RA." ## 1.10 Timing and Referral for Surgery Offer early specialist surgical opinion if persistent pain due to joint damage, worsening joint function, progressive deformity, or persistent localised synovitis do not respond to optimal non-surgical management. Refer urgently, before damage or deformity becomes irreversible, for imminent or actual tendon rupture, nerve compression (for example carpal tunnel syndrome), or stress fracture. Offer urgent combined medical and surgical management for suspected or proven septic arthritis. If cervical myelopathy is suspected, request an urgent MRI scan and refer for specialist surgical opinion. "Do not let concerns about the long-term durability of prosthetic joints influence decisions to offer joint replacements to younger adults with RA."

text: # Rotator Cuff Tears ## Anatomy The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint made up of the humerus (upper arm bone), scapula (shoulder blade), and clavicle (collarbone). The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles that come together as tendons to form a covering around the head of the humerus, attaching it to the shoulder blade and helping lift and rotate the arm. A lubricating sac called a bursa sits between the rotator cuff and the acromion (the bone on top of the shoulder), allowing the tendons to glide freely; this bursa can also become inflamed and painful when the rotator cuff is injured. ## Description When one or more rotator cuff tendons is torn, it becomes partially or completely detached from the head of the humerus — most tears occur in the supraspinatus tendon, but other rotator cuff tendons may be involved.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Description When one or more rotator cuff tendons is torn, it becomes partially or completely detached from the head of the humerus — most tears occur in the supraspinatus tendon, but other rotator cuff tendons may be involved. Tendons often begin by fraying, and as damage progresses can completely tear, sometimes from lifting a heavy object. - **Partial tear**: The tendon is not completely detached — the tear goes only partially through the tendon's thickness, but it is thinner than normal. - **Full-thickness tear**: Part or all of the tendon is detached from the bone. A **full-thickness incomplete tear** detaches only a small part; a **full-thickness complete tear** detaches the tendon completely, leaving essentially a hole in the tendon. ## Cause There are two main causes: injury (acute) and wear (degeneration).

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Cause There are two main causes: injury (acute) and wear (degeneration). - **Injury-related (acute) tear**: Falling on an outstretched arm or lifting something too heavy with a jerking motion can tear the rotator cuff, sometimes alongside a broken collarbone, dislocated shoulder, or wrist fracture. - **Wear-related (degenerative) tear**: Most tears result from gradual wearing down of the tendon that occurs naturally with age and is often relatively painless. Degenerative tears are more common in the dominant arm, and a tear in one shoulder raises the likelihood of a tear in the opposite shoulder, even without pain there. Contributing factors to degenerative tears: - **Repetitive stress**: Repeating the same shoulder motions (baseball, tennis, rowing, weightlifting, many jobs and chores) stresses the muscles and tendons.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Contributing factors to degenerative tears: - **Repetitive stress**: Repeating the same shoulder motions (baseball, tennis, rowing, weightlifting, many jobs and chores) stresses the muscles and tendons. - **Lack of blood supply**: Blood supply to the rotator cuff tendons decreases with age, impairing the body's natural ability to repair tendon damage. People over 40 are at greater risk given normal age-related wear and tear. People who do repetitive lifting or overhead work — such as tennis players, baseball pitchers, painters, and carpenters — are also at risk. Most tears in younger people are caused by traumatic injury such as a fall, rather than overuse. ## Symptoms Common symptoms include: - Pain at rest and at night, especially lying on the affected shoulder - Pain when lifting and lowering the arm or with specific movements - Weakness when lifting or rotating the arm

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Symptoms Common symptoms include: - Pain at rest and at night, especially lying on the affected shoulder - Pain when lifting and lowering the arm or with specific movements - Weakness when lifting or rotating the arm - Crepitus (a crackling sensation) when moving the shoulder in certain positions Tears from a sudden event like a fall usually cause intense pain, a snapping sensation, and immediate weakness. Some rotator cuff tears are not painful at all but still cause weakness and other symptoms. ## Doctor Examination The doctor checks for tenderness, measures range of motion, tests arm strength in different positions, checks for other shoulder joint problems, and may examine the neck to rule out a pinched nerve or arthritis. Imaging tests: - **X-rays**: Usually normal for rotator cuff pain since X-rays don't show soft tissue, but done to rule out other causes such as arthritis, and may reveal a longstanding degenerative tear.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Imaging tests: - **X-rays**: Usually normal for rotator cuff pain since X-rays don't show soft tissue, but done to rule out other causes such as arthritis, and may reveal a longstanding degenerative tear. - **MRI or ultrasound**: Show the soft tissues, including the location and size of a tear. MRI can also indicate how old a tear is based on the quality of the rotator cuff muscles. Ultrasound accuracy depends on the skill of the technician. ## Treatment The goal of treatment is to reduce pain and restore function. Continuing to use the shoulder despite worsening pain can cause further damage and the tear can get larger over time, so early treatment is recommended. Treatment planning considers age, activity level, general health, and the type of tear. ### Nonsurgical Treatment In about 80 to 85% of patients, nonsurgical treatment relieves pain and improves function.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Treatment planning considers age, activity level, general health, and the type of tear. ### Nonsurgical Treatment In about 80 to 85% of patients, nonsurgical treatment relieves pain and improves function. - **Rest** and **activity modification**: Limiting overhead activities and avoiding motions that cause pain. - **Strengthening exercises and physical therapy**: Restore movement, improve flexibility and range of motion, and strengthen supporting muscles. The main advantage of nonsurgical treatment is avoiding major surgical risks (infection, permanent stiffness, anesthesia complications, lengthy recovery, re-tear risk). The disadvantages are that the tear may increase in size over time and activities may need to be limited. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery may be recommended if pain does not improve with nonsurgical methods, or if the patient is very active or uses the arms for overhead work or sports.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Surgical Treatment Surgery may be recommended if pain does not improve with nonsurgical methods, or if the patient is very active or uses the arms for overhead work or sports. Other indicators for surgery include symptoms lasting 6 to 12 months, a large tear (more than 3 cm) with good-quality surrounding tissue, significant weakness and loss of function, or a tear caused by a recent acute injury. Surgery most often involves re-attaching the torn tendon to the head of the humerus; the surgeon will discuss the best procedure for the individual's needs.

text: # Shoulder impingement (rotator cuff related shoulder pain) Note: NHS.uk does not have a page titled specifically "rotator cuff" - rotator cuff tendon problems are covered on the NHS site under shoulder impingement syndrome, since impingement of a rotator cuff tendon is the underlying mechanism. text: # Sciatica Sciatica happens when the sciatic nerve, which runs from your lower back to your feet, is irritated or compressed. It typically improves within a few weeks or months but may recur. ## Symptoms Sciatica usually affects the bottom and back of one leg. Symptoms can include: - sharp, burning pain running down the leg - tingling - numbness - weakness The pain may be worse when moving, sneezing or coughing, and symptoms may develop suddenly or gradually. ## Causes - A slipped disc (the most common cause) - Spinal stenosis - Spondylolisthesis - Back injury ## Self-care **Do:** - continue with normal activities as much as possible - try gentle exercises for sciatica - start doing gentle exercise as soon as you can - put a hot or cold pack on the painful areas - ask a pharmacist about painkillers **Don't:** - do not sit or lie down for long periods ## When to see a GP

text: # Scoliosis Scoliosis is where the spine twists and curves to the side. It can affect people of any age, from babies to adults, but most often starts in children aged 10 to 15. Mild scoliosis often does not need treatment, but more severe cases may need treatment to help stop the curve getting worse or to help improve posture. ## Symptoms - a visibly curved spine - leaning to one side - uneven shoulders - one shoulder or hip sticking out - ribs sticking out further on one side - clothes not fitting well - back pain (this is more common in adults with scoliosis) ## When to see a GP See a GP if you think you or your child might have scoliosis. They may refer you to a specialist and arrange an X-ray to check how severe the curve is. **Scoliosis Support & Research** can help you find specialist centres. ## Causes

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: They may refer you to a specialist and arrange an X-ray to check how severe the curve is. **Scoliosis Support & Research** can help you find specialist centres. ## Causes In around 80% of cases the cause is unknown - this is called idiopathic scoliosis. It's not known to be caused, or made worse, by things like poor posture, exercise or diet, but it does sometimes run in families. Less common causes include: - **Congenital scoliosis** - the bones in the spine did not form properly while the baby was in the womb - **Neuromuscular scoliosis** - abnormal development of the nerves and muscles, associated with conditions such as cerebral palsy - **Degenerative scoliosis** - wear and tear of the spine as you age ## Treatment Treatment depends on age, how severe the curve is, and whether it's likely to get worse.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: - **Degenerative scoliosis** - wear and tear of the spine as you age ## Treatment Treatment depends on age, how severe the curve is, and whether it's likely to get worse. - **Babies and toddlers** - may not need treatment, or a brace may be used to help stop the curve getting worse as they grow - **Older children** - a back brace may be worn while the spine is still growing; surgery is occasionally used to help control growth of the spine Exercise is beneficial for general health, unless a medical professional advises otherwise. ## Living with scoliosis Most people with scoliosis can live a normal, active life. text: # Sesamoiditis and Sesamoid Fracture ## Overview The human body contains a few bones that differ structurally from typical bones. Rather than connecting to other bones through a joint, these specialized bones attach only to a tendon or sit embedded within muscle tissue — these are called sesamoid bones. The largest sesamoid in the body is the kneecap. Two additional tiny sesamoids, about the size of a kernel of corn, are located on the underside of the forefoot near the big toe, one on the outer side and one closer to the center of the foot. This article focuses specifically on sesamoid conditions of the foot. For information about kneecap-related conditions, see separate resources on patellar fractures, patellofemoral arthritis, or patellar tendon injuries. ## Anatomy The pair of sesamoid bones sits beneath the joint of the big toe on the sole of the foot.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Anatomy The pair of sesamoid bones sits beneath the joint of the big toe on the sole of the foot. The tendons responsible for flexing the big toe connect to both sesamoids. The bones are held together by ligaments and a particularly strong plantar plate structure. ## Description and Function Sesamoids work mechanically like pulleys. They provide a smooth gliding surface that lets tendons move easily, increasing the effectiveness with which tendons transmit force generated by muscles. In the forefoot, these bones help distribute weight and assist with lifting the bones of the big toe. Like any bone, sesamoids can break through either a sudden injury or accumulated stress from repetitive use. In addition, the tendons near the sesamoids can become irritated or inflamed — a condition called sesamoiditis, which is a type of tendon inflammation. This condition is seen regularly in ballet dancers, competitive runners, and baseball catchers. ## Symptoms

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This condition is seen regularly in ballet dancers, competitive runners, and baseball catchers. ## Symptoms Discomfort is concentrated under the big toe, in the ball of the foot. The onset differs depending on the specific condition: sesamoiditis typically causes pain that develops gradually, while a sesamoid fracture causes sudden pain following a hyperextension injury (when the toe is bent backward). Affected individuals may or may not develop visible swelling and bruising. Difficulty bending and straightening the big toe is common, and pain often accompanies these movements. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination The doctor will feel the foot and big toe to identify tenderness specifically localized to the sesamoid area, assess active movement of the joints around the big toe and sesamoids, and may gently bend the big toe upward toward the top of the foot to see whether this movement increases pain. ### Imaging **X-rays.** X-rays of the forefoot help establish the diagnosis.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Imaging **X-rays.** X-rays of the forefoot help establish the diagnosis. One notable consideration is that the medial sesamoid (the one closer to the center of the foot) sometimes naturally exists in two separate pieces — a "bipartite" configuration. The way to distinguish this normal variation from an actual fracture is by the appearance of the bone edges: a bipartite sesamoid has smooth borders, while a fractured sesamoid has irregular, jagged edges. Comparison X-rays of the uninjured foot can help with accuracy. **Bone scan.** When initial X-rays appear normal, a bone scan can reveal areas of bone irritation even without a visible fracture line. **MRI.** An MRI is typically not needed for the initial diagnosis.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: **Bone scan.** When initial X-rays appear normal, a bone scan can reveal areas of bone irritation even without a visible fracture line. **MRI.** An MRI is typically not needed for the initial diagnosis. However, when X-rays do not reveal the underlying issue and conservative treatment has not helped, an MRI becomes useful for visualizing soft tissue inflammation near the sesamoids or identifying a stress fracture too subtle to see on X-ray. ## Treatment Management typically starts with conservative methods. Only when nonsurgical approaches fail to relieve symptoms does surgical removal of the sesamoid become a consideration. ### Nonsurgical Treatment **For sesamoiditis:** - Stop the activity causing pain and rest the foot; doctors may recommend either avoiding weight-bearing entirely or limiting it to pain-free positions - Rest and apply cold therapy to the sole of the foot (avoiding direct ice contact with skin by using a protective wrap)

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Rest and apply cold therapy to the sole of the foot (avoiding direct ice contact with skin by using a protective wrap) - Choose footwear with soft soles and minimal heel height; rigid-soled shoes like clogs can also be comfortable - Apply felt-based cushioning to reduce stress on the affected area - Gradually resume activities while continuing to use dense foam padding under the sesamoids for support - Avoid activities that put weight directly on the forefoot - Tape the big toe in a slightly downward-bent position - Use a removable short leg brace for 4 to 6 weeks if symptoms persist **For sesamoid fractures:** - Use rigid-soled shoes or a short leg brace - Tape the toe to restrict movement - Use J-shaped padding around the sesamoid area to reduce pressure during healing - Allow several months for discomfort to fully resolve - Continue using cushioning and orthotic support throughout the healing process ### Surgical Treatment

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Tape the toe to restrict movement - Use J-shaped padding around the sesamoid area to reduce pressure during healing - Allow several months for discomfort to fully resolve - Continue using cushioning and orthotic support throughout the healing process ### Surgical Treatment Surgery is considered for persistent sesamoiditis that has not responded to conservative treatment, for displaced sesamoid fractures where the broken pieces are out of alignment, and for fractures that fail to heal. Surgical repair of a displaced fracture may involve reconstruction with heavy sutures. Surgery for sesamoid pain often involves partial or total removal of the affected sesamoid bone. ## Recovery Recovery time varies depending on the severity of the condition and the intensity of symptoms. An extended period — spanning weeks to months — of protective casting combined with limited weight-bearing is often necessary, since normal walking places substantial force on the forefoot ligaments and sesamoids. The reassuring news is that most sesamoid conditions resolve on their own without surgery.

text: # Shin Splints ## Description Shin splint pain most often occurs on the inside edge of the tibia (shinbone). Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) is an inflammation of the muscles, tendons, and bone tissue around the tibia, with pain typically occurring along the inner border of the tibia where muscles attach to the bone. ## Cause In general, shin splints develop when the muscle and bone tissue (periosteum) in the leg become overworked by repetitive activity. They often occur after sudden changes in physical activity, including: - Changes in frequency, such as increasing the number of exercise days per week - Changes in duration, such as running longer distances - Changes in intensity, such as running on hills after training only on flat surfaces Other contributing factors include having flat feet or abnormally rigid arches, and exercising with improper or worn-out footwear.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Changes in duration, such as running longer distances - Changes in intensity, such as running on hills after training only on flat surfaces Other contributing factors include having flat feet or abnormally rigid arches, and exercising with improper or worn-out footwear. Runners have the highest risk of developing shin splints, along with dancers and military recruits. ## Symptoms The most common symptom is pain along the border of the tibia; mild swelling in the area may also occur. Shin splint pain may be sharp and razor-like or dull and throbbing, may occur both during and after exercise, and may be aggravated by touching the sore spot. ## Doctor Examination After discussing symptoms and medical history, the doctor examines the lower leg. An accurate diagnosis is important, since other problems can affect healing. Additional imaging may be ordered to rule out other causes of shin pain:

text: ## Doctor Examination After discussing symptoms and medical history, the doctor examines the lower leg. An accurate diagnosis is important, since other problems can affect healing. Additional imaging may be ordered to rule out other causes of shin pain: - **Stress fracture**: A small crack in the tibia caused by stress and overuse; if shin splints don't respond to treatment, the doctor may check for this. text: Diagnosis involves measuring pressure within the leg compartments before and after exercise. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment - **Rest**: Since shin splints are typically caused by overuse, standard treatment includes several weeks of rest from the causative activity, substituting lower-impact aerobic activity such as swimming, stationary biking, or elliptical training. - **Ice**: Cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day, not applied directly to the skin. - **Compression**: An elastic compression bandage may prevent additional swelling. - **Flexibility exercises**: Stretching the lower leg muscles may help shins feel better. - **Supportive shoes**: Good cushioning during daily activities helps reduce stress on the shins. - **Orthotics**: People with flat feet or recurrent shin splints may benefit from custom-made or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that align and stabilize the foot and ankle, taking stress off the lower leg.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Orthotics**: People with flat feet or recurrent shin splints may benefit from custom-made or off-the-shelf shoe inserts that align and stabilize the foot and ankle, taking stress off the lower leg. - **Return to exercise**: Shin splints usually resolve with rest and the treatments above. Before returning to exercise, be pain-free for at least 2 weeks, and return at reduced frequency, duration, and intensity compared to before the injury. Guidelines for returning to exercise: warm up and stretch thoroughly beforehand; increase training slowly; if the same pain returns, stop exercising immediately, ice, and rest for a day or two; then resume training for shorter periods, at lower intensity, with more rest between workouts, increasing even more slowly than before. ## Prevention

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Prevention - **Wear a proper-fitting athletic shoe**: Determine foot shape using the "wet test" (stepping out of the shower onto a surface that shows the footprint) — a flat foot shows a full footprint impression, while a high arch shows only the ball and heel. Choose shoes matching the foot pattern and designed for the specific sport. - **Cross train**: Alternate jogging with lower-impact sports like swimming or cycling. - **Barefoot running**: Some people report this helps resolve shin splints, and some research suggests it spreads impact stress among muscles, though there is no clear evidence it reduces injury risk overall. Any such program should start very gradually with short distances to let muscles and feet adjust; barefoot runners are at increased risk of cuts and bruises, and minimalist "toe" shoes also require a slow adjustment period.

text: # Shoulder Impingement/Rotator Cuff Tendinitis ## Anatomy The shoulder comprises three bones: the humerus (upper arm bone), scapula (shoulder blade), and clavicle (collarbone). The rotator cuff tendons attach to the top of the humerus (humeral head) and connect the humerus to the shoulder blade's socket to allow you to move your shoulder and arm. A lubricating sac called a bursa sits between the rotator cuff and the acromion (bony structure on top of the shoulder blade), enabling smooth movement. ## Description Rotator cuff pain stems from three primary causes: - **Tendinitis** — inflammation of the rotator cuff tendons - **Bursitis** — inflammation of the bursa - **Impingement** — the space between the top of your shoulder (acromion) and the rotator cuff tendons becomes smaller when you raise your arm ## Cause

Pain may also develop from minor injuries without obvious causes. ## Symptoms Early symptoms include mild pain at rest and with use, radiating from the front shoulder to the arm side, and sudden pain during lifting. text: # Shoulder Joint Tear (Glenoid Labrum Tear) ## Overview Advances in medical technology have enabled doctors to identify and treat injuries previously undetected 30-40 years ago. A soft fibrous tissue rim called the labrum surrounds the socket to stabilize the joint. The rim deepens the socket by up to 50% so that the head of the upper arm bone fits better, and it serves as an attachment site for several ligaments. ## Description Several types of labral tears exist:

text: # SLAP Tears in the Shoulder ## Overview A SLAP tear involves injury to the labrum, which is the ring of cartilage that surrounds the socket of the shoulder joint. ## Anatomy The shoulder comprises three bones: the humerus (upper arm bone), scapula (shoulder blade), and clavicle (collarbone). The labrum is a rim of strong, fibrous tissue that: - Helps deepen the socket and stabilize the shoulder joint - Serves as an attachment point for shoulder ligaments and a biceps tendon ## Description SLAP stands for "superior labrum anterior and posterior." The injury affects the top (superior) part of the labrum where the biceps tendon attaches, extending from the front (anterior) to the back (posterior) of this attachment point. ## Cause Acute SLAP injuries result from trauma like falls, forceful pulling, rapid arm movements above shoulder level, or dislocations.

text: # Snapping Hip ## Overview Snapping hip is a condition where you experience a snapping sensation or hear a popping sound in your hip during activities like walking, standing from a chair, or swinging your leg. The snapping sensation occurs when a muscle or tendon moves over a bony protrusion in your hip. While typically painless and harmless, it can be bothersome and occasionally progresses to bursitis, which causes painful inflammation. ## Anatomy The hip functions as a ball-and-socket joint where the femur's rounded end fits into a cup-shaped socket (acetabulum) in the pelvis. The acetabulum is surrounded by fibrocartilage called the labrum that provides stability. Ligaments surround and hold the joint together, with tendons attaching muscles from the buttocks, thighs, and pelvis to bones to control movement. Fluid-filled sacs called bursae are positioned strategically around the hip to provide cushioning and facilitate smooth muscle movement over bone. ## Description

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Fluid-filled sacs called bursae are positioned strategically around the hip to provide cushioning and facilitate smooth muscle movement over bone. ## Description ### Outside of the Hip The most common snapping hip location occurs where the iliotibial (IT) band passes over the greater trochanter of the femur. When the hip is straight, the iliotibial band is behind the trochanter. When the hip bends, the band moves over the trochanter so that it is in front of it. The IT band's constant tightness combined with the trochanter's slight protrusion creates the characteristic snapping sound. Repeated snapping may lead to bursitis, involving thickening and inflammation of the fluid-filled bursa. ### Front of the Hip The rectus femoris tendon, running from the front thigh to the pelvis, can cause snapping at the hip's front.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Front of the Hip The rectus femoris tendon, running from the front thigh to the pelvis, can cause snapping at the hip's front. As you bend the hip, the tendon shifts across the head of the thighbone, and when you straighten the hip, the tendon moves back to the side. This back-and-forth motion produces the snapping sensation. Additionally, the iliopsoas tendon may catch on bony prominences at the front of the pelvis bone. ### Back of the Hip Hamstring tendons attaching to the sitting bone (ischial tuberosity) can create snapping in the buttock region when they move across this bony point. This form occurs less frequently than other snapping hip types. ### Cartilage Problems The labrum that lines the socket of the hip can tear and cause a snapping sensation. Damaged cartilage may loosen and float within the joint, causing catching or locking.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This form occurs less frequently than other snapping hip types. ### Cartilage Problems The labrum that lines the socket of the hip can tear and cause a snapping sensation. Damaged cartilage may loosen and float within the joint, causing catching or locking. Although not technically true snapping hip, torn labrum symptoms may resemble it, though typically producing deeper groin pain. ## Cause Snapping hip most commonly results from tightness in surrounding muscles and tendons. People who are involved in sports and activities that require repeated bending at the hip are more likely to experience snapping hip. Dancers face particular vulnerability. Young athletes commonly experience snapping hip due to muscle tightness during adolescent growth spurts. ## Home Remedies For non-painful snapping hip, conservative treatments include: - Reducing activity level and applying ice to the affected area - Modifying sports or exercise activities to avoid repetitive hip movement, such as reducing cycling time or swimming using only arm movements Consult a doctor if discomfort persists after these conservative approaches.

text: # Scapular (Shoulder Blade) Disorders ## Overview The scapula (shoulder blade) is a bone, shaped like a triangle, on the upper back. It's supported by muscles that enable arm movement. When these muscles weaken or become imbalanced, the scapula's position can shift, potentially causing arm movement difficulties, weakness, and shoulder joint misalignment. Treatment typically involves physical therapy targeting muscle strengthening and restoration of proper scapular positioning. ## Anatomy The shoulder functions as a ball-and-socket joint where the head of the humerus (upper arm bone) is the ball, and the scapula (shoulder blade) forms the socket. Multiple muscle and ligament attachments connect the scapula and arm to the body. The acromion connects to the clavicle through the acromioclavicular joint. During arm movement, the scapula must move correspondingly to maintain the ball and socket in normal alignment. ## Description

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The acromion connects to the clavicle through the acromioclavicular joint. During arm movement, the scapula must move correspondingly to maintain the ball and socket in normal alignment. ## Description Scapular disorders involve changes in either resting position or motion patterns. The medical term is scapular dyskinesis ("dys" = alteration of, "kinesis" = movement). Alterations typically become visible from behind, where the medial (inner) border of the affected shoulder blade will appear more prominent. This prominence increases during arm movement, commonly called a "winged" scapula. ## Causes Scapular dyskinesis results from: - Weakness, imbalance, tightness, or detachment of controlling muscles - Nerve injuries supplying the muscles - Bone injuries or shoulder joint injuries ## Symptoms - Pain/tenderness around the scapula, especially top and medial border - Arm weakness or fatigue during vigorous use

If symptoms are relieved and the arc of motion is increased, it is an indication that the muscles are not strong enough to raise the arm. - **Scapular retraction test (SRT):** The physician tests arm strength with the extended arm, then manually retracts the scapula and retests. text: # Lumbar Spinal Stenosis Lumbar spinal stenosis is a common cause of low back and leg pain, or sciatica. The condition develops as the spine ages and degenerative changes narrow the spinal canal, compressing the nerves. It most commonly affects adults over 60. ## Causes Arthritis represents the primary cause. As spinal disks lose water content with age, they shrink and collapse. This settling creates two problems: increased pressure on the facet joints (triggering arthritis) and shrinking of the nerve exit tunnels. Degenerating facet joints develop bone spurs, and thickened ligaments further crowd the nerve space. ## Symptoms Common presentations include: - Back pain (variable intensity) - Burning pain in the buttocks or legs (sciatica) - Numbness or tingling sensations - Leg weakness or foot drop - Cauda equina syndrome (a medical emergency involving bowel/bladder dysfunction)

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) — OrthoInfo
text: - Burning pain in the buttocks or legs (sciatica) - Numbness or tingling sensations - Leg weakness or foot drop - Cauda equina syndrome (a medical emergency involving bowel/bladder dysfunction) Patients typically feel better when leaning forward or sitting; standing and walking worsen the pain. ## Nonsurgical Treatment Options - Physical therapy and core strengthening - Acupuncture and chiropractic manipulation (with caution) - Lumbar traction (limited scientific evidence of benefit) ## Surgical Treatment Two main approaches: **Laminectomy:** Removes bone, spurs, and ligaments compressing the nerves. Can use open or minimally invasive techniques. **Spinal fusion:** Combines decompression with stabilization for arthritis-related instability. Recovery typically involves a hospital stay, physical therapy, and a gradual return to activities over weeks to months.

text: # Adult Spondylolisthesis of the Low Back ## Overview Spondylolisthesis occurs when one of the bones in your spine — called a vertebra — slips forward and out of place. This condition most commonly affects the lower back and may produce no symptoms, or cause pain ranging from mild to severe. ## Anatomy The spine consists of stacked vertebrae connected by flexible intervertebral disks that function as shock absorbers during movement. ## Description When vertebrae slip forward, the spine becomes unstable, potentially causing pain and accelerating bone spur formation and arthritis. ## Causes ### Degenerative Spondylolisthesis (DS) Age-related wear weakens intervertebral disks and supporting ligaments. Women over 50 are more susceptible, with higher incidence among African-American populations. ### Isthmic Spondylolisthesis A stress fracture in the pars interarticularis — typically occurring during adolescence — causes vertebral slippage.

About 4% to 6% of the U.S. population has spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis. ## Symptoms **Degenerative**: Leg weakness when standing or walking, numbness, tingling, and pain relieved by forward bending or sitting. **Isthmic**: Low back pain considered activity-related, sometimes accompanied by leg pain. ## Diagnosis Doctors use medical history, physical examination, X-rays, MRI scans, and CT imaging to confirm diagnosis. ## Treatment Options Surgery becomes an option after 3-6 months of failed conservative treatment, with success rates exceeding 85%.

text: # Cervical Spondylosis: Arthritis of the Neck ## Overview Neck pain frequently stems from age-related changes. Cervical spondylosis, commonly called arthritis of the neck, is the medical term for these age-related, wear-and-tear changes that occur over time. This condition affects over 85% of people older than 60, though many experience no symptoms. ## Anatomy The cervical spine consists of seven vertebrae forming the neck. The spine contains the spinal cord and nerve roots, intervertebral disks (shock absorbers made of an outer annulus fibrosus and soft nucleus pulposus center), and facet joints providing stability. ## Causes Cervical spondylosis results from normal degenerative aging. As disks lose water content and height, they weaken. Increased pressure causes facet joints to deteriorate. Cartilage wearing away can trigger bone spur formation, potentially narrowing the space for nerves (stenosis).

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) — OrthoInfo
text: As disks lose water content and height, they weaken. Increased pressure causes facet joints to deteriorate. Cartilage wearing away can trigger bone spur formation, potentially narrowing the space for nerves (stenosis). **Risk factors include:** - Age (most significant factor) - Family history of neck problems - Smoking - Repetitive occupational neck motion - Depression or anxiety - Previous neck trauma ## Symptoms Many people remain asymptomatic. When present, symptoms include: - Mild to severe neck pain and stiffness - Pain worsening with prolonged neck positioning - Headaches - Grinding sensations during neck movement - Numbness/weakness in arms and hands (if nerve compression occurs) - Balance problems or muscle spasms ## Doctor Examination Physicians conduct thorough physical examinations testing arm and hand strength, reflexes, sensation, flexibility, and gait.

text: # Cervical Spondylosis ## Overview Cervical spondylosis is a prevalent condition affecting individuals over 40, characterized by neck and shoulder pain, often in people over 40. It is the medical term for neck problems caused by age-related "wear and tear" to bones and discs in the neck. ## Symptoms The condition presents with: - Neck and shoulder discomfort or stiffness that fluctuates - Headaches originating at the base of the neck - Many people experience no symptoms at all, as this represents a normal part of aging ## Self-Care Measures Recommended approaches include: - Performing gentle neck exercises - Correcting postural habits ## When to Seek Medical Attention **Non-urgent (see a GP):** Consult a GP if pain persists beyond several weeks or worsens with movement. **Urgent (call NHS 111):** Seek help for severe sudden pain, arm/leg weakness, tingling sensations, or shoulder blade pain.

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: **Urgent (call NHS 111):** Seek help for severe sudden pain, arm/leg weakness, tingling sensations, or shoulder blade pain. **Emergency (call 999):** Call for walking difficulties, loss of bladder or bowel control, sudden loss of coordination, facial drooping, arm weakness, or speech problems. ## Clinical Treatment Medical professionals examine the neck, test reflexes, and may order imaging. Treatment involves exercises, maintaining activity levels, and potentially muscle relaxants for chronic pain. Surgery is reserved for nerve compression or spinal cord involvement. ## Causes Age-related wear and tear of spinal bones and discs cause the condition, with increased risk following previous neck injuries or in people with a family history.
