text: # Sprains, Strains & Other Soft-Tissue Injuries ## Overview Soft-tissue injuries affect muscles, tendons, and ligaments, and typically occur during sports and exercise. Common examples include sprains, strains, and contusions, as well as tendinitis and bursitis, and even with appropriate treatment these injuries may require a long time to heal. ## Cause: Acute vs. Overuse Injuries Soft-tissue injuries fall into two basic categories: **Acute injuries** are caused by a sudden trauma, such as a fall, twist, or blow to the body. Examples include sprains, strains, and contusions. **Overuse injuries** occur gradually over time when an athletic or other activity is repeated so often that the soft tissues do not have enough time to recover. Tendinitis and bursitis are examples of overuse injuries. ## RICE Protocol for Acute Injuries

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: Tendinitis and bursitis are examples of overuse injuries. ## RICE Protocol for Acute Injuries Initial treatment for most acute soft-tissue injuries follows the RICE protocol: - **Rest**: Take a break from the activity that caused the injury. Your doctor may recommend that you use crutches to avoid putting weight on an injured leg. - **Ice**: Use cold packs for 20 minutes out of 1 hour, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly to the skin. - **Compression**: To help stop swelling, wear an elastic compression bandage. - **Elevation**: To reduce swelling, elevate the injury higher than your heart while resting. ## Sprains A sprain is a stretch and/or tear of a ligament, a strong band of connective tissue that connects the end of one bone with another. Ligaments stabilize and support the body's joints.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: ## Sprains A sprain is a stretch and/or tear of a ligament, a strong band of connective tissue that connects the end of one bone with another. Ligaments stabilize and support the body's joints. The most vulnerable areas for sprains are the ankles, knees, and wrists -- for example, ankle sprains from the foot turning inward, knee sprains from a sudden twist, and wrist sprains from a fall onto an outstretched hand. Sprains are classified by severity: - **Grade 1 (mild)**: Slight stretching and some damage to the fibers of the ligament. - **Grade 2 (moderate)**: Partial tearing of the ligament, with abnormal looseness (laxity) in the joint. - **Grade 3 (severe)**: Complete tear of the ligament, causing significant instability. Common symptoms across all grades include pain, bruising, swelling, and inflammation.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: - **Grade 3 (severe)**: Complete tear of the ligament, causing significant instability. Common symptoms across all grades include pain, bruising, swelling, and inflammation. **Treatment** begins with the RICE protocol and physical therapy. Moderate sprains often require bracing (for example, CAM walking boots for ankle sprains, or hinged knee braces). Severe sprains may require surgery to repair torn ligaments. ## Strains A strain is an injury to a muscle and/or tendon. Tendons are fibrous cords of tissue that attach muscles to bone. Common locations for strains include the back, neck, and legs (particularly the hamstring). A strain may involve a simple stretch of a muscle or tendon, or it may involve a partial or complete tear. Symptoms include pain, muscle spasm, muscle weakness, swelling, inflammation, and cramping.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: A strain may involve a simple stretch of a muscle or tendon, or it may involve a partial or complete tear. Symptoms include pain, muscle spasm, muscle weakness, swelling, inflammation, and cramping. Sports at risk for strains include contact sports (soccer, football, hockey, boxing, wrestling) and quick-start sports (basketball, sprinting), which can cause hamstring strains; running-heavy sports (football, soccer, tennis, basketball), which can cause calf strains; gymnastics, tennis, rowing, and golf, which can cause hand strains through extensive gripping; and racquet, throwing, and contact sports, which can cause elbow strains. **Treatment** is the same as for sprains: rest, ice, compression, and elevation, followed by exercises to relieve pain and restore mobility. Surgery may be needed for severe tears. ## Contusions (Bruises)

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: **Treatment** is the same as for sprains: rest, ice, compression, and elevation, followed by exercises to relieve pain and restore mobility. Surgery may be needed for severe tears. ## Contusions (Bruises) Contusions occur when a direct blow (or repeated blows) by a blunt object strikes part of the body, crushing underlying muscle fibers and connective tissue without breaking the skin. Discoloration results from blood pooling around the injury. Most contusions respond well to the RICE protocol. Quadriceps contusions specifically benefit from a compression wrap and temporary immobilization of the thigh with the knee in a bent position. Persistent symptoms warrant medical evaluation to prevent permanent damage. ## Tendinitis Tendinitis is an inflammation or irritation of a tendon or the covering of a tendon (called a sheath). It results from a series of small stresses that repeatedly aggravate the tendon, with symptoms of swelling and pain that worsens with activity.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: It results from a series of small stresses that repeatedly aggravate the tendon, with symptoms of swelling and pain that worsens with activity. Sports with high risk for tendinitis include overhead sports (baseball, softball, swimming, tennis, volleyball, golf), which affect the shoulders and elbows, and running and jumping sports (soccer, basketball, running, aerobic dancing), which affect the knees and ankles. Persistent inflammation may cause significant damage to the tendon, which may require surgery. ## Bursitis Bursae are small, jelly-like sacs located throughout the body, including around the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, and heel. They contain fluid and act as cushions to reduce friction. Bursitis results when repeated small stresses and overuse cause the bursa to swell, and it often accompanies tendinitis.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: They contain fluid and act as cushions to reduce friction. Bursitis results when repeated small stresses and overuse cause the bursa to swell, and it often accompanies tendinitis. Surgery is rarely needed unless infection occurs; removal may be performed via standard incision (open procedure) or as an arthroscopic procedure with small incisions. ## Prevention Injuries often occur when people suddenly increase the duration, intensity, or frequency of their activities. Many soft-tissue injuries can be prevented through proper conditioning and training. Specific prevention strategies include: - **Equipment**: Replace athletic shoes as they wear out, and wear comfortable, loose-fitting clothes that let you move freely. - **Fitness balance**: Develop a balanced fitness program that incorporates cardiovascular exercise, strength training, and flexibility. Add activities and new exercises cautiously, no more than one or two new activities per workout. - **Warm-up**: Warm up to prepare for exercise, even before stretching.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: Add activities and new exercises cautiously, no more than one or two new activities per workout. - **Warm-up**: Warm up to prepare for exercise, even before stretching. Warming up increases your heart and blood flow rates and loosens up muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints. - **Stretching**: Begin stretches slowly and carefully until reaching a point of muscle tension. Hold each stretch for 10 to 20 seconds, then slowly release. Never stretch to the point of pain, always maintain control, and never bounce on a muscle that is fully stretched. - **Hydration**: Drink 1 pint of water 15 minutes before you start exercising and another pint after you cool down. Have a drink of water every 20 minutes or so while you exercise. - **Cool-down**: Make cooling down the final phase of your exercise routine. It should take twice as long as your warm-up, for at least 10 minutes before you stop completely.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: - **Cool-down**: Make cooling down the final phase of your exercise routine. It should take twice as long as your warm-up, for at least 10 minutes before you stop completely. - **Rest and pacing**: Schedule regular days off from vigorous exercise and rest when tired. Fatigue and pain are good reasons not to exercise. Avoid being a "weekend warrior"; aim for at least 30 minutes of moderate physical activity every day, and resume sports slowly after extended breaks.

text: # Sprains and Strains ## Overview Sprains and strains are common injuries that affect the muscles and ligaments. Most can be treated at home without needing to see a GP. ## Symptoms It's likely to be a sprain or strain if you have pain, tenderness or weakness - usually around your ankle, foot, wrist, thumb, knee, leg or back - along with swelling, bruising, being unable to put weight on the injury or use it normally, and muscle spasms or cramping. ## Sprain vs Strain A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. Sprains are most common in your wrists, ankles, thumbs and knees. A strain is an overstretched or torn muscle (sometimes called a "pulled" muscle). Strains most often happen in your feet, legs or back. ## Self-Treatment: PRICE Therapy For the first 2 to 3 days, follow the five steps known as PRICE:

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: Strains most often happen in your feet, legs or back. ## Self-Treatment: PRICE Therapy For the first 2 to 3 days, follow the five steps known as PRICE: 1. **Protection** - protect the area from further injury, for example by using a support 2. **Rest** - stop exercising and try to avoid putting weight on the injury 3. **Ice** - apply an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel) to the injury for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours 4. **Compression** - wrap a bandage around the injury to support it 5. **Elevation** - keep it raised on a pillow as much as possible During this time, try to avoid heat (such as hot baths), alcohol, running, or massage, as this may increase swelling. When you can move the injured area without pain stopping you, try to keep moving it so the joint or muscle does not become stiff.

Severe sprains and strains can take months to heal fully. ## When to Get Further Help Call NHS 111 or get help from 111 online if: - the pain or swelling gets worse, or does not start to improve after a few days of treating it at home - you cannot put any weight at all on the injury or you cannot use the affected joint - the area feels stiff and it's hard to move it - you have a very painful lump on the muscle - you have tingling or loss of sensation - the injury has not improved after 2 weeks

text: # Tennis Elbow (Lateral Epicondylitis) ## Overview Tennis elbow, or lateral epicondylitis, is a painful condition of the elbow caused by overuse, involving degeneration or microtearing of the tendons that join the forearm muscles on the outside of the elbow. Treatment for tennis elbow in most cases involves a team approach with primary care doctors, physical or occupational therapists, and sometimes surgeons working together. ## Anatomy The elbow joint is made up of the humerus (upper arm bone) and the radius and ulna (forearm bones). Bony prominences called epicondyles are where forearm muscles begin; the bony prominence on the outside of the elbow is the lateral epicondyle. Tennis elbow involves the muscles and tendons responsible for extending the wrist and fingers, particularly the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon, which connects the ECRB forearm muscle to the lateral epicondyle.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Tennis elbow involves the muscles and tendons responsible for extending the wrist and fingers, particularly the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) tendon, which connects the ECRB forearm muscle to the lateral epicondyle. ## Cause - **Overuse**: The ECRB muscle helps stabilize the wrist when the elbow is straight. When weakened from overuse, microscopic tears form in the ECRB tendon where it attaches to the lateral epicondyle. The muscle's anatomical position contributes to wear and tear as the elbow bends and straightens. - **Activities**: Beyond athletes, many people with tennis elbow have jobs or hobbies requiring repetitive, vigorous forearm use — painters, plumbers, carpenters, auto workers, cooks, and butchers have higher rates. - **Age**: Most people who get tennis elbow are between 30 and 50, although anyone with risk factors can develop it.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Age**: Most people who get tennis elbow are between 30 and 50, although anyone with risk factors can develop it. - **Unknown cause**: Lateral epicondylitis can occur without any recognized repetitive injury — this is called idiopathic (of unknown cause). ## Symptoms Symptoms develop gradually; in most cases pain begins as mild and slowly worsens over weeks and months. Common signs include pain or burning on the outer elbow, weak grip strength, and sometimes pain at night. Symptoms are often worsened by forearm activity such as holding a racquet, turning a wrench, or shaking hands. The dominant arm is typically affected, though both arms can be involved. ## Doctor Examination The doctor considers how the symptoms developed and any occupational or recreational risk factors, discussing which activities trigger symptoms and where the pain is located.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The dominant arm is typically affected, though both arms can be involved. ## Doctor Examination The doctor considers how the symptoms developed and any occupational or recreational risk factors, discussing which activities trigger symptoms and where the pain is located. During examination, the doctor applies gentle pressure to the lateral epicondyle to check for pain and tenderness, and may test resistance by having the patient try to straighten the wrist and fingers with the arm fully extended. Tests that may be used: - **X-rays**: Rule out elbow arthritis. - **MRI scans**: Show soft-tissue detail, the extent of tendon damage, or rule out cervical (neck) issues. - **Electromyography (EMG)**: Rules out nerve compression, since several nerves around the elbow can cause similar symptoms. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Approximately 80 to 95% of patients have success with nonsurgical treatment.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment Approximately 80 to 95% of patients have success with nonsurgical treatment. - **Rest**: Stopping or decreasing participation in sports, heavy work, and other symptom-triggering activities for several weeks. - **Physical or occupational therapy**: Exercises to strengthen the forearm muscles; therapists may also use ultrasound, ice massage, or muscle-stimulating techniques. - **Brace**: A brace centered over the back of the forearm can rest the muscles and tendons and relieve symptoms. - **Platelet-rich plasma (PRP)**: Blood is drawn and centrifuged to concentrate platelets and their growth factors, which are then injected; results have been mixed, though some studies show promise. - **Extracorporeal shock wave therapy**: Sound waves create microtrauma intended to promote healing; many doctors consider it experimental.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Extracorporeal shock wave therapy**: Sound waves create microtrauma intended to promote healing; many doctors consider it experimental. - **Equipment check**: For racquet sports, ensuring proper equipment fit — stiffer or looser-strung racquets can reduce forearm stress. ### Surgical Treatment If symptoms do not respond after 6 to 12 months of nonsurgical treatment, surgery may be recommended. Most procedures involve removing diseased tendon and reattaching healthy tendon to bone; the approach depends on the scope of the injury, general health, and personal needs. - **Open surgery**: The most common approach, involving an incision over the outside of the elbow, usually performed as outpatient surgery. - **Arthroscopic surgery**: Uses miniature instruments and small incisions, also outpatient. Surgical risks include infection, nerve and blood vessel damage, prolonged rehabilitation, loss of strength, loss of flexibility, and the possible need for further surgery.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Arthroscopic surgery**: Uses miniature instruments and small incisions, also outpatient. Surgical risks include infection, nerve and blood vessel damage, prolonged rehabilitation, loss of strength, loss of flexibility, and the possible need for further surgery. After surgery, the arm may be splinted temporarily; sutures and splint are typically removed about a week later, stretching exercises begin after splint removal, light strengthening starts around 2 months after surgery, and return to athletic activity typically occurs 4 to 6 months after surgery. Tennis elbow surgery is considered successful in 80 to 90% of patients, though some loss of strength is not uncommon. ## Related Condition: Golfer's Elbow

text: # Tennis elbow Tennis elbow is a condition that causes pain around the outside of the elbow. It usually goes away with rest but can sometimes last over a year. This NHS page covers tennis elbow specifically; it does not also cover golfer's elbow. ## Symptoms - pain on the outer part of the elbow, ranging from mild to severe - tenderness or swelling in the elbow - pain that spreads into the forearm - difficulty fully straightening the arm - symptoms worsen with lifting, gripping, or twisting the wrist Tennis elbow is more common in people aged 35 to 54. ## Causes Tennis elbow is caused by inflamed tendons in the elbow, usually from repetitive gripping and wrist-twisting movements - for example from typing, manual work, racquet sports, or playing a musical instrument. ## Self-care - avoid the activities that make the pain worse - apply a hot or cold pack to the elbow for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours

source_note: NHS (National Health Service, UK)
text: ## Self-care - avoid the activities that make the pain worse - apply a hot or cold pack to the elbow for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours - try simple exercises such as gently bending the arm - wear a forearm strap or brace ## When to see a GP See a GP if you still have elbow pain after resting your elbow and trying self-care treatments for at least 2 weeks. ## Treatment - a GP may prescribe anti-inflammatory tablets - physiotherapy - usually offered after 6 weeks without improvement - may include massage, stretching exercises, and ultrasound therapy - surgery may be considered if symptoms persist for 6 to 12 months despite other treatment

text: # Muscle Strains in the Thigh ## Overview A muscle strain (muscle pull or tear) is a common injury, particularly among people who participate in sports. The thigh has three sets of strong muscles: - The hamstring muscles in the back of the thigh - The quadriceps muscles in the front of the thigh - The adductor muscles on the inside of the thigh The quadriceps and hamstrings work together to straighten (extend) and bend (flex) the leg. The adductor muscles pull the legs together. The hamstring and quadriceps muscle groups are particularly at risk for muscle strains because they cross both the hip and knee joints. They are also used for high-speed activities, such as track and field events (running, hurdles, long jump), football, basketball, and soccer. Muscle strains usually happen when a muscle is stretched beyond its limit, tearing the muscle fibers.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: They are also used for high-speed activities, such as track and field events (running, hurdles, long jump), football, basketball, and soccer. Muscle strains usually happen when a muscle is stretched beyond its limit, tearing the muscle fibers. This injury frequently occurs near the point where the muscle joins the tough, fibrous connective tissue of the tendon. A direct blow to the muscle may also cause a similar injury. Muscle strains in the thigh can be quite painful. Once a muscle strain occurs, the muscle is vulnerable to reinjury. It is important to let the muscle heal properly and to follow preventive guidelines from your doctor. ## Symptoms - A person who experiences a muscle strain in the thigh will frequently describe "a popping or snapping sensation as the muscle tears." - Pain is sudden and may be severe. - The area around the injury may be tender to the touch, with visible bruising if blood vessels are also broken.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Pain is sudden and may be severe. - The area around the injury may be tender to the touch, with visible bruising if blood vessels are also broken. - Swelling and areas of ecchymosis ("black and blue") may often extend below the thigh into the calf and ankle, possibly occurring 1 or 2 days after the injury. ## Doctor Examination - Your physician will ask about the injury and examine your thigh for tenderness or bruising. - You may be asked to bend or straighten your knee and/or hip so the doctor can confirm the diagnosis. - An X-ray may be needed if there is a possible fracture or other injury to the bone. - Your doctor may also order a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to further evaluate the muscles and tendons in your leg. Muscle strains are graded according to their severity.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Your doctor may also order a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan to further evaluate the muscles and tendons in your leg. Muscle strains are graded according to their severity. A grade 1 strain is mild and usually heals fairly quickly, whereas a grade 3 strain is a severe tear of the muscle that may take months to heal. ## Treatment Most muscle strains can be treated with the RICE protocol. RICE stands for: - **Rest**: Take a break from the activity that caused the strain. Your physician may recommend that you use crutches to avoid putting weight on the leg. - **Ice**: Use cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly to the skin. - **Compression**: To prevent additional swelling, lightly wrap the injured area in a soft bandage or ace wrap. - **Elevation**: To minimize swelling, elevate your leg up above the level of your heart.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Compression**: To prevent additional swelling, lightly wrap the injured area in a soft bandage or ace wrap. - **Elevation**: To minimize swelling, elevate your leg up above the level of your heart. As the pain and swelling subside, physical therapy will help improve range of motion and strength. The muscle should be at full strength and pain-free before you return to sports. This will help prevent additional injury. ## Prevention ### Risk Factors Several factors can increase your risk of muscle strains, including: - **Muscle tightness**: Tight muscles are vulnerable to strain. Athletes should follow a year-round program of daily stretching exercises. - **Muscle imbalance**: Because the quadriceps and hamstring muscles work together, if one is stronger than the other, the weaker muscle can become strained. - **Poor conditioning**: If your muscles are weak, they are less able to cope with the stress of exercise and are more likely to be injured.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Poor conditioning**: If your muscles are weak, they are less able to cope with the stress of exercise and are more likely to be injured. - **Muscle fatigue**: Fatigue reduces the energy-absorbing capabilities of muscles, making them more prone to injury. ### Precautions You can take the following precautions to help prevent muscle strain: - Condition your muscles with a regular exercise program. You can ask your physician about exercise programs for people of your age and activity level. - Warm up before any exercise session or sports activity, including practice. A good warm up prepares your body for more intense activity. It gets your blood flowing, raises your muscle temperature, and increases your breathing rate. Warming up gives your body time to adjust to the demands of exercise and can help increase range of motion and reduce stiffness. - Take time to cool down after exercise. Stretch slowly and gradually, holding each stretch to give the muscle time to respond and lengthen.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - Take time to cool down after exercise. Stretch slowly and gradually, holding each stretch to give the muscle time to respond and lengthen. - If you are injured, take the time needed to let the muscle heal before you return to sports. Wait until your muscle strength and flexibility return to preinjury levels. This can take 10 days to 3 weeks for a mild strain, and up to 6 months for a severe strain, such as a hamstring strain. ## Be Aware of Other Similar Injuries While muscle strains can occur at the junction of the muscle and tendon or in the middle of the muscle, it is important to make sure you have not sustained a high-grade or complete injury of the tendon where it attaches to bone. A hamstring tear — when the hamstring detaches from the ischial tuberosity, or "sit bone," part of the ischium bone in the pelvis — can resemble a hamstring strain, with a similar bruising pattern.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: A hamstring tear — when the hamstring detaches from the ischial tuberosity, or "sit bone," part of the ischium bone in the pelvis — can resemble a hamstring strain, with a similar bruising pattern. But unlike a strain, a tear can be a time-sensitive injury that may benefit from surgical reattachment. If you injure your hamstring and the pain is closer to your ischium (the bottom of your pelvis) you may need to be evaluated for a tear of the hamstring tendons off of the ischial tuberosity.

text: # Thoracic Outlet Syndrome ## Overview Thoracic outlet syndrome represents a term used for several rare and different conditions that can occur when nerves and/or blood vessels in the thoracic outlet are compressed (squeezed) or irritated. The thoracic outlet is the anatomical space between the collarbone and first rib. When shoulder and chest muscles lack adequate strength to stabilize the collarbone, it may slip downward and forward, compressing underlying nerves and blood vessels. ## Cause Thoracic outlet syndrome develops from: - Injury - Disease - Congenital abnormalities (such as an abnormal first rib) The condition occurs more frequently in women than men. Poor posture and excess weight can exacerbate symptoms. Psychological changes often accompany this syndrome, though causation remains unclear. ## Symptoms Symptom presentation depends on which nerves or blood vessels experience compression. Nerve compression symptoms are more prevalent and easier to diagnose than vascular compression. **Nerve Pressure Effects:**

text: Physicians will: - Review symptom history thoroughly - Conduct comprehensive physical examination - Attempt reproducing symptoms through positional examination ### Diagnostic Tests **Elevated Arm Stress Test:** Patients raise arms overhead and open/close fists for approximately three minutes. Symptom reproduction suggests thoracic outlet syndrome, though false positives occur. **Imaging Tests:** - X-rays - Computed tomography (CT) scans - Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans - Ultrasound **Additional Testing:** Physicians may order blood circulation tests and nerve conduction tests to confirm diagnosis, ruling out similar conditions like cervical nerve compression. Many institutions employ multidisciplinary teams including orthopaedic surgeons, physiatrists, physical therapists, peripheral nerve surgeons, and vascular surgeons. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment **Physical Therapy:** Exercises strengthen shoulder muscles supporting the collarbone. Postural exercises reduce nerve and vessel pressure by improving posture alignment. **Weight Loss:** Overweight individuals should consider weight loss programs, as excess weight stresses supportive shoulder musculature.

text: # Sprained Thumb ## Overview A sprained thumb occurs when the ligaments supporting the thumb stretch beyond their limits, typically from a strong force bending the thumb backward away from the palm. The most common cause is falling onto an outstretched hand. Most thumb sprains involve the ulnar collateral ligament (UCL), located on the inside of the joint where the thumb meets the palm. An injury to this ligament can be painful and may make the thumb feel loose or unstable, potentially weakening the ability to pinch or grasp objects between the thumb and index finger. Treatment usually involves wearing a splint or cast to keep the thumb immobilized while the ligament heals. For more severe sprains or ligament tears, surgery may be needed to restore joint stability. ## Description Ligaments are strong, fibrous tissues that typically connect bones to other bones. The ligaments in the thumb help keep the bones in proper position while allowing for joint motion. **Sprain Types:**

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Description Ligaments are strong, fibrous tissues that typically connect bones to other bones. The ligaments in the thumb help keep the bones in proper position while allowing for joint motion. **Sprain Types:** - Sprains occur when ligaments stretch beyond their limit, potentially causing small, incomplete tears in the fibers. The ligament remains intact. These are known as partial-thickness tears. - Ligaments can also be torn completely — either in the middle of the ligament or at the end(s), where it can pull off the bone(s). These are known as full-thickness tears. ### Grades of Thumb Sprains Sprains are graded based on the degree of ligament injury: - **Grade 1 sprain (mild).** The ligament is stretched, but not torn. - **Grade 2 sprain (moderate).** The ligament is partially torn. This type of injury may involve some loss of function.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Grade 2 sprain (moderate).** The ligament is partially torn. This type of injury may involve some loss of function. - **Grade 3 sprain (severe).** The ligament is completely torn in the middle or is pulled off its attachment to the bone. These are significant injuries that require medical or surgical care. If the ligament tears away from the bone, it may take a small chip of the bone with it. This is called an avulsion fracture. ### Injury to the Ulnar Collateral Ligament of the Thumb The ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) of the thumb is a strong band of tissue running along the inside of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, which is where the thumb meets the palm. This ligament keeps the thumb stable, especially when pinching and grasping things.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: This ligament keeps the thumb stable, especially when pinching and grasping things. A thumb UCL injury is commonly called "skier's thumb," because falling on the ski slopes with the hand strapped to a ski pole is a common cause of this injury. The ligament can also be injured more gradually, over time, from repetitive grasping or twisting activities. This type of chronic injury is known as "gamekeeper's thumb" because originally, it was most commonly a work-related injury seen among Scottish gamekeepers (workers who manage wildlife and areas of land used for hunting). The ulnar collateral ligament can tear in different ways. For example, it may be: - Pulled off its attachment at the base of the first bone (the proximal phalanx) in the thumb - Pulled off the metacarpal bone, where it originates - Torn through its middle, though this is less common ## Cause

text: - Pulled off the metacarpal bone, where it originates - Torn through its middle, though this is less common ## Cause Any strong force that bends the thumb backward and away from the palm of the hand can stretch or tear the ulnar collateral ligament. This most often occurs by falling onto an outstretched hand. Sprained thumbs are also common in skiers and in athletes who participate in sports that involve catching and throwing a ball, such as football, baseball, softball, and basketball. ## Symptoms - Depending on the severity of the sprain, pain may or may not occur at the time of the injury. - Bruising, tenderness, and swelling around the base of the thumb, near the palm, may develop. - If the ulnar collateral ligament is completely torn, the end of the ruptured ligament may cause a lump or swelling on the inside of the thumb.

The thumb joint may also feel loose or unstable, with difficulty grasping items between the thumb and index finger. It is important for a doctor to evaluate even a mild thumb sprain if it does not improve quickly. Proper and prompt diagnosis and treatment of a thumb injury is necessary to avoid long-term complications, including chronic pain, instability, and arthritis. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination The doctor will: - Ask how and when the injury occurred - Ask the patient to describe symptoms - Carefully examine the thumb and hand. To help determine whether the ulnar collateral ligament is partially or completely torn, the doctor will move the thumb in different positions to test the stability of the MCP joint. If the joint is loose and unstable, it is an indication that the ligament may be completely torn. ### Imaging Tests

A special type of X-ray, called a stress X-ray, may also be ordered. During this test, the doctor applies tension to the thumb while it is being X-rayed to learn more about the stability of the MCP joint. **Other imaging tests.** If more information is needed, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan or an ultrasound may be ordered. text: These tests can help determine the severity of the injury and inform decisions about treatment and return to activity. ## Treatment Treatment for a sprained thumb depends on the severity of the injury. ### Home Care Mild thumb sprains will usually improve with home treatment that includes the RICE protocol: - **Rest.** Try not to use the hand for at least 48 hours. - **Ice.** Apply ice immediately after the injury to keep the swelling down. Use cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly on the skin. - **Compression.** Wear an elastic compression bandage to reduce swelling. Do not make the bandage too tight, as this could cut off blood flow to the thumb. - **Elevation.** As often as possible, rest with the hand raised up higher than the heart. If, however, pain and swelling continue for more than 48 hours, see a doctor. ### Nonsurgical Treatment For a moderate sprain, the doctor will probably immobilize the thumb joint with a bandage, thumb spica cast, or splint until it heals. To ease pain and swelling, a cold pack can be applied to the thumb twice a day for 2 to 3 days after the injury. Do not apply ice directly on the skin. Depending on the severity of the injury, the splint or cast may need to be worn at all times. After surgery, a short arm cast or a splint may need to be worn for 6 to 12 weeks to protect the thumb ligament while it heals. ## Outcomes When diagnosed and treated properly, most thumb sprains will heal well with no complications. text: # Trigger Finger ## Description Trigger finger, also called stenosing tenosynovitis, is a condition affecting the tendons in the fingers or thumbs that prevents them from bending normally. It causes a sensation of catching, locking, or "triggering" of the finger or thumb when trying to bend or straighten it, along with pain and stiffness. It affects approximately 2% of the general population, most commonly the ring finger and thumb, though any finger may be involved. When it affects the thumb it is called "trigger thumb." ## Anatomy The flexor tendons are cord-like structures connecting the forearm muscles to the finger and thumb bones. When bending the fingers, these tendons on the palm side pull the fingers into a fist. Each tendon passes through tunnel-like structures called pulleys that keep the tendon close to the bone, similar to guides on a fishing rod.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: When bending the fingers, these tendons on the palm side pull the fingers into a fist. Each tendon passes through tunnel-like structures called pulleys that keep the tendon close to the bone, similar to guides on a fishing rod. The A1 pulley, located in the palm at the base of each finger, is the pulley most involved in trigger finger. The tendon sheath attaches to the finger and thumb bones, keeping the flexor tendon in place during movement. ## What Happens Trigger finger involves a size mismatch between the finger tendons and the A1 pulley. The tendon may thicken or develop a bump, and the A1 pulley may also thicken and narrow, leaving less room for the tendon to pass through.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: The tendon may thicken or develop a bump, and the A1 pulley may also thicken and narrow, leaving less room for the tendon to pass through. This prevents the tendon from gliding smoothly, causing catching or locking, often painfully — a thickened nodule on the flexor tendon pops through the A1 pulley during deep finger flexion and then catches against the pulley on attempted extension, making straightening difficult and painful. In some cases the finger locks and remains bent, sometimes requiring manual straightening with the other hand, or in worst cases professional medical help. ## Cause Most cases have no identifiable cause, with symptoms often beginning without any change in activity. It is more common in: - Women between the ages of 40 and 60 (rare in children, though congenital trigger thumb can cause a child's thumb to lock in flexion) - People with medical conditions including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and amyloidosis

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - People with medical conditions including diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and amyloidosis - People who do repetitive gripping or pinching activities for work or recreation - People with certain differences in tendon structure ## Symptoms Symptoms typically start slowly and get worse over time, and may include: - A tender lump at the base of the finger or thumb on the palm side - A catching, popping, or locking sensation with movement - Pain below the finger when bending or straightening, which may travel up the finger or down into the palm - The finger getting stuck in a bent position Stiffness and locking tend to be worse after periods of inactivity, such as first thing in the morning, and symptoms may improve throughout the day with gentle, consistent hand use. ## Diagnosis Doctors typically diagnose trigger finger through discussion of symptoms and a hand examination; X-rays or other tests are usually unnecessary.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## Diagnosis Doctors typically diagnose trigger finger through discussion of symptoms and a hand examination; X-rays or other tests are usually unnecessary. The exam checks the affected digit for tenderness over the flexor tendon sheath in the palm, thickening or swelling of the tendon sheath at the base of the finger or thumb, and a clicking or catching sensation with bending and straightening. ## Treatment ### Nonsurgical Treatment The goal is to reduce pain and help the tendon glide more freely. Most cases respond well to nonsurgical treatment. - **Activity modification**: Resting the hand and avoiding repetitive gripping or pinching. - **Splinting**: A night splint keeping the affected finger or thumb straight during sleep. - **Exercises**: Gentle stretching to decrease stiffness and improve range of motion. ### Surgical Treatment Surgery may be needed if symptoms are severe or don't improve with other treatments, or if the finger is stuck in a bent position and cannot be straightened.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Surgical Treatment Surgery may be needed if symptoms are severe or don't improve with other treatments, or if the finger is stuck in a bent position and cannot be straightened. - **Trigger finger release**: An outpatient procedure done the same day under local numbing (with the patient awake or lightly sedated). The doctor makes a small cut in the palm, or uses a needle tip, to open the A1 pulley and give the tendon more room to move. Opening the A1 pulley does not harm hand function since the other pulleys remain intact. Occasionally part of the tendon is removed if opening the pulley alone doesn't resolve triggering, more common in patients with longstanding symptoms. - **Complications**: Rare, but may include infection, stiffness, or return of symptoms; some pain and swelling after surgery is normal and should improve. - **Recovery**: Most patients begin moving the finger immediately after surgery. Keeping the hand raised above the heart helps reduce pain and swelling.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Recovery**: Most patients begin moving the finger immediately after surgery. Keeping the hand raised above the heart helps reduce pain and swelling. The incision usually heals within weeks, though swelling and stiffness may take 4 to 6 months to fully resolve, with full recovery averaging about 6 months. Hand therapy may be recommended if stiffness, swelling, or pain persist. ## Outcomes Most people with trigger finger improve with appropriate treatment, whether nonsurgical or surgical. Early intervention and following the treatment plan are key to successful recovery.

text: # Turf Toe ## Overview Turf toe is a sprain of the main joint of the big toe. It occurs when the toe is forced upward into extreme extension, typically when an athlete pushes off forcefully while the toe stays planted flat on the ground and the rest of the foot continues moving. While the condition gained its name from American football, it can develop across many sports and recreational activities. ## Anatomy The big toe has two joints, and the metatarsophalangeal joint (MTP) is the larger one. It forms where the first long bone of the forefoot (the metatarsal) connects with the first toe bone (the phalanx). In turf toe, this joint is the one that gets injured. Several important structures surround the MTP joint and work together to keep it stable. Collectively, these structures are known as the plantar plate complex:

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: In turf toe, this joint is the one that gets injured. Several important structures surround the MTP joint and work together to keep it stable. Collectively, these structures are known as the plantar plate complex: - **Plantar plate.** A thick fibrous layer beneath the MTP joint that limits how far the big toe can bend upward. - **Collateral ligaments.** Positioned on each side of the big toe, these connect the phalanx to the metatarsal and prevent the toe from moving side to side. - **Flexor hallucis brevis.** A muscle that passes under the first metatarsal and attaches to the base of the phalanx, providing stability and power during push-off. - **Sesamoids.** Two small bones embedded within the flexor hallucis structure that allow smoother movement while helping stabilize the MTP joint by distributing weight in the forefoot. ## Description

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Sesamoids.** Two small bones embedded within the flexor hallucis structure that allow smoother movement while helping stabilize the MTP joint by distributing weight in the forefoot. ## Description Turf toe involves damage to any part of the plantar plate complex, including the plantar plate itself and the collateral ligaments. Severity ranges from a simple stretching injury through a partial tear to complete disruption of the MTP joint. Doctors classify these injuries into three grades: - **Grade 1 (mild).** The plantar complex is stretched, causing focused tenderness at one point and little swelling. - **Grade 2 (moderate).** Partial tearing of the plantar complex causes a broader area of tenderness, moderate swelling, bruising, and restricted, painful toe movement. - **Grade 3 (severe).** Complete tearing of the plantar complex causes intense tenderness, significant swelling and bruising, and considerable difficulty and pain moving the big toe.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **Grade 3 (severe).** Complete tearing of the plantar complex causes intense tenderness, significant swelling and bruising, and considerable difficulty and pain moving the big toe. ## Cause Turf toe develops when the forefoot is fixed against the ground, the heel lifts, and a force drives the big toe into hyperextension. The injury became particularly common in American football once artificial playing surfaces became widespread, which gave the condition its name. Artificial turf is harder and absorbs less energy than natural grass, and it gives less under applied force. In addition, football cleats designed for artificial surfaces tend to be less stiff and more flexible, giving athletes better agility but much less support for the forefoot. ## First Aid Treatment The RICE approach is useful for most acute sports injuries: - **Rest.** Stop the activity that caused the injury and avoid walking or putting weight on the affected foot.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ## First Aid Treatment The RICE approach is useful for most acute sports injuries: - **Rest.** Stop the activity that caused the injury and avoid walking or putting weight on the affected foot. - **Ice.** Apply cold therapy in 20-minute intervals several times a day, avoiding direct skin contact. - **Compression.** Use an elastic wrap to help limit further swelling. - **Elevation.** Keep the leg raised above heart level while resting to reduce swelling. Depending on the severity, prompt medical evaluation is advisable, or recommended if symptoms continue. Documenting exactly how the injury happened beforehand helps your doctor with diagnosis and treatment planning. ## Doctor Examination ### Medical History and Physical Examination The doctor will ask about your overall health, your toe symptoms, and exactly how the injury occurred. During the physical exam, the doctor evaluates swelling, bruising, and how freely the MTP joint moves.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: ### Medical History and Physical Examination The doctor will ask about your overall health, your toe symptoms, and exactly how the injury occurred. During the physical exam, the doctor evaluates swelling, bruising, and how freely the MTP joint moves. The toe will be flexed upward, moved side to side and up and down, and checked for instability that might indicate a plantar complex tear. Testing the uninjured toe provides comparison. Range-of-motion testing can be uncomfortable. ### Imaging Tests Confirming the diagnosis may include: - **X-rays.** These show the bony anatomy well. Although the plantar complex is made of soft tissue, X-rays help rule out other injuries, including small fractures where the plantar complex attaches to bone and abnormal sesamoid positioning. - **MRI.** MRI gives a much better picture of soft tissue than X-rays and can show damage to soft tissue and cartilage.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: - **MRI.** MRI gives a much better picture of soft tissue than X-rays and can show damage to soft tissue and cartilage. It is particularly useful for Grade 2 and 3 injuries or when X-ray findings are abnormal. ## Nonsurgical Treatment Most turf toe injuries heal without surgery. Nonsurgical management depends on the grade of injury: **Grade 1.** RICE — rest, ice, compression, and elevation — is the primary treatment. Taping the big toe to the neighboring toes limits movement. Athletes often tolerate acceptable pain levels and continue participating in sports using stiff-soled shoes. Custom inserts with rigid forefoot support reduce tension on the plantar plate and improve stability. **Grade 2.** Doctors may recommend a protective walking boot for about seven days to immobilize the MTP joint. After this period, treatment shifts to taping combined with Grade 1 interventions. Most athletes need somewhere between three and fourteen days away from competition before returning.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: After this period, treatment shifts to taping combined with Grade 1 interventions. Most athletes need somewhere between three and fourteen days away from competition before returning. **Grade 3.** Severe injuries usually require a longer period of immobilization. Athletes may use protective footwear or a cast that holds the big toe in slight downward flexion. As recovery progresses, management gradually shifts to Grade 2, then Grade 1, strategies. Rehabilitation may start as tolerated and includes exercises for flexibility and strength of the big toe. Starting movement early is important for preventing or minimizing permanent stiffness. ## Surgical Treatment Surgery is not necessary for many turf toe injuries. However, ongoing symptoms or compromised athletic performance may require it. Doctors typically recommend surgery for significant Grade 3 injuries involving: - Extensive tearing of the plantar complex - A fracture of a sesamoid bone - Up-and-down instability of the MTP joint - Displaced bone fragments within the joint

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: Doctors typically recommend surgery for significant Grade 3 injuries involving: - Extensive tearing of the plantar complex - A fracture of a sesamoid bone - Up-and-down instability of the MTP joint - Displaced bone fragments within the joint - Damage to the joint's cartilage surface - Developing or worsening hallux valgus (the big toe angling toward the other toes) The specific surgical approach varies based on the details of the injury. The goal of surgery is to restore soft tissue integrity and recover the MTP joint motion needed to preserve normal foot function. ## Long-Term Outcomes Early management of turf toe injuries typically produces a good recovery. Persistent mild-to-moderate symptoms — particularly pain and restricted movement — are the most common lasting effect. Other possible lasting complications include reduced push-off strength, decreased mobility, a developing bunion, and an upward curl of the big toe.

text: # Ulnar Tunnel Syndrome of the Wrist ## Overview The ulnar nerve is one of three primary nerves supplying sensation and function to the hand, originating from the spinal cord and traveling from the neck through the arm into the hand. Ulnar tunnel syndrome occurs when the ulnar nerve is compressed at the wrist. This compression reduces blood flow to the nerve and impairs its function. When compressed at the wrist, the condition causes numbness and tingling in the little finger (pinky) and the outside of the ring finger, along with weakness in hand pinch and grip strength. ## Cause The most common cause involves soft tissue tumors pressing on the nerve. The tumor is typically a benign (noncancerous) cyst called a ganglion which originates from the wrist joint. Ganglion cysts contain thick gel and vary in size.

text: # Whiplash Whiplash is a neck injury caused by sudden movement of the head. It usually gets better within 2 to 3 months. It's most often caused by road traffic accidents or falls, and symptoms can take several hours to appear after the injury. ## Symptoms - neck pain and stiffness, with limited movement of the head - headaches - pain and muscle spasms in the shoulders and arms ## Self-care **Do:** - try to carry on with your normal activities as this can help you recover more quickly **Don't:** - do not wear a neck brace or collar - these are not recommended - do not keep your neck still for long periods ## When to get help urgently Contact NHS 111 or get an urgent GP appointment if you have: - severe pain that isn't helped by painkillers - tingling or pins and needles - difficulty walking or standing normally - an electric shock feeling in your neck and back that spreads to your arms or legs

text: - severe pain that isn't helped by painkillers - tingling or pins and needles - difficulty walking or standing normally - an electric shock feeling in your neck and back that spreads to your arms or legs - weakness in your arms or legs These symptoms can be a sign of nerve damage. ## Treatment If symptoms haven't improved after a few weeks, you may be referred for physiotherapy, to see a pain specialist, or for psychological support. Physiotherapy is available both on the NHS and privately.

text: # Wrist Sprains ## Overview Wrist sprains are common injuries that occur when the wrist is bent or twisted forcefully. When this happens, the strong ligaments that support the wrist can stretch beyond their limits or tear. Wrist sprains are typically caused by a traumatic event, such as a fall onto an outstretched hand. They can range from mild to severe, depending on how much damage there is to the ligaments. ## Description Ligaments are strong, fibrous tissues that connect bones to other bones. The ligaments in the wrist help to keep the bones of the wrist in proper position and stabilize the joint. The wrist joint is made up of the radius, the ulna, and eight smaller carpal bones. This complex system relies heavily on ligaments for stability. Thus, injuries to these ligaments can result in pain and dysfunction of the wrist.

text: The wrist joint is made up of the radius, the ulna, and eight smaller carpal bones. This complex system relies heavily on ligaments for stability. Thus, injuries to these ligaments can result in pain and dysfunction of the wrist. Sprains can range from a stretch or tiny tear in the fibers that make up the ligament to a complete tear through the ligament or through its attachment to the bone. Typically, higher grade/worse injuries require more advanced treatment and more time to recover. ### Grades of Wrist Sprains Sprains are graded based on the degree of injury to the ligaments: - **Grade 1 sprain (mild).** The ligaments are stretched but not torn. - **Grade 2 sprain (moderate).** The ligaments are partially torn. This type of injury may involve some loss of function.

text: - **Grade 2 sprain (moderate).** The ligaments are partially torn. This type of injury may involve some loss of function. - **Grade 3 sprain (severe).** The ligament is completely torn, or the ligament is pulled off of its attachment to bone. These are significant injuries that may require more advanced medical or surgical care. If the ligament tears away from the bone, it may take a small chip of bone with it. This is called an avulsion fracture. ## Cause A variety of traumatic events can cause a wrist sprain. They are most often caused by a fall onto an outstretched hand. This might happen during everyday activities, but it most frequently occurs during sports and outdoor recreational activities. ## Symptoms A sprained wrist is typically painful. Other symptoms may include: - Swelling - Bruising - Tenderness to touch - A feeling of popping or tearing inside the wrist - A feeling of warmth around the wrist

text: ## Symptoms A sprained wrist is typically painful. Other symptoms may include: - Swelling - Bruising - Tenderness to touch - A feeling of popping or tearing inside the wrist - A feeling of warmth around the wrist Even a wrist injury that seems mild with minimal swelling could still involve a torn ligament and may even require surgery to avoid long-term problems. Similarly, an unrecognized (occult) fracture can be mistaken for a mild or moderate sprain. If left untreated, the fracture may not heal properly, and a surgical procedure that might have been avoided with early, appropriate treatment could become necessary. The most common example of this is an occult fracture of the scaphoid, one of the small bones in the wrist. Thus, it is important for a doctor to evaluate even a mild wrist injury if it does not improve quickly. This is especially important if the injury causes persistent wrist pain (pain that does not go away).

Proper diagnosis and treatment of wrist injuries is necessary to avoid long-term problems, including chronic pain, stiffness, and arthritis. ## Doctor Examination ### Physical Examination After discussing medical history and general health, the doctor will: - Likely ask about any previous injuries to the hand or wrist. - Ask how and when the current injury occurred. - Ask the patient to describe symptoms, including whether there is any numbness in the hand or pain in any other locations. - Carefully examine the wrist to see where it hurts and to check how it moves. Tenderness in certain areas may also be consistent with a broken bone or torn ligament. - Possibly examine the entire hand and arm to make sure there are no other injuries. ### Imaging Tests

An X-ray can also help identify a broken bone in the wrist. **Other imaging tests.** If more information is needed, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan, computerized tomography (CT) scan, or arthrogram may be ordered. In an arthrogram, a special dye is injected into the wrist joint. This makes the joint and ligaments show up more clearly on an imaging study. ## Treatment Treatment for a wrist sprain depends on the severity of the injury. ### Home Care

text: This makes the joint and ligaments show up more clearly on an imaging study. ## Treatment Treatment for a wrist sprain depends on the severity of the injury. ### Home Care Mild wrist sprains will usually improve with home treatment that includes the RICE protocol: - **Rest.** Avoid strenuous activities that aggravate the strain. - **Ice.** Apply ice immediately after the injury to keep the swelling down. Use cold packs for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly on the skin; use an ice pack or bag, or wrap the ice in a towel or cloth. - **Compression.** Wear an elastic compression bandage to reduce swelling. Do not apply the bandage too tightly, as this can be harmful. - **Elevation.** As often as possible, rest with the wrist raised up higher than the heart to reduce swelling.

text: Do not apply the bandage too tightly, as this can be harmful. - **Elevation.** As often as possible, rest with the wrist raised up higher than the heart to reduce swelling. However, if pain and swelling persist for more than 48 hours (2 full days), see a doctor. ### Nonsurgical Treatment Moderate sprains may need to be immobilized with a wrist splint. Because immobilization may cause some stiffness in the wrist, stretching exercises may be recommended to help regain full mobility. Formal therapy can be quite helpful when recovering from a significant wrist sprain. ### Surgical Treatment Severe sprains may require surgery to repair the fully torn ligament. Surgery involves reconnecting the ligament to the bone or using a tendon graft to reconstruct the injured ligament. After surgery, there will be a period of rehabilitation that includes immobilization, followed by exercises to strengthen the wrist and restore range of motion.

source_note: AAOS (American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons), OrthoInfo
text: After surgery, there will be a period of rehabilitation that includes immobilization, followed by exercises to strengthen the wrist and restore range of motion. Although the ligament usually heals in 8 to 12 weeks, it can take 6 to 12 months for a full recovery. The length of the recovery process and outcomes will depend on the severity of the sprain/tear. ## Outcomes The ultimate outcome of a wrist sprain is highly variable. - **Mild wrist sprains** often result in a full recovery over several weeks. - **Moderate sprains** may take longer to recover from and may require surgical intervention in those patients who do not recover well. - **Severe sprains/tears** may require surgery to achieve a reasonable outcome. - **In some patients with severe sprains/tears**, even surgery cannot fully restore wrist function. This depends on the type of tear, age of the patient, and timing from injury to surgery.

text: - **In some patients with severe sprains/tears**, even surgery cannot fully restore wrist function. This depends on the type of tear, age of the patient, and timing from injury to surgery. For this reason, it is important to seek care rapidly if a serious injury to the wrist is suspected. Some patients with severe sprains/tears who either do not seek treatment or do not have a successful outcome following treatment will develop arthritis of the wrist in the long term. This often will take several years to develop. If it does develop, further treatment may be necessary. ## Prevention Because wrist sprains usually result from a fall, care should be taken when: - Walking in wet or slippery conditions - Going up and down stairs or hills - Stepping down off of curbs - Walking on uneven or unstable surfaces (e.g., brick or cobblestone streets, grass, and pavement with a lot of cracks or missing pieces)

text: - Going up and down stairs or hills - Stepping down off of curbs - Walking on uneven or unstable surfaces (e.g., brick or cobblestone streets, grass, and pavement with a lot of cracks or missing pieces) - Walking a dog; never wrap the leash around the hand or wrist Wrist sprains also occur during sports, such as skating, skateboarding, and skiing. Wearing wrist guards or protective tape when participating in these activities will help support the wrist and can prevent it from bending too far backward in the event of a fall.
